abstract.para: One of the most effective and compelling ways to communicate is through a good story. This course introduces key elements of storytelling and illustrates ways to enhance messaging and better engage with audiences. Topics covered may include compositional structure, grammar, and storytelling strategies to address business and communication needs.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 1. This week, you will read the following topics:

listitem.para: : Storytelling—Clarity with Charm
: Sentences—The Raw Material of Writing

section.para: We’ll learn about what stories are made of, and then we’ll begin our study of good writing. Writing well is essential if we want to communicate our stories with power.

section.title: Stories

figure.title:
Your favorite movie.
Photo by Taryn Elliott via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Two people holding drinks while watching a movie.

section.para: Think about your favorite movie. What comes to mind? It might be an action film, a character study, or a romance. You might be imagining Luke Skywalker battling Darth Vader in Star Wars,Kershner, I. (Director). (1980, May 17). Star wars: The empire strikes back [Film]. Lucasfilm Ltd. Vito Corleone plotting against his rivals in The Godfather,Coppola, F. F. (Director). (1972, March 24). The godfather [Film]. Paramount Pictures; Alfran Productions. or Joe Fox promising to send Kathleen Kelly a bouquet of newly sharpened pencils in You’ve Got Mail.Ephron, N. (Director). (1998, December 18). You’ve got mail [Film]. Lauren Shuler Donner Productions.

You may have thought of countless other films as well. On the surface, many of them probably seem like they have little in common. The story of Corleone’s downfall, for example, doesn’t much resemble Kelly’s efforts to save her bookstore. The drama of The Princess BrideReiner, R. (Director). (1987, September 25). The princess bride [Film]. Act III Communications; Buttercup Films; The Princess Bride Ltd. doesn’t seem anything like the raw power of Chiron’s life in Moonlight.Jenkins, B. (Director). (2016, October 21). Moonlight [Film]. A24; Plan B Entertainment; Pastel Productions. But when we look a bit deeper—as we’ll learn to do in this course—we find that these movies and many others all have a compelling story.

section.title: Capturing Attention with Stories
section.para: Each of the movies mentioned earlier has a story that jumps off the screen, looks us in the eye, and demands that we pay attention. The characters and events capture our minds and transport us from the real world to a new one where anything could happen. A good story can make us happy, sad, or angry, and some can even move us to action or change the way we see the world.

This course is all about stories. Our goals will be to understand what stories are and, more importantly, to learn how to use this marvelous power of stories for ourselves. Stories aren’t just in movies or books, after all. We use stories to understand ourselves, interact with others, and make sense of our lives.

section.title: What Is a Story?

figure.title:
Telling stories.
Photo by Andrea Piacquadio via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A family sits on the floor reading a book.

section.para: So, what exactly is a story, anyway? Giving a definition of the word might actually make it more obscure because the definition may appear to exclude some things that we definitely think are stories. But for our course, we’ll understand a storyAny account of characters or events. as any account of characters or events. Our definition includes characters and what they do in not only movies, books, and plays but also news reports, professional journal articles, and even commercials. Many pieces of communication across many forms of media contain elements of a story, and we want our definition to capture them all. Stories aren’t just limited to books and movies or other media we commonly associate with them. In fact, the opposite is true—stories are everywhere. They’re in sports, politics, science, history, families, the lives of individuals, and in many other places as well.

section.title: Humans Can’t Help but Tell Stories
section.para: Stories are so widespread because they allow us to make sense of people and events so effortlessly. Stories string together events that may seem disconnected from each other. We connect them through the actions of characters and the meaning of these events in the lives of those characters.

In fact, we really can’t help but tell stories about many aspects of our lives, whether to ourselves or to others. We use stories to understand where we’ve been as people, why we’re here now, and where we intend to go. We use narrative arcs to connect otherwise disparate parts of our lives across time, knitting together a coherent picture of who we are and what we’re about. All these explanations that we tell ourselves are stories.

section.title: Understanding the World through Stories
section.para: We do the same for the lives of other people and their interactions with us. We might tell ourselves that our partner or our spouse was meant for us by analyzing the many seemingly improbable occurrences that led to our meeting. That tale is a story. On a larger scale, we might understand the rise of social movements in terms of stories as well when certain groups of people show us the importance of certain causes or ideas. We can use stories to explain what other people are doing and why.

figure.title:
Stories are everywhere.
Photo by Alexandr Podvalny via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Two women sit around a campfire talking.

section.para: In short, stories are everywhere, and humans can’t help but tell them. We have a natural inclination to understand chains of events as connected through their meaning for each other and for people. This inclination gives stories their power: we readily accept stories and are interested in them, even when we believe that they might be false. Effectively using stories, then, is a powerful tool for communication and a way to share messages that may not be able to be shared in any other way.

section.title: Stories Aren’t Necessarily True or False
section.para: Sometimes people use the term “story” in a derogatory way to imply that someone is just making up a report about what happened to them. “Some story,” we might say with skepticism when a friend tells us something that we find unbelievable.

But that’s not how we’ll use the term “story” in our course. For us, a story will just be any account of characters and events—without any prejudgment about whether or not that account is true. It could be true, or it could be false; parts of it could be true and other parts false. Judging the truth or falsity of stories is not a significant concern in this course.

This course is about understanding how stories work and how to present them in a compelling way. Whatever stories we’re presenting, whether about ourselves, our work, our relationships, our goals, or something else, the same storytelling principles will apply. Those principles function independently of whether our stories accurately depict the world.

section.title: Every Piece of Writing Tells a Story
section.para: We usually associate stories with novels and movies. Those works are specifically written to tell a story; that is, the story is the reason they exist. While they may be communicating many other things along the way, the story is the focus, and every part of the work contributes in some way to that story.

section.title: Looking for a Story

title.para: Photo by Nikhil Prasad via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A small home build inside a hill with a circle door.

section.para: So, when we read the first line in the Lord of the RingsTolkien, J. R. R. (1954–1955). The lord of the rings [Book series]. Allen & Unwin. series of novels, “When Mr. Bilbo Baggins of Bag End announced that he would shortly be celebrating his eleventy-first birthday with a party of special magnificence, there was much talk and excitement in Hobbiton,”Tolkien, J. R. R. The fellowship of the ring. (1954, July 29). The Lord of the Rings: The fellowship of the ring. George Allen & Unwin, 1. we know we’re looking for a story.

And right away, we’ve found one! We’ve got a character with an unusual name, Bilbo Baggins. He’s celebrating his “eleventy-first birthday,” whatever that is, with a “party of special magnificence.” Everyone in Hobbiton is excited, and as readers, we are too. We’re there for the story, and the first sentence serves it up for us. Telling a story about good characters, evil characters, and their choices was Tolkien’s goal in writing those novels. Each part of the book series adds to that goal.

But if stories really are everywhere, then we need to learn to look beyond the familiar homes of stories to places where we might not normally expect them. In this course, we’ll try to make the case that every piece of writing—at least, every compelling piece of writing—tells a story. That’s as true for a fantasy novel as it is for an article in a scientific journal, as we’ll see shortly.

section.title: Every Communication Is a Story
section.para: Even more broadly, we’ll try to show that every compelling piece of communication, from a book to a movie to a press release to a news report, features elements of a story. Characters, conflicts, hooks, and stakes are parts of stories that feature in many human interactions, whether we mean for those interactions to be about a story or not. We can learn to use those story elements to make our communications compelling.
But how is that possible? How can writing or other communications use storytelling techniques when their authors aren’t really trying to tell a story?

section.title: Stories Frame Information
section.para: The answer is that stories can be the frame to communicate other pieces of information. The frame for a piece of communication is how it is presented or pitched to the audience. We can think of the frame as the packaging we use to deliver our messages. Aspects of the frame include a message’s tone, how technical it is, whether we use humor as we present it, and so on.

Other aspects of the frame include elements of storytelling. We can present any message, for example, by setting up a conflict that our message is intended to resolve, and this is true regardless of what our message actually says. We can use other parts of stories, like characters or stakes, to do the same thing.

section.title: Framing Science with a Story: DNA

figure.title:
DNA.
Pop Nukoonrat © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A scientist in the background of a DNA helix.

section.para: Let’s take a look at an example. In the 1940s and early 1950s, scientists were struggling to understand the structure of important molecules inside cells. Deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, had been discovered in the nineteenth century, but its exact shape was still unknown. The shape of molecules, like DNA, determines some of their functions and interactions with other cells, so it was important for scientists to know more about DNA’s shape.

Then, in a landmark proposal in 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick suggested that DNA formed a double helix, or two spirals wrapping around themselves. This suggestion gave an elegant, unifying explanation for what was then known about DNA. Watson and Crick published their results in the scientific journal Nature.
Let’s take a look at the opening lines of that paper:

blockquote.emphasis: We wish to suggest a structure for the salt of deoxyribose nucleic acid (D.N.A.). This structure has novel features which are of considerable biological interest.

A structure for nucleic acid has already been proposed by Pauling and Corey. They kindly made their manuscript available to us in advance of publication. Their model consists of three intertwined chains, with the phosphates near the fibre axis, and the bases on the outside. In our opinion, this structure is unsatisfactory for two reasons: (1) We believe that the material which gives the X-ray diagrams is the salt, not the free acid. Without the acidic hydrogen atoms it is not clear what forces would hold the structure together, especially as the negatively charged phosphates near the axis will repel each other. (2) Some of the van der Waals distances appear to be too small.
blockquote.footnote: Watson, J. D., & Crick, F. H. (1953). Molecular structure of nucleic acids: A structure for deoxyribose nucleic acid. Nature, 171(4356), 737–738.

section.para: Now, unless you’ve recently had a course in biochemistry, some of this will be incomprehensible. But you don’t need to know what phosphates or van der Waals distances are to spot the elements of a story. The first sentence tells us the purpose of the authors’ communication, and the second sentence sets up the stakes: they’re high because DNA is so fundamental to life. The second sentence also gives a potential payoff, or reward. If the story Watson and Crick are telling is true, that payoff will be real.

The next sentences introduce two new characters, Pauling and Corey. These two researchers have proposed an alternative model for the structure of DNA. With other characters and different points of view comes conflict, and the conflict escalates as Watson and Crick immediately set forth the reasons why they think the alternative model is wrong.

So just in the first few lines of this milestone scientific paper, we see several elements of a story: characters, stakes, a payoff, and conflict. The stage has been set for Watson and Crick to share the technical details of their proposal and deliver on the promise they offer in the opening line. Those details may be inaccessible to us, but we can easily recognize and understand how storytelling is used to make the article a compelling piece of writing.

Whether we’re communicating scientific discoveries, history, or a short story about aliens, the term “story” helps us remember that we are presenting an account of characters and events to an audience. The idea of a story focuses on the fact that we are sharing messages with particular people, and since those people are disposed to understand things in terms of stories, we can use storytelling techniques to our advantage. Those techniques will benefit us no matter what messages we are sharing or what we ultimately want our audiences to receive.

section.title: Creating Stories
section.para: We tell stories for their own sake, and we also use them to communicate other kinds of messages. We want those messages to be as clear as possible to make sure that others can understand us and what we hope to accomplish. We also want to present those messages in the most engaging way possible to interest the audience and keep their attention. Putting these two desires together, we can say that good storytelling combines clarity and charm: clarity makes our messages understood, and charm captivates our audience.

section.title: Writing Stories

figure.title:
Creating our own stories.
Photo by Pixabay via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man lying in the grass writing in a notebook.

section.para: As we learn about stories and how to use them, we’ll want to create many of our own stories to communicate with others and share our points of view. This means that we’ll write many of our stories down—we’ll create them by drafting a few sentences, a paragraph, or something much longer.

Our focus in writing stories will need to be on writing itself, at least at first. Of course, there are other ways of creating and telling stories, like a dance or a musical composition. But the stories we will discover and practice within this class involve words. Learning some principles and strategies for effective writing will prepare us to create our messages with real clarity and authentic charm.

section.title: The Nuts and Bolts of Writing

figure.title:
Nuts and bolts of writing.
Photo by cottonbro via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man and woman sit at a table surrounded by books.

section.para: Effective writing requires a basic understanding of English composition, as well as a sense of how readers read our stories. The words we choose and the way we arrange them are almost everything we have in crafting compelling stories, so we need to learn to use these tools correctly.

Choices about writing take place at different levels. At smaller levels, we decide which words we will use and how we will arrange them in relation to other words. From there, we design sentences that convey more complete ideas. We string sentences together to form paragraphs, whole units that offer a substantial amount of information about something. Larger pieces of writing, like news articles, books, or scripts, are composed of paragraphs and maybe other units as well, like sections, chapters, or acts.

In this course, we will look at the decisions we make at all these levels to see how those decisions influence the precision and appeal of our stories. We will study tools that help us control our narratives at each level so that each part makes a clear and unique contribution to the story as a whole.
Let’s look at some examples of how decisions at different levels can affect the stories we tell.

section.title: Sentences
section.para: A sentenceA basic unit of discourse that conveys a complete idea, consisting of a subject and predicate. is a basic unit of discourse that conveys a complete idea. Fundamentally, a sentence is composed of a subject (the “character” of the sentence) and a predicate (the “event” of the sentence). Most sentences affirm or deny that the predicate is true of the subject.
Consider the following sentence:

blockquote.emphasis: They watched me.

section.para: In this sentence, the pronoun “they” is the subject of the sentence, and everything else—“watched me”—is the predicate. According to this sentence, the predicate “watched me” is true of whoever “they” are. The predicate “watched me” would be false if whoever “they” are wasn’t watching me or if the sentence was stating something false.
We’ll get a bit more background in these concepts later on, but for now, let’s see how decisions about constructing sentences can make a difference in how we tell a story.

section.title: Active and Passive Voice

figure.title:
Voice.
Photo by Pressmaster via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man holds a megaphone to his mouth.

section.para: The sentence above is in active voiceA feature of a sentence in which the subject of the verb performs the action in the predicate. , which means that the subject of the sentence is doing the action spoken of in the predicate. In contrast to the active voice is passive voiceA feature of a sentence in which the subject receives the action of the predicate. , or when the subject is receiving the action (done by someone or something else) named in the predicate. In this example, the corresponding sentence in the passive voice would be “I was being watched by them.” Here, the object of the original sentence, “me,” becomes the subject, and the predicate now states that the subject receives the action, or that the action is done to it. In the passive voice, we mark the agentIn grammar, the entity which performs the action in a passive-voice sentence. of the action, or whatever’s doing it, with “by.”

Sentences in the active voice are usually shorter and more direct than passive voice sentences. Active voice sentences also closely connect the subject to the action of the predicate, which can make them a bit easier to understand. In general, sentences in the active voice are just more active themselves, suggesting a sense of motion and activity that passive voice sentences lack.

section.title: Voice Tells a Story
section.para: Later in our course, we will learn that most writing is better with active-voice sentences. But this isn’t always the case, and, in fact, the decisions we make about active and passive voice influence how we tell the stories we want to share. Imagine, for example, that the following sentence was the very first line in a book:

blockquote.emphasis: They watched me.

section.para: What comes to your mind when you read it? Maybe it’s a story about a child whose parents have come out to watch her play soccer. Maybe it’s about a figure skater hoping to impress the judges. Whatever it is, the emphasis is on the subject.
Now imagine that we begin a story with the same line, but this time in passive voice:

blockquote.emphasis: I was being watched by them.

section.para: Sounds ominous! For even more effect, we can cut out “by them” and leave the rest:

blockquote.emphasis: I was being watched.

section.para: Now we’re talking! Since we don’t know yet whether the person being watched knows who she’s being watched by, we’re left wondering what could be going on. Are there cameras in her home? Is someone tailing her car? We can add two more sentences to increase the suspense:

blockquote.emphasis: I was being watched. I didn’t know who it was or why they were doing it, but I was sure of it. I was being watched.

section.para: All of a sudden, we’ve got the beginnings of a story. Notice how the sentence-level decision of active versus passive voice impacts how our story unfolds.

section.title: Paragraphs

figure.title:
Paragraphs.
Photo by Mehmet Ali Turan via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Piles of open books with a mug of coffee in the middle.

section.para: A paragraphA logical collection of sentences organized around some theme. is a collection of sentences that usually form part of a larger work, like a section, chapter, or book. This textbook contains many short paragraphs; longer paragraphs are common in more professional settings.

Later, we will learn some useful guidelines for constructing effective paragraphs. It isn’t just about throwing sentences together, skipping a line, and calling our creation a paragraph. Paragraphs have a logic of their own, and clear paragraphs will allow readers to digest them easily. The logic of paragraphs gives us the guidelines for building good ones.

In fact, the previous paragraph attempts to follow some of those guidelines explicitly. Many effective paragraphs begin with a sentence that sets the theme for the paragraph, and the sentences that follow it develop that theme or provide evidence for it. The final sentence then connects all of those middle sentences back to the theme as a kind of summary. Each paragraph tries to follow a similar pattern.

Different kinds of writing have different rules for paragraphs. In a novel, for example, it’s common to start a new paragraph not only when the story changes focus but also when one character stops speaking and another begins. We should know and follow the conventions governing the story we’re telling, and we’ll learn a few of them in this course.

section.title: Grammar
section.para: The rules we use to arrange words and sentences make up the grammarThe set of rules and conventions for forming words and sentences in a language. of English. A story that makes lots of grammatical mistakes is not easy to understand. On the other hand, clear, grammatically correct prose allows our story ideas to shine through the text unimpeded.

The focus of this course is on storytelling; it isn’t an English class. This means our study of grammar will focus on common mistakes and how to decide for ourselves the best way to construct phrases and sentences.

section.title: Word Choice
section.para: We make decisions about sentences, paragraphs, and grammar based on principles of good writing and the English language. In some cases, as with sentences, those principles allow a lot of flexibility to accommodate an author’s style and goals; in others, as with grammar, the rules are more rigid.

figure.title:
Words.
Photo by Pixabay via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A pile of scrabble letters.

section.para: Decisions about word choiceThe decision of which word to include in some part of a piece of writing, and for what purpose. give us another area in which we can play with style and set the tone for an interesting story. Consider the following two examples, built off the sentence we mentioned earlier:

blockquote.emphasis: I was being watched—and I loathed it.
I was being watched—and I cherished it.

section.para: In most circumstances, being watched isn’t a good thing, so “loathing” it may seem like a more natural attitude to have. “Cherishing,” on the other hand, is pretty different from “loathing,” and it is not the attitude we’d expect someone to have if they were being watched. Why do they cherish being watched? Is there something special about the watchers or about the experience of being watched? The choice of one word over another kindles our interest by going against our expectations about how someone should feel toward being watched.

The process of revising our stories is the time when we’ll make many word-choice decisions. Revision also cleans up grammar and other mistakes, smooths the narrative flow of a story, and deepens our ideas.

section.title: Improving Our Writing: The Keats Fallacy
section.para: Gaining skills with the English language will allow us to tell clearer, more engaging stories. And these skills really are ones that we can gain—when we understand the principles and apply them, we’ll improve. And we’ll only get better with practice.

This point about practice runs contrary to the idea that many people have about writing: that being a good writer is an innate gift that some people have and others simply don’t. In our course, we will call this idea the “ Keats fallacyThe erroneous idea that being a good writer is an innate gift that cannot be learned. ,” named after the English poet John Keats, who was famous for producing brilliant writing on the first try in very little time.

But few people are like John Keats, which is why the idea that writing is an innate gift is a fallacy. Most good writers have become good by practicing and are able to tell compelling stories because they understand how. We, too, can learn those same skills and create impactful stories.

section.title: Elements of a Story
section.para: While stories differ in many ways, almost all stories have some general elements in common. Mastering these elements and their functions will help us better understand how stories work.

section.title: Narrative
section.para: The driving force behind any story is the narrativeThe sequence of events that unfolds over the course of a story; also known as “plot.” , the sequence of events that unfolds over the course of the story. Most of the time, these events are closely connected to each other, but the connections aren’t always obvious.

In our course, we can also refer to this sequence of events by the term “plotAnother term for “narrative.” . This word appears in certain phrases that help us analyze a narrative—a plotline is one branch of the unfolding events, a plot hole is a logical gap between events, and so on.

As an example, let’s consider a simple narrative—the sequence of events in Dr. Seuss’s book The Cat in the Hat.Dr. Seuss. (1957). The cat in the hat. Random House; Houghton Mifflin. We’ll model the main events on individual lines in and connect them with arrows to represent their development over the course of the story.

figure.title: The main events in “The Cat and the Hat.”

imagedata.alt: The main seven events in “The Cat and the Hat.” 1. Too cold to play outside. 2. Cat shows up. 3. Warning from fish. 4. Cat causes a lot of mischief. 5. Fish: “Mom on her way home!” 6. Clean up the mess. 7. Mom gets home and everything is fine.

section.para: In this diagram, each line represents an event or group of events. The narrative unfolds as each event causes or contributes in some way to the event after it. We divide up the events in whatever way best preserves the structure of the narrative—here, the line “Cat causes a lot of mischief” actually represents a big portion of the book, while “Fish: ‘Mom on her way home!’” happens in just a couple lines. But the fish’s warning marks a turning point in the narrative, so we make sure to point that out.

section.title: Characters

figure.title:
Characters.
kudryashka © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Sketches of many different people.

section.para: A second primary element of a story is a characterThe entity in a narrative that makes events happen or that events happen to. or characters, which are the entities in a narrative that make events happen or that events happen to. We use the general term “entities” to refer to these characters because characters are usually people but can also be animals, robots, aliens, or anything else we want.

Through characters, we connect with the events in the narrative. Characters may be like us or completely different, but as we see the world through their eyes, we come to experience some of the same things they do.

section.title: Characters in The Cat and the Hat
section.para: The Cat in the Hat contains a number of characters: Sally and her brother, the fish, the Cat in the Hat, Thing One and Thing Two, and at the end, the children’s mother. The characters have different functions in the story, and their actions as they perform those functions tell us something about them. The Cat seems to be up to no good but really just wants to have fun; the children are bystanders for almost the entire book; the fish has some stern words for anyone who looks like they’re having a good time, and so on.

In this book, the narrative allows the characters to act or experience events on their own, so we learn about the characters by seeing what they do and how they react. We learn that the fish is stern by watching his prudish behavior; we learn that the Cat likes having fun because he’s starting a new party every few pages. The narrative and the characters work together to create a zany atmosphere that keeps children coming back for more.

Characters don’t have to be living things, at least not in the way we’ve been describing them here. Settings can be characters too, for example. In Ernest Hemingway’s novel The Old Man and the Sea,Hemingway, E. (1952). The old man and the sea. Charles Scribner’s Sons. the sea itself is a character because it interacts with the old man, Santiago. We learn of Santiago’s character and life as he struggles with the sea, and the fish he tries to catch becomes another character as well.

section.title: Message
section.para: Not all stories have messages that go beyond the events recounted in the story. Of course, we can always interpret a story as having a message, even when there doesn’t really seem to be one. We could say, for example, that The Cat in the Hat is really a commentary on Elvis Presley’s third and final appearance in The Ed Sullivan Show.Sullivan, E. (Executive Producer). The Ed Sullivan Show. (1957, January 6). Sullivan Productions; CBS Productions. No one would take that interpretation seriously outside of a literary theory class, but we could still try to make the case.

Even though not all stories have underlying messages, we will treat messages here as important elements of a story. We do this because, in many professional and organizational settings, stories are created in order to share a message—the message is integral to the story and may be the reason for its existence in the first place. As we saw before, a story can be the frame through which we convey some other piece of information. That information is the message, whose content drives some or all of the narrative, characters, and other elements of the story.

section.title: Telling Engaging Stories
section.para: Story elements like the overall narrative, individual plot events, characters, and settings are all part of the raw material that makes up a story. Good stories have other elements as well, and the ones we’ll see next are not easily identified by many people. We can see these parts of stories as techniques that authors use to engage an audience’s interest and advance the narrative.

section.title: The Hook

figure.title:
Hook.
Sergiy Tryapitsyn © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A fishing hook in the ocean.

section.para: A hookAn element near the beginning of a story designed to capture a reader’s attention. is whatever a story uses to grab a reader’s attention. Most readers begin at the beginning, so the hook always comes first—either in the first few pages or in the very first line. The hook is what makes a reader want to stick around for the rest of the story.
Hooks can be exciting, mysterious, disturbing, or anything else that will convince a reader to keep going. Here are some examples:
section.blockquote: “You better not tell nobody but God. It’d kill your mammy.”Walker, A. (1982). The color purple. Harcourt Brace Jovanich, 1.

“I’d never given much thought to how I would die—though I’d had reason enough in the last few months—but even if I had, I would not have imagined it like this.”Meyer, S. (2005). Twilight. Little, Brown and Company, 1.
“‘We should start back,’ Gared urged as the woods began to grow dark around them.”Martin, G. R. R. (1996). A game of thrones. Bantam Spectra; Voyager Books, 1.
section.para: In all three of these examples, we read the hook and are immediately left wondering what’s going on: what is so bad that you could only tell God? Who is about to die, and why? What is frightening Gared so much that he wants to go back? Good hooks leave readers wanting more as the story becomes the focus of their attention.

section.title: The Conflict
section.para: A conflictAny struggle between two entities in a story. is a struggle between two entities in a story. Conflicts can be simple, like two people disagreeing about what restaurant to go to, or larger and much more complex, like Batman’s fight against the Joker in The Dark Knight.Nolan, C. (Director). (2008, July 18). The dark knight [Film]. Warner Bros. Pictures; DC Comics; Legendary Pictures; Syncopy.

figure.title:
Conflict.
Przemyslaw Koch © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Two men playing tug-of-war with a rope.

section.para: Conflicts can arise naturally out of the characters with their personalities and interactions, or characters may be pushed into conflicts that they are unwilling participants in. In The Hunger Games,Collins, S. (2008–2010). The hunger games [Book series]. Scholastic Press. Katniss Everdeen is drawn into the titular event when she volunteers to take the place of her sister. Katniss’s conflicts include struggles against not only other children and the government but also the deadly landscape itself.
Characters and their conflicts help drive the events of a story. As characters act and react to what is happening around them, their choices allow a narrative to unfold.

section.title: The Stakes
section.para: The stakesSomething of value whose outcome depends on events in a story. of a story are what is up for grabs or in play due to the events in the narrative. The stakes can be small, involving only some children and their relationship with their mother, as in The Cat in the Hat. They can also span the entire universe, as in a movie like Avengers: Endgame.Russo, A., & Russo, J. (Directors). (2019, April 26). Avengers: Endgame [Film]. Marvel Studios.

Stories become compelling as authors increase the stakes. Lives are in danger, fortunes are at risk, and worlds teeter on the brink of destruction as the stakes rise and the importance of the narrative grows. When we learn to properly manage what is at stake for our characters and the world, we can pull our readers along for the ride.

section.title: Storytelling Attracts Audiences

figure.title:
Storytelling attracts an audience.
Photo by Daria Shevtsova via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A group of people gather in a living room.

section.para: Story elements like narrative and characters, along with techniques like hooks, conflicts, and stakes, work together to create compelling tales that can grip audiences for hours, days, or months at a time. It is the story and its quality that have these gripping powers rather than ancillary concerns like production values or marketing. Without a good story, even the shiniest project dissolves into a Pompeii,Anderson, P. W. S. (Director). (2014, February 27). Pompeii [Film]. Constantin Film; Impact Pictures. Jupiter Ascending,Wachowski, Lily, & Wachowski, Lana. (Directors). (2015, February 26). Jupiter ascending [Film]. Village Roadshow Pictures; RatPac-Dune Entertainment; Anarchos Productions. or Mortal EnginesRivers, C. (Director). (2018, December 14). Mortal engines [Film]. Universal Pictures; Media Rights Capital; WingNut Films.—you likely don’t remember those movies because few people watched them. They weren’t popular because the stories weren’t interesting.

It isn’t just novels and movies that need good stories, either. As we’ve seen, scientific articles sell their findings by telling a story about characters, conflict, and high stakes. They set up a narrative in which the heroes—the authors of the article—provide the key piece of knowledge or the crucial next step. Even though scientists are discovering truths about the natural world, they’re sharing those truths by telling stories about them.

section.title: Telling Stories to Audiences
section.para: Stories attract audiences—readers, viewers, listeners, reviewers, or anyone else who experiences the story. Elements of stories are there not only to make up the story but also to cater to audiences—to give them a story worth caring about.

section.title: An Audience’s Needs
section.para: Audience members have needs: things necessary to their enjoyment of a story. These needs usually include a comprehensible narrative, relatable characters, and conflicts and stakes that cohere with the events in the narrative. Not delivering these elements in a story risks alienating an audience or, perhaps even worse, never generating one in the first place.

figure.title:
Audience needs.
Photo by Zen Chung via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Two women sit on a bridge reading a book.

section.para: In creating our stories, we’ll want to remember who our audiences are and what they need. Many story choices are made by asking ourselves how an audience would think or feel about some aspect of the story. The needs and expectations of our audience should always be near the front of our minds in designing stories and determining how events will unfold. We can violate those needs and expectations, but we probably want to do so only for good reasons because violating them always involves a risk.

Audiences are always right in the sense that they are the final judges over what they like. If an audience decides it likes a book, then it will read that book, maybe two or three or a dozen times, regardless of what critics or others have to say. When we fail to engage a target audience with our story, the fault probably lies with us, not them.

section.title: Storytelling and Communication
section.para: The stories we tell will have many purposes, but at their heart, stories wish to communicate something. It may be something about the story’s narrative and characters or a latent message only dimly represented in the events of the story. Whatever it is, we’ll want that information to come through as clearly as possible.

But storytelling is about more than just sending a message—it’s about sending a message in a way that impacts audiences. Clarity combined with charm gives our ideas unmistakable appeal and will have audiences listening. We’ve also discussed other tools that can enhance our storytelling, such as voice, characters, the hook, and so on. As we continue with this course, we will learn even more skills we can use to captivate an audience and create a memorable message.

section.title: The Neuroscience of Storytelling
section.para: So far we’ve introduced stories by talking about how each piece of writing tells a story, and how each story has certain elements that help us hook audiences, raise the stakes, and deliver a satisfying conclusion. Humans have known about the power of stories for millennia. In tales as old as the ancient Greek poets Homer and Hesiod, and even in ones much older than them, we find characters, narrative, tension, and other elements of stories that we’ll discuss in this course.
In more recent times, neuroscience has been uncovering the way that our brains process stories, and these scientific results shed light on why we receive and retain story-based information so easily.

Let’s look at an example of this science in the work of Paul Zak, a professor of economics, psychology, and management who also directs the Center for Neuroeconomics Studies at the Claremont Graduate University.

In one of Zak’s studies, researchers showed one group of participants a video with emotional content (a father explaining his experiences with his young, terminally ill son), while another group saw a neutral control video with no emotional content. Among those who watched the emotional video, some then participated in a further task where they had the opportunity to share a fixed sum of money with a stranger in an ultimatum game. After completing all tasks, participants then had the option to donate to a charity.

Zak and colleagues made three main findings. First, they observed that viewing the video with emotional content raised the level of a certain chemical, oxytocin, in participants’ blood by an average of 47 percent over those who watched the neutral video. They also found a positive correlation between the degree of empathy that participants reported feeling and the change in oxytocin levels. Finally, they noted that an increase in the empathy someone experienced also correlated positively with greater generosity in the ultimatum game.Barrazza, J. A., & Zak, P. J. (2009). Empathy toward strangers triggers oxytocin release and subsequent generosity. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1167(1), 182–189.

These findings help us understand why stories are so effective in communicating messages to human beings. The chemical oxytocin has been linked to positive emotional states in the context of personal relationships; Zak himself, along with other researchers, found that elevated levels of oxytocin led to increases in how much a group of study participants trusted each other.Kosfield, M., Heinrichs, M., Zak, P. J., Fischbacher, U., & Fehr, E. (2005). Oxytocin increases trust in humans. Nature, 435, 673–676. In general, oxytocin is connected with prosocial behavior, or behavior that is likely to develop or enhance social relationships.

Given that watching an emotional video induced a greater amount of oxytocin in the bloodstream, we can see what kind of effect our stories may have on the brains of our audiences. If we can craft our stories so that they create similar kinds of emotional reactions in our audiences, we’ll be able to tap into the deep ways that the human brain connects to life as lived through stories.

In the end, we’re telling stories to our audiences for a reason: to sell a book or product, or to get them to change their behavior in other ways. Neuroscience is helping us understand the effect that stories have on the brain and on the choices we make after receiving information through stories.

section.title: Summary

figure.title:
Everyone tells stories.
Photo by Ketut Subiyanto via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A couple sits in their doorway talking.

section.para: Everyone tells stories—about themselves, others, and their lives. This course is all about stories and how they work.

We can use stories to communicate all sorts of messages. Sometimes there’s nothing more to a story than the story itself, but we can also use stories to frame other information. The elements of stories are flexible enough to be used in many different circumstances. Combining good writing with a knowledge of stories will help us communicate clearly.

section.title: What Sentences Are
section.para: A sentence is a string of words that expresses a complete idea. You just read a sentence. Then you read another one. Speech is based around sentences; they are the minimum unit of language that conveys a complete, self-contained idea.

All writing is also composed of sentences. We use sentences to state ideas or parts of ideas. We build sentences on each other to create paragraphs that tell more about those ideas, and we keep going until we’ve got an entire piece of writing that shares some kind of message. Writing is built from top to bottom by sentences organized in logical ways.

Words have meanings of their own, and individual words or phrases can have great power outside of sentences. In other words, we don’t always need sentences to communicate meanings or ideas. It’s possible to write something that isn’t a sentence, and readers may still understand us. Writing in this way is common online and is becoming common elsewhere too.

section.title: Short Forms of Language

figure.label: Figure 2.1
figure.title:
Writing sentences.
Photo by fotografierende via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Somone writing in a notebook with one hand and holding a cup of coffee in the other.

section.para: For example, we can use one of the oldest internet acronyms, “lol,” to mean “laughing out loud.” Or, if someone texts us to ask why we didn’t go to the party last night, we could respond with “because Netflix.” Neither “lol” nor “because Netflix” is a sentence according to the rules we’ll discuss later, but both expressions carry meaning that many people comprehend.

Notice, however, that we must use sentences in order to explain what these short forms of language mean. If our grandmother asks us what “lol” stands for, we could just say “laughing out loud.” Then our grandmother could follow up by asking who is actually laughing. We’d then have to clarify that when we put “lol” in a message, we mean that we are laughing out loud and not that someone else is. The same is true for “because Netflix,” which is just a shorthand way of saying something like “I didn’t go to the party last night because I was watching Netflix.” Only a complete sentence can adequately summarize the meaning of acronyms and other shortcuts.

section.title: Sentences Are the Foundation of Writing
section.para: For this reason and others that we’ll discuss below, sentences are the foundation of writing. They are the most important building blocks of clear communication, and as such, they’re the most important building blocks of stories as well. Learning how to write good sentences is essential to telling good stories. If we can’t assemble a string of a dozen words that make sense together, then we’ll never be able to share a compelling narrative that will require tens, hundreds, or even thousands of sentences to communicate.

This topic will offer some principles for constructing sentences. We’ll learn about parts of sentences and where sentences commonly go wrong, but the emphasis will be on learning how to write clear sentences to tell clear stories.

section.title: Clarity through Good Sentences
section.para: The term “clarity” refers to how comprehensible the meaning of something is. We use the adjective “clear” to describe a sentence, paragraph, or other piece of writing that exemplifies the virtue of clarity. Clear writing, in particular, writing clear sentences, is the way we achieve clarity in our stories, messages, and other communications.

section.title: Something to Avoid

figure.title:
Academic writing.
Photo by Andrea Piacquadio via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman uses a pointer to point to a chalkboard full of notes.

section.para: Let’s take a look at an example. Here is a sentence from an academic paper:
section.blockquote: “It is not at all hard to find utility assignments such that it is true that I prefer that I do A to that I do B iff I prefer that I do A to that I do B conditional on law x being in force, and I prefer that I do A to that I do B iff I prefer that I do A to that I do B conditional on law y being in force, but I do not prefer that I do A to that I do B iff I prefer that I do A to that I do B conditional on law x being in force and law y being in force.”Hawthorne, J., & Stanley, J. (2008). Knowledge and action. The Journal of Philosophy, 105(10), 576.
section.para: There may be some unfamiliar terms in this passage, like “utility assignments” and “iff” (which stands for “if and only if”), but other than that, it’s perfectly clear, right? Everyone would agree that any competent English speaker could take one look at this sentence and instantly grasp what the authors had in mind.

Hopefully the sarcasm came through in the previous paragraph—that sentence is absolutely incomprehensible. It is 116 words long! Even if we knew all the terms and understood the gist of what the authors wanted to communicate, the sentence would still utterly fail to communicate any useful meaning. The sentence has more subordinate clauses than most other sentences have words. It is a disastrous failure of writing regardless of the audience because it fails to communicate effectively.

section.title: Failure to Understand Is a Failure to Communicate
section.para: Sometimes we read sentences like the above and think to ourselves, “I don’t get it because I don’t have the right background.” A lack of background knowledge does sometimes explain why we can’t understand something, but that is not the case here. In many cases, the writing is just bad. And bad writing begins at the sentence level.

We achieve clarity in our writing when we assemble sentences that simply and directly state the ideas we want to communicate. Some ideas are complex and rely on many other ideas, as is true for the sentence we quoted above. But that just means complex ideas require greater attention on our part as writers. We must unravel our meanings and display them as intelligibly and as transparently as possible. The burden for making a meaning understood lies primarily with the author of a sentence, not the reader.

section.title: How Readers Experience Sentences
section.para: Authors assume the burden of making their meanings clear by understanding how readers experience sentences. We say that readers experience sentences, rather than just read them, to acknowledge the effort it can take to grasp what someone else has said. Following all but the most basic sentences requires effort and concentration, a process that authors can ease or exacerbate depending on how they write.

section.title: Reading Sentences—Underwater

figure.label: Figure 2.3
figure.title:
Coming up for air.
Photo by Jacub Gomez via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man coming up for air while swimming in the ocean.

section.para: The following metaphor may help put us in the mind of a reader. Reading a sentence is like going underwater. Getting to the period at the end of a sentence is the moment we come back to the surface and can breathe again.

To go underwater, we can dunk our heads just below the water level, or we can dive deeply. When we’re just below the surface, it’s easy to come back up, and the air is never far away. This can be compared to a short, easy-to-understand sentence. As readers, we can dive into the sentence, fully comprehend it, and finish it with more than enough air to spare.

Long, complex sentences, on the other hand, can be compared to diving deeply underwater. When we dive deeply, we may not have enough breath to reach the bottom, and coming back up to breathe may not be easy. Similarly, if the period is too far off, readers will be gasping for air near the end of the sentence. They may forget what the earlier parts of the sentence were even about. A reader’s struggle is compounded when the sentence has many phrases and clauses or relies on complex ideas. Those sentences require the most care to create. As writers, we need to make sure that readers experience each sentence in a gentle, thoughtful way. We do not want our readers to drown in the complexity of our writing as they struggle to break the surface of understanding.

Readers need the assurance of fresh air as they experience our writing, and their experiences help us outline some guidelines for how to construct effective sentences. We write sentences with readers in mind. We must ask ourselves, How will they experience what we write? If we are careful and willing to work, we can make sure that their experiences are clear and even enjoyable. Well-built sentences will allow compelling narratives, vibrant characters, and fascinating ideas to shine through.

section.title: Good Sentences Are Sentences We Control
section.para: Good sentences are sentences that we control. We control a sentence when we understand its purpose, and we make it do what is relevant to accomplishing that purpose.
Likewise, a bad sentence is one that we’ve lost control of. The words have escaped us and are running amok on the page, far beyond the limits of what the sentence hopes to accomplish.

The rest of this topic will discuss the principles of good sentence construction and their use. The discussion is based on the idea that sentences with fewer parts are easier to control than sentences with many parts. When authors keep their sentences under control, readers experience the writing as a gentle dip into pleasant waters. There may still be a struggle to understand complex ideas, but it won’t be because the writing failed to give the reader a chance.

section.title: Parts of Sentences
section.para: Earlier, we said that a sentence is a string of words that expresses a complete idea. We now need to be a little more specific about what we meant. Learning about the parts of sentences and then a bit more about other aspects of language will help us lay down some principles for the controlled construction of good sentences.

section.title: Not Just Any String of Words Is a Sentence

figure.label: Figure 2.4
figure.title:
Bananas.
Photo by Iona Cristiana via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Many bunches of bananas.

section.para: First off, not just any string of words counts as a sentence. Here’s one string that doesn’t:

blockquote.emphasis: Jackrabbit unusually twenty banana.

section.para: That string contains four words, but together they do not make a sentence. We can see that by reading the string, but soon, we’ll be able to state precisely why it isn’t a sentence.

section.title: Sentences Don’t Have to Have Meaning
section.para: Here’s another string of words. Does it make a sentence?

blockquote.emphasis: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.

section.para: Unlike the first string, this one is a sentence—even though it doesn’t make any sense. Something can’t be colorless and green at the same time, and ideas cannot sleep; the sentence is nonsensical. But its parts are arranged in such a way that they, together, make up a sentence.

section.title: Syntax and Semantics
section.para: Based on these examples, it’s clear we can analyze strings of words from two different perspectives. The first is through syntaxThe rules for forming grammatical expressions in a language. , the rules that govern how the words are arranged in a string. The second is according to the way we interpret the string, and this perspective is called semanticsThe interpretation of linguistic items, such as words or sentences, as meaningful units..

The rules of syntax determine whether a string counts as a sentence at all. The rules of good sentence construction are a combination of syntactical and semantic rules. This topic won’t refer to this terminology again, but we should remember that the rules and principles we’ll learn below have both syntactical and semantic sides.

section.title: Subjects

figure.label: Figure 2.5
figure.title:
Colorless green ideas.
Photo by Paul Blenkhorn via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: An abstract painiting with a green tone.

section.para: In general, a string of words counts as a sentence if it has both a subject and a predicate.
Let’s start with the subjectThe entity that a sentence says something about. . Every sentence has to have a subject. That’s the first requirement to have a sentence in the first place.
The subject of a sentence is the entity that the sentence says something about. Here is an example:

blockquote.emphasis: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.

section.para: The subject of this sentence is “colorless green ideas” because that’s what the sentence is about. The sentence says something about those ideas—namely, that they sleep furiously.
Here’s another example:

blockquote.emphasis: The cat is on the mat.

section.para: The subject here is “the cat.” The sentence tells us something about the cat by saying that it’s on the mat.
Let’s look at another example:

blockquote.emphasis: All my people have escaped from the jaws of death.

section.para: To identify the subject, we ask ourselves, What entity is this sentence about? This one tells us something about “all of my people,” so that must be the subject.
We can practice finding the subject in any sentence by asking ourselves that same question: What entity is this sentence about?

section.title: Predicates
section.para: The second requirement to have a sentence is that the string of words must say something about the subject. It must tell us that something is true or false of the subject. The technical term for what we say about the subject is the predicateWhat a sentence says about the subject. .
Let’s go back to this example:

blockquote.emphasis: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously.

section.para: We already know the subject, so what’s the predicate? It has to be “sleeps furiously” because those words tell us something about the colorless green ideas: they are sleeping in a furious manner. Again, that doesn’t make much sense, but it doesn’t have to. The rule of sentence formation just says that we need a subject and a predicate. If we have those two parts, we’ve got a sentence, whether or not it makes sense.

section.title: Subjects and Predicates Make Sentences
section.para: A string of words counts as a sentence if it has a subject and a predicate. By that rule, the following string isn’t a sentence:

figure.label: Figure 2.6
figure.title:
The calm blue ocean.
Photo by Anastasia Taioglou via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: The sun shining on the surface of the ocean.

blockquote.emphasis: The calm blue ocean.

section.para: Why isn’t it a sentence? What is it missing? This string has only a subject. The string names an entity—the calm blue ocean—but doesn’t tell us anything about that entity. It’s missing a predicate. We can make the string into a sentence by adding a predicate:

blockquote.emphasis: The calm blue ocean shines.

section.para: All we’ve done here is add one word, “shines,” and we’ve turned a string into a sentence. The subject is still “the calm blue ocean,” and the sentence tells us something about that subject: it shines.
Though they won’t make a complete sentence, predicates can also appear alone. Here are some examples:

blockquote.emphasis: Is blue.
Flies badly.
Discovered a cure for what ails you.

section.para: We could make each of these lone predicates into a complete sentence by adding a subject.

blockquote.emphasis: The sky is blue.
He flies badly.
She discovered a cure for what ails you.

section.title: Predicates and Verbs
section.para: Sometimes a sentence is described as containing a subject and a verb instead of a subject and a predicate. This description is true for the English language, which always includes a verb in the predicate.
Verbs are words that indicate the action or state of the subject. In the sentence about colorless green ideas, the verb is “sleep.” In the sentence about the calm blue ocean, the verb is “shines.”

In other languages, however, it doesn’t make sense to say that a sentence is made up of a subject and a verb. Ancient Greek and biblical Hebrew, for example, can both create complete sentences by combining a subject with an adjective and leaving out the “is” that English requires. “The tree green,” if written in ancient Greek, would be a complete sentence because the rules of Greek syntax allow the “is” to be left out. In English, we have to write, “The tree is green.” For this reason, it’s more accurate to say that a sentence consists of a subject and predicate rather than a subject and verb.
Let’s now learn about some other parts of speech. Later, we’ll combine those parts with what we’ve said about sentences and review some common mistakes in constructing sentences.

section.title: Other Parts of Speech
section.para: Other parts of language fill in spots in both the subject of a sentence and the predicate. This course isn’t about English grammar, so we won’t cover all those parts of speech here. We’ll only see a few that will help us understand ways to make our writing clear and simple.

section.title: Nouns
section.para: A nounA part of speech that identifies an entity, such as a person, place, or thing. is the subject of a predicate. Nouns most often refer to people, places, things, or ideas. Nouns can be common, like “cat” and “person,” or can refer to specific named instances, like “Fluffy,” “Barack Obama,” and “Los Angeles.” Nouns also have a number, meaning that a noun always refers to either one thing or more than one thing. When a noun refers to one thing, it’s a singular noun; when it refers to more than one thing, it’s plural.

section.title: Pronouns

figure.label: Figure 2.7
figure.title:
The cat is on the mat.
Photo by Jennifer Griffin via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A cat sitting on a mat.

section.para: A pronounA part of speech that refers to someone or something previously identified and includes “I,” “them,” or “it.” is a word that replaces a noun. Instead of saying, “The cat is on the mat,” we can say, “She is on the mat.” “She” is a pronoun that refers to “the cat.” We could use a pronoun for “the mat” as well. Then we could write, “She is on it.” The pronoun “it” refers to “the mat.”

We use pronouns in English both because they are short and because we don’t want to keep referring to entities by their full names. Using pronouns clearly is an important part of writing good sentences, as we’ll see below.

section.title: Prepositions
section.para: A prepositionA part of speech describing the relationship between two entities. is a word that expresses a relation between two entities. “On” is a preposition expressing a relation between “the cat” and “the mat.” The relation is that the cat is above the mat and touching it. The word after a preposition is in a prepositional phrase. A prepositional phraseA grammatical construction consisting of a preposition and its object. includes the preposition itself.

There are many different prepositions. Some, like “on,” have a primary use in describing spatial relations between things: “upon,” “over,” “under,” “through,” “next to,” and others have this use. Other prepositions describe relations of time, like “before,” “after,” or “during.”

Spatial and temporal relations aren’t the only ones that can be represented by a preposition. Some prepositions, like “because of” and “due to,” represent causal relations, or relations of cause and effect. Other prepositions represent other relations as well.

section.title: Objects

figure.label: Figure 2.8
figure.title:
I give money to Dana.
Photo by Karolina Grabowska via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man gives a woman money at a coffee shop.

section.para: An objectAn entity in a sentence that plays a certain grammatical role, such as receiving the action of a verb or being inside a prepositional phrase. , in the grammatical sense, refers to an entity that receives the action of the verb or an entity that is in a prepositional phrase.

In the sentence “The girl hit the ball,” “the ball” is the object of the verb “hit” because the ball is being hit—it receives the action of the verb. In “I give money to Dana,” both “money” and “Dana” are objects of the verb “give” because the action of giving is done to the money, and Dana receives the result of that action, or is given the money.
In the prepositional phrase “on the mat,” “the mat” is the object of the preposition “on.” In “because of the forest fire,” “the forest fire” is the object of the preposition “because of.”

section.title: Adverbs
section.para: An adverbA part of speech that describes the way in which something is done or exists. is a word that modifies a verb by telling how or in what way the verb was done. In the sentence “Lilly went quickly,” the word “quickly” is an adverb because it tells us how Lilly went—she went quickly. Many adverbs have an “-ly” ending, but not all; “well,” “fine,” and “often” are examples of common adverbs that don’t have that ending.

section.title: Conjunctions
section.para: A conjunctionA word used to connect different linguistic items, like two nouns or two sentences. connects two sentences or parts of sentences. There are several kinds of conjunctions, but only two will concern us here: coordinating conjunctions and subordinating conjunctions.

section.title: Coordinating Conjunctions
section.para: A coordinating conjunctionA conjunction used to connect two items that could stand independent of each other. connects two items that could stand independent of each other. These items may be two nouns, two adjectives, two sentences, two adverbs, and so on. When we say the items are independent of each other, we don’t mean that each item could stand on its own as an independent sentence. We just mean that the items are separate from each other and play a distinct role in a sentence.
“And” is the most common coordinating conjunction, as in the following sentence:

blockquote.emphasis: Taylor and Arianna sing.

section.para: “And” connects two nouns here, but it can also connect two complete sentences:

blockquote.emphasis: Taylor sings and Arianna sings.

section.para: In these sentences, the items connected by “and” could be independent of each other; they do not depend on each other in order to make sense. Any conjunction that connects items in these ways is a coordinating conjunction.
The acronym FANBOYS may be helpful for remembering some common coordinating conjunctions: “for,” “and,” “nor,” “but,” “or,” “yet,” and “so.” (See .)

figure.label: Figure 2.9
figure.title: FANBOYS acronym.

imagedata.alt: A graphic showing “F” is “for,” “A” is “and, “N” is “nor,” “B” is “but,” “O” is “or,” “Y” is “yet,” and “S” is “so.”

section.title: Subordinating Conjunctions
section.para: A subordinating conjunctionA conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause. connects two items where one of the items is dependent on the other or subordinate to it. A common subordinating conjunction is “because.” Let’s look at an example:

blockquote.emphasis: Taylor sings because she wants to cheer everyone up.

section.para: In this sentence, “because” introduces a subordinating conjunction clause, or string of words, and everything that follows it belongs to that clause.
The key for subordinating conjunctions is that they depend on the sentence they are a part of—they cannot stand alone or be independent of that sentence because their meaning would be incomplete.

section.title: Subordinate Clauses Are Not Independent
section.para: Let’s look at an example:

blockquote.emphasis: Because she wants to cheer everyone up.

section.para: Together, these words make sense, but they do not form a complete sentence. Although “She wants to cheer everyone up” is a complete sentence, introducing this sentence with a subordinating conjunction causes the meaning of the words after “because” to become dependent on another sentence. The entire clause, including the “because,” can then no longer stand on its own as a complete sentence. This is why: a clause introduced by a subordinating conjunction must be a part of another sentence.
“After,” “that,” “if,” and “where” are other common subordinating conjunctions. lists more examples.

figure.label: Figure 2.10
figure.title: Subordinating conjunctions.

imagedata.alt: A list of subordinating conjunctions: “after,” “although,” “as,” “because,” “before,” “even,” “if,” “even though,” “if,” “in order to,” “once,” “provided that,” “rather than,” “since,” “so that,” “than,” “that,” “though,” “unless,” “until,” “when,” “whenever,” “where,” “whereas,” “wherever,” “whether,” “while,” and “why.”

section.para: In the following examples, notice how the subordinate clause could not be a sentence on its own and depends on the rest of the sentence in order to make sense:

blockquote.emphasis: After Taylor sings, Arianna will sing.
I know that Taylor can sing.
Taylor will sing if Arianna sings.
Where Taylor goes, Arianna goes.

section.title: Coordinating or Subordinating Conjunction?
section.para: To determine whether a conjunction is coordinating or subordinating, we ask ourselves, could the clause introduced by this conjunction be a complete sentence if we include the conjunction? If the conjunction and the clause together could be a complete sentence, not dependent on their meaning on any other sentence, then it’s a coordinating conjunction. But if the clause and the conjunction together depend on another sentence, then it’s a subordinating conjunction.

You can also remember that conjunctions that connect two nouns, two verbs, two adjectives, or two adverbs are always coordinating conjunctions. Here are some examples with the coordinating conjunctions in italics:

blockquote.emphasis: Jack and Jill went up the hill.
Jack and Jill ascended and descended the hill.
Jack and Jill went up the brown but lovely hill.
Jack and Jill went quickly yet stealthily up the hill.

section.title: Conjunction Practice

figure.label: Figure 2.11
figure.title:
Flowers all around the house.
Photo by Matthew Perrier via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Flowers in vases on a table.

section.para: Take a look at the following sentences. Conjunctions are in italics—see if you can tell whether the word is a coordinating or subordinating conjunction and why.

blockquote.emphasis: Orlando rode the horse, but he didn’t ride the pony.
Silvia put flowers all around the house because she liked the way they smelled.
Wilma said that everyone who drives a car made of stone is old.

section.para: You can find the answers to these sentences at the end of this section.

section.title: Voice
section.para: As noted in , we say that a sentence is in active voice when the subject is performing the action of the verb. A sentence is in passive voice when the subject receives the action of the verb.

section.title: Active Voice
section.para: Here are some examples of active-voice sentences:

blockquote.emphasis: I sent a package to Benny.
The printer did a fine job.
No one would have guessed that.

section.title: Passive Voice
section.para: Here are some related examples in the passive voice:

blockquote.emphasis: A package was received by Benny.
A fine job was done by the printer.
That would not have been guessed by anyone.

section.para: Notice how the emphasis of each sentence shifts depending on whether it is in active or passive voice. Generally, a sentence in the active voice is more direct and specific, and the sentence emphasizes the subject doing the action. A sentence in the passive voice is often less specific and longer, and the sentence emphasizes that something was done without worrying too much about who was responsible for it.

section.title: Conjunction Practice Answers
section.blockquote: Orlando rode the horse, but he didn’t ride the pony. (Coordinating)
Silvia put flowers all around the house because she liked the way they smelled. (Subordinating)
Wilma said that everyone who drives a car made of stone is old. (Subordinating)

section.title: Sentence Mistakes
section.para: So far, we’ve learned about sentences, how readers experience them, and what their parts are. We’re now ready to apply this knowledge in order to see some common mistakes made at the sentence level.

We won’t discuss all the possible sentence-level mistakes here, nor even all the most common ones. Our focus is on mistakes that are especially harmful to a reader trying to understand our sentences. Not all sentence-level mistakes are created equal. Some have no ill effects and may not be noticed, while others can make a sentence extremely difficult to comprehend.

section.title: Subject-Verb Disagreement
section.para: When a noun is the subject of a sentence, it must agree with the verb in the predicate in number. This means that when the noun is plural—when we’re talking about more than one thing—the verb must be plural as well. “The cat are on the mat” is incorrect because “the cat” is a singular noun, but the verb “are” requires a plural subject. “The cats is on the mat” is incorrect for a similar reason.

figure.label: Figure 2.12
figure.title:
Honey.
Photo by Alexander Mils via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Honey on a honeycomb on a table.

section.para: In English, the subject of a sentence is always singular or plural—one thing or more than one thing. The verb for the subject must reflect this number. If the subject is singular, the verb must be singular; if the subject is plural, the verb must be plural too. If the subject and the verb do not match, the sentence has a subject-verb disagreement.See if you can spot the mistake here:

blockquote.emphasis: A man living down by the river visit us.

section.para: Here we have a singular subject but a plural verb—“visit” should be “visits” to agree with the subject. Subject-verb mistakes like this one almost always cause attentive readers to return to the beginning of the sentence to see if they missed something or misunderstood the first few words. Here is another example:

blockquote.emphasis: The bear in the leaves were eating honey.

section.para: In this example, the subject is singular, “bear,” but the verb is plural, “were.” It’s a mistake of subject-verb agreement. This example is even more confusing because this sentence has a plural word—“leaves”—before the verb. A reader may end up thinking that the leaves, not the bear, were eating honey.
Subjects and verbs must always agree in number.

section.title: Subject and Verb Too Far Apart
section.para: Every subject in a sentence needs a verb. Without the verb telling us something about the subject, the string of words isn’t a complete sentence. The tight relationship between subject and verb suggests that those words should appear close together in actual sentences.

Sometimes, however, the subject and verb are very far from each other, and the resulting sentence requires readers to return to the beginning to make sure they know what is going on. Here is an example:

blockquote.emphasis: The farmer who lives down by the river trickling through the glade across from the road near the gas station drives.

section.para: In this sentence, we get the subject, “the farmer,” in the first two words. But we don’t get the verb until the very last word. By the time we get to “drives,” we have to go back to the beginning to check again who we’re talking about.

section.title: Keep Subjects and Verbs Close

figure.label: Figure 2.13
figure.title:
Sally.
Photo by Thgusstavo Santana via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A little girl holds her hand to her cheek, looking slightly upset.

section.para: Remember, we construct sentences by keeping in mind how readers experience sentences. A reader encountering our example sentence is underwater for a very long time, struggling to find the verb to complete the meaning.
A related problem occurs when the completion of a predicate is very far from the verb. Here is an example of a sentence like that:

blockquote.emphasis: Sally grew, more than we expected, but less than most other people thought, upset.

section.para: The word “upset” at the end of this sentence completes the predicate by adding to the meaning of “grew.” The idea is that Sally grew upset. But when completion of the predicate is placed far away from the verb, the sentence becomes much more difficult to understand. Most readers will assume that the core of the sentence is “Sally grew,” so when they get to “upset,” they’ll have to re-read the entire sentence.

section.title: Too Many Adverbs
section.para: We should use adverbs with care. They can bog a sentence down with words and may not add much to the meaning. Fewer is better.

Sometimes we can cut adverbs by choosing more descriptive verbs. Instead of writing “Yolanda ran fast,” for example, we could write “Yolanda sprinted.” We’ve cut the adverb “fast” by using “sprinted,” which means to run fast.

section.title: Overuse of “Of”
section.para: Like sentence mistakes, not all prepositions are created equal. Some prepositions are “light,” in that using them tends not to increase the complexity or difficulty of a sentence very much. Light propositions include “after,” “before,” “in,” and “on.”

Other prepositions are heavier, and “of” may be the heaviest of all. “Of” has so many meanings that denote so many relationships between entities that a reader must rapidly sort through them to find the correct relationship each time the reader encounters the word. When “of” occurs multiple times in quick succession, the sentence can quickly get out of control. Here’s an example:

blockquote.emphasis: The discovery of the candle of light of the king of the ancient land of Sparta was important.

section.para: The five “of” prepositions in a row make it difficult for a reader to discern the correct meaning of the sentence. Is the candle of light the king’s, or does it belong to Sparta? Is the king the king of the ancient land of Sparta or just the ancient land? It’s impossible to say.
When we use “of,” we should be mindful of the experiences we are setting up for our readers.

section.title: Vague Pronouns

figure.label: Figure 2.14
figure.title:
They walked the dog.
Photo by mentatdgt via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man and woman walk their dog in a park.

section.para: A vague pronoun is one that could refer back to multiple nouns, with no way to tell which is correct. Here is an example:

blockquote.emphasis: They walked the dog through the obstacle course at the park and loved it.

section.para: Here, “it” could refer to “the obstacle course,” “the park,” or even the whole event of walking the dog. We could rewrite the sentence to be more precise:

blockquote.emphasis: They loved the obstacle course when they walked the dog through it at the park.

section.para: This use of “it” must refer to “the obstacle course,” so the pronoun isn’t vague anymore.

section.title: Run-On and Overly Long Sentences
section.para: Remember, for a reader, encountering a sentence is like going underwater. As authors of sentences, we don’t want to keep our readers underwater too long, so we should be conscientious of the ways our sentences begin and end.

One problem with beginnings is run-on sentences. A run-on sentenceA sentence made by improperly combining two other complete sentences. is a sentence built of two complete sentences that are not properly connected. Here is an example:

blockquote.emphasis: Video games are the best I have a lot of fun with them.

section.para: This one sentence contains two complete sentences, but the sentences run right next to each other with no warning. We can fix the problem by adding a period separating these sentences.

blockquote.emphasis: Video games are the best. I have a lot of fun with them.

section.para: Or we can add a coordinating conjunction and connect the sentences.

blockquote.emphasis: Video games are the best, and I have a lot of fun with them.

section.para: A related problem has to do with the endings of our sentences—sometimes the endings never come. Many sentences are just too long. Long sentences keep our readers underwater for much longer than necessary.
