Thesauruses, especially searchable ones online, are useful for suggesting new frames and new ways of approaching a topic. But they are not simply lists of words that mean the same thing.

section.title: Avoiding Uncommon or Fancy Words
section.para: In writing, simple and direct phrases are usually best. This means that choosing simpler and direct words is usually better than choosing long or uncommon words that even a professional writer might have to look up in a dictionary.
For example, consider the difference between these possible sentences, describing a character in a story:

para.emphasis: 1. The speaker was prolix.
2. The speaker was verbose.
3. The speaker was wordy.

section.para: These three sentences are identical except for the last word. Most people will have never heard the word “prolix.” Most people will know “verbose,” though they may never actually use it. And most everyone knows and uses the word “wordy.” But all three words mean the exact same thing—using too many words to express a point.

Think, then, of the frame communicated by an author in choosing one sentence over another. Choosing sentence 1 may be an author’s way of saying something like “I’m smarter than you,” or “Look at my fancy word,” or “I don’t care whether you understand this or not.” Those frames are bad; we should avoid them. Choosing sentence 2 indicates that the author has chosen a formal frame for the story, perhaps hinting at other formal aspects still to come. By choosing sentence 3, the author shows the reader that he is taking a more commonly known and general approach to his writing.

For most purposes, sentence 3 is preferable, though sentence 2 does have a place in more formal contexts. “Prolix” in sentence 1, however, is so uncommon that it is probably better to avoid it for most audiences. There are few sentences describing a wordy person or text that would become better if they contained “prolix.”

figure.label: Figure 4.8
figure.title:
A laconic man.
Ion Chiosea © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man makes a motion that looks like he is zipping his lips.

section.para: Other words are like this too. Look at these two choices:

para.emphasis: 1. He’s a man of few words.
2. He’s laconic.

section.para: Virtually every English speaker both understands and uses the construction in sentence 1 to say that someone doesn’t talk much. Only academics and owners of word-a-day calendars would use sentence 2. Simpler and more direct words are usually preferable.

Of course, as we’ll notice right away, the distinction between simple words and fancy words doesn’t depend on how long they are. Some long words, like “incomprehensible,” are common and understood by everyone; it’s a simple word because it’s so widely used. On the other hand, “quaff” is very short, but how many people know it just means “drink”? Not many, and if we write it, we’ll be sending many readers to a dictionary to figure it out.

We can ask ourselves how we would explain or describe something to an intelligent friend with no background in what we’re saying. The words that come to mind will probably be simple and direct ways of communicating our point—then we should write those words.

This is not to diminish the importance of expanding one’s vocabulary or using expressive words for a more powerful effect in communication. In fact, it is important to develop a wide vocabulary to be able to know and choose the best words to use in a given context. Using words the audience doesn’t understand will undermine the message, but carefully choosing words to express a specific meaning will convey the message more clearly and naturally.

As always, these suggestions depend on the audience we’re writing to and the frame we want to communicate. Sometimes we may choose to use higher-level vocabulary to let the audience know that we’re playing the same game as them or playing it on the same level. So be it. But let’s at least be aware of the clarity and simplicity we abandon when we write that way.

section.title: Jargon and Buzzwords
section.para: JargonTechnical language that is specific to a certain profession or group. is extremely technical language specific to a certain profession or group. The Latin phrase “stare decisis” is a piece of jargon in the legal profession because only someone who’s gone through law school would understand what it means.

In most contexts, we can avoid jargon just by choosing simpler words. But in other cases, it isn’t always possible or even advisable to avoid jargon. A law clerk writing a memo to judges will probably want to use “stare decisis” because it’s the exact phrase describing a certain meaning. But communicating the same meaning outside of a legal context calls for a different approach and less technical language.

Unlike jargon, a buzzwordA popular term within a certain community. is a term that is usually easy to understand but that has become popular in a certain community. Authors then use the buzzword not because it is clearer than other words but simply because it is popular.

An example is the term “leverage.” This word is widely written and spoken in business circles within sentences such as “We’ll leverage the new software to open the market.” But “leverage” in this context just means “use,” and authors leverage the word “leverage” not because of its meaning but because of its popularity.
We will stand out with a distinct voice among storytellers when we choose words for their descriptive value and impact on audiences, not for their popularity.

section.title: Know Exact Meanings

figure.label: Figure 4.9
figure.title:
Fire.
Photo by Nathan Lindahl via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A campfire under a starry sky.

section.para: The final suggestion is to know the exact meaning of our words. Take the term “ignominious.” The letters “ign” at the start also appear in words like “ignition” and “ignite,” which may give us the sense that “ignominious” has something to do with fire or burning. But it doesn’t. Instead, the word describes something involving disgrace or shame. Using the word to describe fire would be odd at best.
When in doubt, use the dictionary. We shouldn’t use a word whose meaning we don’t know well.

section.title: Simple and Direct Is Best
section.para: The words we choose communicate the frame of our stories and messages. The best advice is to choose simple, direct words whenever possible. That choice is possible much more often than we may think, and those kinds of words will make our communications shine.

section.title: Writing Is Thinking
section.para: Including previous topics, we have now covered sentences (), paragraphs (), grammar, and word choice (). We have learned skills that will help us write more effectively and tell more compelling stories. The most important subject left to cover is revision. As a bridge to that subject, this section will discuss the writing process itself.

section.title: Writing Is Difficult

figure.label: Figure 4.10
figure.title:
Writing is difficult.
Photo by Joshua Hoehne via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A broken pencil on a wood table with notches.

section.para: Writing is difficult. Even experienced writers sometimes have trouble conveying what they mean. Sometimes it’s a battle to hammer out a paragraph or even a sentence. This is normal—writing is hard! Nothing is wrong with us when we find writing a challenge—everyone does.

Writing is difficult exactly because the process of writing is the process of coming to understand what we think or of discovering the story we want to tell. Writing is thinking; we arrive at our points of view by writing. We have rarely made our thoughts precise enough to be able to spill pristine words onto a page with no errors. Most of the time, we work out our ideas as we go, uncovering new possibilities that couldn’t have occurred to us before we started writing. Writing is thinking, and thinking is discovery.

section.title: Writing Is Discovery
section.para: In many cases, we won’t know what we want to say until we start to write. We won’t have bulletproof arguments before committing them to paper. We won’t have our views, a plotline, a character, or anything else completely worked out before we start to type. This is normal. Writing is hard. As we learn to embrace uncertainty and write, we will discover the right way to say something as we go along.

section.title: Writing Takes Work
section.para: Many people accept a version of the Keats fallacy, which we mentioned in the introduction to this course. John Keats was a poet who became famous for his work partly because he produced such brilliant lines with apparently very little revision. He composed the following lines in the spring of 1819, along with 70 others, in a single morning:

blockquote.emphasis: Darkling I listen; and, for many a time
I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Call’d him soft names in many a mused rhyme,
To take into the air my quiet breath;
Now more than ever seems it rich to die,
To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
In such an ecstasy!
Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—
To thy high requiem become a sod.Keats, J. (2017). Ode to a nightingale (complete edition). e-artnow, 6. (Original work published 1820)

section.para: Truly remarkable! And the circumstances of their creation make these lines of poetry even more amazing. But what Keats did in 1819 is not common for anyone, poet or otherwise. Such stories of genius and lightning-strike brilliance give rise to the impression that all good writing is created in Keats’s way, with very little revision.

section.title: Refuting the Keats Fallacy

figure.label: Figure 4.11
figure.title:
Writing takes time.
Photo by freestocks via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A clock, a notebook, and a pen on a white table.

section.para: But we call this impression the Keats fallacy for a reason—it is an incorrect way of thinking about writing and our relationship to it. There may well be a Keats out there, but the rest of us just show up in front of the computer every day, typing and, sometimes, struggling to type. Over time, our work becomes better and, eventually, good. But we cannot expect ourselves to churn out publication-quality work on the first try, the second, or even the third or fourth. Writing is thinking, and thinking takes time.

As a consequence of all this, the first step in good writing is to produce a draft. When writing our first draft, we don’t need to worry much about how good it is. Our first draft doesn’t need to be good—it just needs to exist. Once it does, we’ll have material to work on and improve. We can't start refining until we have a draft.

section.title: First Drafts Are for Writers, Not Readers
section.para: Our first drafts don’t need to be for anyone but us, and we should feel that we can write them freely, without concern for how good they are. Once they are done and we can step back from the creation process, we’ll be able to see places where they can improve. But punishing ourselves for not creating something good on the first try isn’t going to get us anywhere.

Always remember that good writing and storytelling are skills that we can learn by practicing. The Keats fallacy tempts us to believe otherwise, assuming that good writers have some innate genius. Lucky writers have talent, but good writers become good by working hard and learning. They face their fears and put words to paper even when they aren’t feeling it. In that way, good writers learn the skills that make them good writers.

figure.label: Figure 4.12
figure.title:
The solution: write.
Photo by Green Chameleon via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A woman writing at her desk.

section.title: The Solution to Writing Problems: Write
section.para: We will face problems as we write. Fortunately, the solution to most writing problems, including writer’s block, is the same: write. We will overcome the problems as we put words on the page. Even when we have serious anxiety about the quality of our work, the solution is still the same. Nothing can get better unless we actually write.

Writing is thinking, and thinking is an arduous process. We don’t always know where our thinking will take us nor the route we’ll travel to get there. But we discover it all while writing. And as we write, we come to truly understand the stories we want to tell—maybe even for the very first time.

section.title: Writing Is Revising
section.para: Writing is thinking, but writing is also revising. Revising is the process of making improvements to a piece of writing after we’ve written it. After we write a paper, we revise it by reading it again and changing it. Depending on what we’re writing and why, revising can take a long time, sometimes much longer than it took to create the original draft.

section.title: Revising Improves Writing

figure.label: Figure 4.13
figure.title:
Revising improves writing.
Photo by Andrea Piacquadio via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man writes at his desk, which is full of papers and pencils.

section.para: We say that writing is revising because revising is where the writing begins to improve. Revision is taking something rough, uneven, and unclear and turning it into something sparkling. Revision clarifies our thoughts and sharpens our narratives. It brings the essential ideas to the surface and cuts out anything superfluous. It will allow our writing to be good writing; we cannot expect to produce good writing without the revision process.

Revision is also creation. The revision process doesn’t just tinker with what we already have; it creates new material to fill in gaps or develop crucial points. Just as our thinking isn’t finished after we state a thought for the first time, a piece of writing isn’t finished after it first takes form. Revisions will change it, build on it, erase part of it, and even contradict it as the writing improves.

Revision is also the process in which we clean up issues of grammar and word choice and make decisions about how to express the frame of our message or story. It can be paralyzing to worry too much about grammar and word choice when writing a first draft. Since our first drafts will never be our best work, we don’t need to care too much if everything is not exactly right. We’ll fix the problems in revision, and we will adapt the grammar and word choice to match the frame and expectations of our audience.

section.title: Revising Is Writing
section.para: In short, revision is everything that writing is: thinking, improving, creating, organizing, building, cutting, choosing, and refining. The more we do all those things, the more we learn and the better we’re able to give voice to the stories we want to tell.

We offer specific guidance for revising sentences in section and paragraphs in section . We will also offer some general revision advice here. Keep in mind that not every piece of writing advice applies to every writer. Different writers have different strategies for creating drafts and revising. You should try out different approaches to discover what works for you.

section.title: Take a Step Back
section.para: One of the biggest problems students have with term papers in college is that they write them the day before they are due. As we’ve discussed, the first drafts of our work usually aren’t very good, especially when we write under pressure. But writing papers the day before they’re due leaves authors no time to revise them, so they’re stuck with whatever they produce the first time through.

figure.label: Figure 4.14
figure.title:
Writing under pressure.
Photo by Black Ice via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A clock and a notebook surrounded by numbers.

section.para: The first thing to learn from students’ experiences is to produce written material early. But the more important point is that, whenever possible, we should take some time away from a draft of our writing before we begin to revise.

During the writing process, we are neck-deep in the ideas we’re trying to formulate. Our views are also evolving as we write the draft, and we sometimes reach the end of a document believing something entirely opposite from what we believed when we started. Our minds are consumed with the words, sentences, and paragraphs we’ve worked so hard to create.

After taking a few days or more away from a piece of writing, we’ll return to our work with new eyes. We will be able to clarify what we actually believe and see how our writing does or doesn’t support the points we want to make. We’ll see spots where we were confused, sentences that don’t make sense, and many things that we can cut without affecting the writing. Our revision will improve simply because the writing is less familiar to us.
When possible, we should take a step back from our writing so that we can evaluate it later. We will revise more effectively, and our writing will be better for it.

section.title: Read Slowly Out Loud

figure.label: Figure 4.15
figure.title:
Reading out loud.
Photo by nappy via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man reading a book outside.

section.para: As we revise, it is useful to read our work out loud. Reading something out loud forces us to read more attentively and to try to match the natural rhythms and inflections of speech to the writing. When those aspects of speech have trouble matching up with what we’ve written, we’ll find places to revise.

Reading out loud can also help with problems like sentence length. If we’re drowning in sentences of our own making in a desperate attempt to find the end, we can be sure that other readers will also struggle.

section.title: Keep Old Drafts
section.para: When we revise, we should begin by creating and saving a new document. The new document will usually be an exact copy of the old one, and we’ll begin our revision in the new document, leaving the old one alone. The new document will house all our changes and cutting, and the old version will be there if we decide we need something from it.

We can repeat this same process for each major revision. Many authors deeply revise their work ten or twenty times or more, each time creating a substantially different version. Most people won’t need to do that, but it’s still a good idea to save our old work and keep track of it clearly with descriptive file names.

Many document-writing programs, like Microsoft Word, offer the ability to track changes, or make changes to a document while leaving old or deleted material in the background. Authors then have the option to view their work with or without the old material.

This feature is useful for many projects, but sometimes the deleted material can turn into an incomprehensible mess. Try different approaches to discover what works, but always, always save what you’ve written.

section.title: Cut with Abandon

figure.label: Figure 4.16
figure.title:
Cut with abandon.
Photo by Karolina Grabowska via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Scissors cutting a blank piece of paper.

section.para: Our first draft, and even our second and third drafts, often comes complete with sentences or even whole paragraphs that utterly fail in various ways. They may not support the point we want to make, they may make a terrible argument, or they may be jumbled wrecks beyond saving. We might even wonder how we could possibly have written them.

We should be merciless in our attitude toward material like this in our own writing. Cut, cut, cut, and then cut again. If we’ve saved our previous versions, then we lose nothing because what we’re cutting lives on in another document. And it’s more likely that we’ve gained clarity by eliminating weak writing to keep and develop the best ideas.

Some writers are afraid to cut because they feel an emotional attachment to what they have created. They will need to cut anyway—the love we feel for a particular sentence or turn of phrase says nothing about the effectiveness of that writing in conveying a point.

section.title: Have Others Read Our Work
section.para: Even after we’ve taken a step back from our work and adopted a ruthless attitude toward editing, there are still things we will miss. We simply cannot see all the weaknesses of our writing, no matter how many times we read it.

The solution is to get others to read our work. They will be able to identify places where we need to make changes and point out unclear points that we missed. Don’t be afraid to ask others for help, and make sure to listen to their feedback.

section.title: Proofread at the End
section.para: Finally, we should learn the difference between revision and proofreading. Revision is just writing at a different stage, and it involves everything that writing does. Proofreading is checking for small errors in punctuation, formatting, and spelling without regard for the ideas or large-scale organization of the writing.
Save proofreading for the end, when the document is near completion. There’s no sense in paying careful attention to small issues when we’re going to change much of what we’re writing anyway.

section.title: Revising Sentences
section.para: Many problems with writing trace back to problems at the sentence level. When our sentences aren’t clear or don’t flow cleanly, readers will struggle to get through our writing, no matter what else we’ve done.

We covered sentences in . The most important point from our discussion is that simple, direct sentences are better whenever possible. “Simple” means carefully choosing words and avoiding complex internal structure, like multiple subordinate clauses. “Direct” means that sentences say only what they need to say and nothing else.

section.title: To Revise: Simplify

figure.label: Figure 4.17
figure.title:
Eliminate anything superfluous.
Photo by David Pennington via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Erasers on a pencil.

section.para: The key for revising sentences, then, is to simplify. Use fewer subordinate clauses, or break apart a long sentence into multiple, simpler sentences. Use fewer words. Choose words that are easier to understand, and eliminate anything superfluous.

Sometimes we may worry that simplifying sentences will force us to sacrifice the meaning of a sentence. In reality, most authors do not have that problem because they can easily simplify their writing without cutting anything meaningful. Almost everyone can pare things down, especially after a first draft.
To see how this revision works, we’ll look at a few sentences to see what we can do.

section.title: Sentence 1

blockquote.emphasis: The rationale was that the increase in hormonal function would make units otherwise unavailable for the formation of the building block assembly available.

section.para: Read this sentence again a few times to get a handle on it. The internal structure of this sentence is not too complex; it has a single subordinate clause, introduced by “that.” A bigger problem is that the adjective “available,” which completes the meaning of “units” to finish the thought, is very far from the noun it modifies.
We could revise the sentence to put these words closer together:

blockquote.emphasis: The rationale was that the increase in hormonal function would make otherwise unavailable units available for the formation of the building block assembly.

section.para: It may even be better to choose a verb that better includes the idea of availability:

blockquote.emphasis: The rationale was that increasing hormonal function would free up units for forming the building block assembly.

section.para: In this version, we’ve also replaced two constructions involving prepositions (“increase in hormonal function” and “for the formation of the building block assembly”) with simpler constructions relying on “ing” (“increasing hormonal function” and “for forming the building block assembly”). This is a common way to eliminate prepositional phrases, especially those involving “of.”
Finally, we could even get rid of the subordinate clause:

blockquote.emphasis: Increasing hormonal function, they thought, would free up units for forming the building block assembly.

section.para: Adding “they thought” in the middle of the sentence does not add the same kind of structure that a subordinate clause does, though it may not be totally necessary.
Let’s compare the two final versions in .

td.emphasis: The rationale was that the increase in hormonal function would make units otherwise unavailable for the formation of the building block assembly available.
Increasing hormonal function, they thought, would free up units for forming the building block assembly.

section.para: The revised version may not be perfect, but it’s much simpler and says the same thing with seven fewer words—a 32% reduction in the word count.

section.title: Sentence 2

blockquote.emphasis: Alexandra scudded along the quay.

section.para: This sentence is simple and direct, but it uses two words that most people won’t know: “scudded” and “quay.” “Scud” means to move fast as if driven forward; “quay” means “dock.” The change is simple:

blockquote.emphasis: Alexandra ran along the dock.

section.para: The revised version of this sentence uses words everyone understands. In that respect, it is better. But it is also very different and may not produce the feel an author wants. Remember that our word choices communicate frame, and we determine the frame of a story by considering our audience. Simplifying a sentence with simpler words may not always be the right decision. Let’s see the difference in .
Although the word count is the same between the sentences, the revised sentence is much easier to understand.

section.title: Sentence 3

blockquote.emphasis: “Our intention, rather, is to emphasize the need to be circumspect and explicit about the subjective construction of such quantitative datasets, and thereby to better understand underlying biases and ultimately improve the construction and use of such data.”Herrera, Y. M., & Devesh, K. (2007). Improving data quality: Actors, incentives, and capabilities. Political Analysis, 15(4), 369.

section.para: This sentence breaks down pretty obviously into two parts. Our first step will be to separate them out:

blockquote.emphasis: Our intention, rather, is to emphasize the need to be circumspect and explicit about the subjective construction of such quantitative datasets. That way, we will better understand underlying biases and ultimately improve the construction and use of such data.

section.para: Now, these two sentences have a lot of verbs masquerading as nouns and prepositional phrases. We can change them, simplify the words, and drop the “intention” bit at the beginning:

blockquote.emphasis: Instead, we emphasize care and clarity in subjectively constructing quantitative datasets. That way, we will better understand biases and improve how we construct and use such data.

section.para: These sentences drastically improve when we reshape them to follow a simple subject-verb-object model, without so much stuff in between. This reshaping requires changing prepositional phrases, using verbs more clearly, and dropping unnecessary material. But the result is a pair of sentences that state the very same ideas much more clearly. We can see that in .

td.emphasis: Our intention, rather, is to emphasize the need to be circumspect and explicit about the subjective construction of such quantitative datasets, and thereby to better understand underlying biases and ultimately improve the construction and use of such data.
Instead, we emphasize care and clarity in subjectively constructing quantitative datasets. That way, we will better understand biases and improve how we construct and use such data.

section.para: The original is 39 words; the revised is 28—a 28% reduction that comes with a big gain in clarity.

section.title: Sentence 4

blockquote.emphasis: “While the constraining effect of the pre-accession process on political competition was universal across all 10 cases as the EU applied a one-size-fits-all approach to the Eastern enlargement, it is instructive to determine the extent to which the pre-accession process had a differentiated effect on different party systems.”Meka, E. (2016). European integration, democratic consolidation, and democratic regression in CEE: An institutional assessment. Journal of European Integration, 38(2), 179.

section.para: Yikes! This sentence requires us to wade through two complete lines before we even get to the main verb! When we have leading subordinate clauses that long, they are better off as separate sentences. We’ll then want to eliminate the “while” at the start of the first new sentence and add a sentence transition to the start of the second one to mark their relationship:

blockquote.emphasis: The constraining effect of the pre-accession process on political competition was universal across all 10 cases as the EU applied a one-size-fits-all approach to the Eastern enlargement. For this reason, it is instructive to determine the extent to which the pre-accession process had a differentiated effect on different party systems.

section.para: These sentences are still full of verbs masquerading and nouns; we must determine the actual meaning of each sentence, and change them to state that meaning more directly:

blockquote.emphasis: The pre-accession process constrained political competition in all 10 cases because the EU took a one-size-fits-all approach to Eastern enlargement. For this reason, we should determine whether that process affected different party systems differently.

section.para: It is not easy to change the construction “it is instructive” into a strong verb without knowing exactly what the author had in mind; the attempt here is just one way of doing it.

Notice again that these two new sentences both have a straightforward subject-verb-object structure. They are far simpler and more direct than the original sentence, and the meaning of the new sentences is much clearer. We can see that in .

td.emphasis: While the constraining effect of the pre-accession process on political competition was universal across all 10 cases as the EU applied a one-size-fits-all approach to the Eastern enlargement, it is instructive to determine the extent to which the pre-accession process had a differentiated effect on different party systems.

The pre-accession process constrained political competition in all 10 cases because the EU took a one-size-fits-all approach to Eastern enlargement. For this reason, we should determine whether that process affected different party systems differently.

section.para: The original sentence has 48 words, and the revised one has 34. That’s a 30% reduction, and the new sentence is much clearer.

In the three examples that required significant rewriting, our reduction in word count hovered around 30%. That’s nearly a third of the original writing that was not only bloating the sentence but also making it harder to understand.
It can be a difficult skill to learn, but we should try to take this same approach to our own writing. Clarity is the goal.

section.title: Revising Paragraphs
section.para: We discussed paragraphs in . A paragraph is a logical collection of sentences organized around some theme. We also learned about the uneven “U” model of paragraph structure.

section.title: Revise with the Uneven “U”
section.para: The best way to think about paragraph-level revision is according to the uneven “U” shape. We can test our paragraph structure by assigning each sentence a number based on its level of detail. Many good paragraphs begin with a medium level of detail before getting into specifics and then finish with a broader statement of how that material connects to other aspects of a work. If we find that most of our paragraphs have an uneven “U” shape, we’re on our way to using paragraphs effectively. If we don’t see that shape, we can revise our paragraphs to follow it.
Remember that not all paragraphs need to follow the uneven “U” shape to effectively communicate a point. The model is a guide for what we want to produce, not a fixed requirement.

section.title: Other Suggestions for Paragraph Revision
section.para: We can also add a few other suggestions for paragraph revision. To check the contribution of each sentence within a paragraph, we can write the point of the paragraph in the margin as a complete sentence. Then we can see how each sentence contributes or doesn’t contribute to that point. If we find material that doesn’t meaningfully add to the point, then we can cut it or move it somewhere else. We may also find that the sentences don’t do enough to support the point. In that case, we will need to add more material.

figure.label: Figure 4.18
figure.title:
Linked threads.
lightwise © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Ropes of many different colors are knotted together.

section.para: Like sentences, paragraphs should be logically connected to each other. There is more than one way to check the logical relationships between paragraphs. We can check the transitions between paragraphs, which may be implicit or explicit, to see whether there is a logical connection. If the words we’ve written don’t suggest an answer to the question, Why does this paragraph immediately follow that one? then we may need to link them more explicitly.

In addition, we can list the point of each paragraph in a list. A comprehensible thread should link them together. Seeing one-sentence descriptions of our paragraphs in a list will help us determine whether we should shuffle paragraphs around or add new ones to fill gaps in the logic.

Finally, revising paragraphs involves decisions about not only individual paragraphs but also larger-scale organization as well. An attentive reader should always know her current position in our writing and how what she is reading contributes to the larger purposes of the work.

We mark a position by using signpostsWords or phrases that mark where a reader is in a narrative and help show the relationships between sentences, paragraphs, and other units; also known as “transitions.” , which connect some piece of writing to the larger whole. Sentence and paragraph transitions are signposts, but on a larger scale, we can consider whole paragraphs to be signposts as well. An introductory paragraph in a chapter or section can explain what that piece of writing contributes to the purposes of the whole work.
Good paragraph revision looks at single paragraphs and groups of them, as well as relationships between paragraphs and even larger units. Organizing those units ties a work together.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 4.19
figure.title:
Improving our writing.
Photo by Frans Van Heerden via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A pile of sticky notes, highlighters, and pencils.

section.para: In this topic, we first covered grammar and word choice. The rules of grammar are usually not very flexible, but decisions about word choice are. Since so many different words could be used to communicate a single idea, our word choice reflects the frame of our messages and stories.

We then focused on revision, learning specific strategies to improve our writing at the sentence and paragraph level. These strategies are not always easy to implement. Writing is thinking, and thinking is difficult. We will not always know exactly what we want to say before we start writing. But during the writing process, we will clarify our thoughts and discover the opinions and stories that we want to share.
Writing is difficult, but it is a skill. We become better by practicing, making mistakes, and revising.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 3. This week, you will read the following topics:

listitem.para: : Narrative—What Happens and Why
: Character—Who It Happens To
: Message—The Meaning Behind the Story

section.para: We’ll dive in deep with stories! We’ll be learning about the most important parts of stories, narrative and character. We’ll also discuss how stories work to send messages beyond their events and characters.

section.title: Narrative: Telling a Story

figure.label: Figure 5.1
figure.title:
Stories.
Photo by Karolina Grabowska via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A stack of books on a stool.

section.para: , , and focused on writing. We learned about sentences, paragraphs, grammar, word choice, revision, and other aspects of the writing process. We also discussed strategies for keeping our writing clear so that others can understand the messages we want to share.

All those subjects were a preparation for the remaining topics, which are about stories. The writing skills we’ve gained will allow us to express our thoughts clearly, but now, we need to learn how stories work. Combining the elements of stories with good writing leads to compelling plots, interesting characters, and audiences that can’t pull themselves away.

section.title: Narrative
section.para: The first topic in this series will deal with narrativeThe sequence of events that unfolds over the course of a story; also known as “plot.”the . A narrative is a sequence of events that unfolds over the course of a story. We also refer to this sequence of events by the term “plot.” A narrative is what happens or what actually takes place in a story. What do the characters do? What happens in the world around them? How do they interact with each other? How do they struggle, win, lose, live, and die? All these questions ask about events in a plot.

The narrative of a story is the story’s heart. In the Harry Potter book seriesRowling, J. K. (1997–2007). Harry Potter [Book series]. Bloomsbury; Arthur A. Levine/Scholastic; Raincoast. for example, the driving narrative across all seven books is the back-and-forth battle between Harry and Lord Voldemort. Behind all the Quidditch, chocolate frogs, and Yule Balls is a set of urgent interactions between Harry and his adversary. J. K. Rowling, the author of the series, created a memorable world of witches and wizards, but the world doesn’t amount to much without the things happening in it. As readers, we care about the world because of the narrative.

The goal of this topic is to understand how narratives work. Future topics will then take up more specific elements of stories, such as characters, hooks, and conflicts. The topics will then show how those elements arise from and contribute to a story’s narrative.

section.title: Narrative Analysis
section.para: At its core, a narrative consists of a set of events. A narrative can comprise a small number of events or may include many spanning millions of years. The events can be broad and world-shaking, such as those in the alien-invasion movie Independence Day,Emerich, R. (Director). (1996, June 25). Independence Day [Film]. Centropolis Entertainment. or they may be local and mundane, like those in George Eliot’s book Middlemarch.Eliot, G. (1871). Middlemarch: A study of provincial life. William Blackwood and Sons. Where there are one or more events, there’s a narrative.

figure.label: Figure 5.2
figure.title:
Narrative events.
iStock.com/Rawpixel Ltd.

imagedata.alt: A whiteboard full of different sizes and shapes of sticky notes that are connected by lines.

section.title: Events
section.para: We keep referring to “events,” but what are those exactly? For our purposes, an eventAnything that happens. is anything that happens. That definition includes almost everything, which is by design because a narrative can be about pretty much anything. Sitting down to breakfast in the morning is an event. The Big Bang is an event. A French baker making loaves of bread on May 3, 1722, is an event. My memory of my seventh birthday party is an event. The history of the United States is a large event composed of many smaller events. We can classify all these happenings and many more as events.

We don’t, however, impose any restriction on how events are related to each other. In most narratives, events clearly connect to each other as the actions of characters move a plot along: I sit down to breakfast, and that causes me to be late for work, which causes me to be fired, and so on. The connections between those events are apparent and make sense; they give backbone to a plot about how I lost my job.

But not all plots contain connected events like those. A narrative could consist of randomly chosen occurrences with no relations to each other. Such a narrative might be incomprehensible and the resulting story bizarre, but it would still be a narrative.

section.title: Causal Connections between Events
section.para: In our course, we’ll focus on narratives in which events have clear connections to each other. These connections won’t always be apparent to the readers, but the authors had them in mind when they were structuring the story and its parts.

The connections between events in our narratives are usually causal connections or involve causal relations. A causal relationThe relation between a cause and its effect. is a relation of cause and effect—we throw a baseball, which causes the ball to travel through the air, which causes it to hit a window, which causes the window to shatter. Each event in that chain is either a cause, an effect, or both. The ball traveling through the air is not the cause of it hitting the window, but an effect of being thrown.

Causal relationships involve events. And because pretty much anything can count as an event, pretty much anything can enter into a causal relationship. Ideas cause people to act, people cause the natural world to change, the natural world changing causes places to evolve, and so on. Causal relationships could include all these entities and many more.

section.title: Narrative Causal Relations
section.para: Narratives involve causal relations—one event causes another, which causes one more, and so on through the chain. We saw some of these connections in section , when we looked at the narrative structure of the Dr. Seuss book The Cat in the Hat.Dr. Seuss. (1957). The cat in the hat. Random House; Houghton Mifflin. Here is that structure again in :

figure.label: Figure 5.3
figure.title: The main events in “The Cat and the Hat.”

imagedata.alt: The main seven events in “The Cat and the Hat.” 1. Too cold to play outside. 2. Cat shows up. 3. Warning from fish. 4. Cat causes a lot of mischief. 5. Fish: “Mom on her way home!” 6. Clean up the mess. 7. Mom gets home and everything is fine.

section.para: Each line of text in this figure is an event, like “warning from fish,” or group of events, like “Cat causes a lot of mischief.” The arrows indicate that the events are connected to each other in some way. Frequently the connection we intend is a causal connection: the Cat showing up causes the fish to issue a warning, which causes the Cat to create even more mischief, and so on. As readers, we readily understand these causal relationships and grasp the narrative easily.

section.title: Other Event Relations
section.para: But a causal relation isn’t the only kind of relation between events. Sometimes, events are simply related temporally, or in time, in that one event precedes another. For example, in the Cat in the Hat, the Cat’s mischief doesn’t cause the children’s mother to come home; she was coming home anyway. The relation between the Cat’s mischief and the mother’s arrival isn’t causal but temporal—the former precedes the latter in time.

The Cat’s mischief, however, does cause the fish to react in a certain way to the mother coming home. The flow of events in The Cat in the Hat thus includes both causal relations and temporal relations: a sequence of events is unfolding over time in the course of the story, and many of those events are causing others to happen.

section.title: Narrative Analyses
section.para: For our course, a narrative analysisAn examination of a narrative’s structure that includes major events in the narrative and their relations to each other. is an examination of a narrative’s structure. We can perform a narrative analysis in many ways, but one of the simplest is to write a flow chart like the one we’ve created for Cat in the Hat. We add key events and then connect them with arrows to show relationships between events. The flow chart from a narrative analysis shows how an entire plot makes sense.
Most narratives will have a natural beginning, middle, and ending. We will discuss these aspects of storytelling in greater detail later.

section.title: A Sample Narrative Analysis
section.para: For now, let’s do another narrative analysis of something a bit more complicated than Dr. Seuss. Our target will be the original Star Wars movie, A New Hope.Lucas, G. (Director). (1977, May 25). Star wars: A new hope [Film]. Lucasfilm Ltd. Since many things happen in this movie, we’ll keep our events at a high level so that we don’t get bogged down in the details. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 5.4
figure.title: The main events in “Star Wars: A New Hope.”

imagedata.alt: The seven main events in “Star Wars: A New Hope.” 1. Leia gives R2-D2 a message. 2. Luke takes R2-D2 to Obi-Wan. 3. Luke and Obi-Wan get a ride from Han Solo. 4. Luke and Han resuce Leia; Obi-Wan dies. 5. Luke, Han, Leia, and others prepare to attack Death Star. 6. Luke succeeds in destroying Death Star. 7. Everyone gets a medal.

section.para: Of course, anyone who’s seen the first Star Wars movie knows that many other things happen than what we’ve listed here. The beauty of a narrative analysis is that it works at the level we need it to. If we’re just interested in major plot events, then the structure we’ve charted here will do. A more thorough analysis would break down each event we’ve listed into groups of smaller events. The event “Luke and Han rescue Leia” involves the three characters plunging into a garbage compactor, narrowly escaping, seeing Darth Vader, and so on. We’ve just chosen not to represent those events here in our narrative analysis.

section.title: Branching Plotlines
section.para: A more thorough analysis of the narrative in A New Hope could also include parallel branches of events that intersect at key points. While Luke and Obi-Wan are meeting Han Solo, Princess Leia is busy being interrogated by representatives of the Empire. Our analysis could represent the interrogation as part of an independent sequence of events. But when Luke and Han meet Leia in the prison, Leia’s branch isn’t independent anymore, and the two sequences merge to drive toward the ending.

Putting together a narrative analysis helps us understand how events in a plot fit together. Watching A New Hope makes us familiar with the events, but analyzing the narrative of the movie forces us to clarify exactly how events relate to each other. In our analysis of Star Wars, some relations are causal and some temporal, but seeing the plot from a high level shows how events drive the narrative forward to create a compelling story.

And if a narrative analysis can help us understand plots from Cat in the Hat to Star Wars, then it’s also going to help us understand the plots we create. We can develop a narrative from scratch by writing down a few key events and seeing how they relate. We can do the same thing when we’re working on a plot we’ve already developed: making a flow chart to analyze our own narratives will help us see where the relationships between events make sense and where they don’t.

section.title: Developing a Narrative: What Happens?
section.para: We can use the core idea behind a narrative analysis to develop a simple narrative. As we’ll see, our human inclination for stories makes coming up with a basic narrative extremely easy.

Compelling stories feature narratives full of great ideas. Movies like InterstellarNolan, C. (Director). (2014, October 26). Interstellar [Film]. Paramount Pictures; Warner Bros. Pictures; Legendary Pictures; Syncopy; Lynda Obst Productions. and Fight ClubFincher, D. (Director). (1999, September 10). Fight club [Film]. Fox 2000 Pictures; Regency Enterprises; Linson Films. or books like The Way of KingsSanderson, B. (2010, August 31.) The way of kings. Tor Books; Gollancz. and FrankensteinShelley, M. (1818, January 1). Frankenstein. Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor & Jones. draw us in with awesome, mind-bending possibilities; more cerebral works, like Howards EndForster, E. M. (1910, October 18). Howards end. Edward Arnold. and I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings,Angelou, M. (1969). I know why the caged bird sings. Random House. dive into the depths of human psychology and experience. What all these stories have in common is a narrative in which one interesting idea is connected to another and another in a chain linking characters, settings, and events together.

section.title: Connecting Events

figure.label: Figure 5.5
figure.title:
Connecting events.
iStock.com/alexsl.

imagedata.alt: A blackboard with several shapes drawn on it that are connected by various lines.

section.para: When we turn to the stories we want to tell, we may feel intimidated by the great works we know, thinking that no idea of ours will ever be as good as those. But as readers, we only see the finished product—the great battles, triumphant characters, and immortal victories. We must remember that all compelling stories started in the same way: as a single idea in the mind of an author. The author then built out that idea into a connected narrative, one piece at a time. Compelling stories don’t spring from an author’s mind fully developed and ready to sweep an audience away through imagination. Great ideas take time.

And the more sophisticated the plot, the more time an author must spend developing the narrative. The books in the series A Song of Ice and FireMartin, G. R. R., (1996–2011). A Song of Ice and Fire [Book series]. Bantam Books; Voyager Books. feature hundreds of named characters from dozens of families inhabiting a living, detailed world. This world and its narratives took years to create, and the author of the series, George R. R. Martin, must have vetted and discarded countless ideas before he was left with the best ones for his books.

We want to focus on simpler plots in our course, so we’ll leave such sophisticated narratives aside for now. But the simpler narratives we deal with here can reach the heights of any epic if given enough work and time.

section.title: Begin with an Event
section.para: Developing a narrative starts with an event. We then take that event and pair it with a second, third, and fourth. Done! Narrative created. Now, the plot we develop at first may not be the most compelling tale ever to see print, but creating a basic narrative really is that easy. Our minds can even make connections between events that seem totally unrelated.

section.title: Story Dice
section.para: Our ability to make these connections is the basis for a game I play with my children. They’ve got some “story dice,” or a set of six-sided dice where each face has an image of a different object. The dice show things like swords, birds, cars, waterfalls, and other objects. The game is easy to play: all we do is roll the dice and then start making up a story. Each face showing on a die gives us an event in the narrative.

The fun of the game is in connecting events that seem to have little to do with each other. For example, I might roll a tree, an airplane, a diamond, and a fish. It takes no effort at all to tell a story involving events with those objects. We’ll refer to it as “Story A.”

blockquote.emphasis: Once upon a time, there was a large tree standing on a hill. The tree proudly overlooked the village below. Unfortunately, an airplane crashed into the tree one day. This started a landslide, which destroyed the village and all its people. There was a silver lining for the search-and-rescue teams, however, because the landslide uncovered a diamond mine that had been hidden in the hillside. All the first responders at the village that day became rich. One of them used his money to buy an exotic fish, which promptly died one day when he forgot to feed it.

section.title: Story Dice Narrative Structure
section.para: The narrative structure for this goofy story is simple. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 5.6
figure.title: Main events in “Story A.”

imagedata.alt: The five main events in “Story A.” 1. Airplane hits tree. 2. Landslide destroys village. 3. Diamond mine discovered. 4. Everyone is rich. 5. Fish dies.

section.para: Our analysis hits on the major events of the story. But the dice roll I made could go in a completely different direction, either by introducing different events or by taking the objects in a different order. Here’s a new story formed by taking the latter approach. We’ll refer to it as “Story B.”

blockquote.emphasis: Once upon a time, there was a diamond smuggler. He had hidden his diamonds in the lining of his jacket so they wouldn’t be discovered. On his flight across the ocean, the plane had mechanical troubles and was forced to make a water landing in the middle of the sea. The passengers survived by floating on large branches of a tree they found in the plane’s cargo hold. The smuggler’s jacket was heavy from the diamonds, though, and because he refused to remove it, he sunk to the bottom of the ocean. As he descended, one passenger said to another, “The diamond smuggler sleeps with the fishes.”

section.para: It’s hard to tell whether this story is more bizarre than the first, but it’s still easy to analyze the narrative. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 5.7
figure.title: Main events in “Story B.”

imagedata.alt: The four main events in “Story B.” 1. Diamond smuggler boards plane. 2. Plane lands in sea. 3. Smuggler refuses to ditch jacket. 4. Smuggler meets his end.

section.para: This story uses the same objects as the first but arranges them differently and introduces other objects to create new events and a new narrative. Even with such a small number of objects, the possibilities are infinite.

section.title: Filling in the Gaps
section.para: The fact that children can play the story dice game tells us something about narratives. Humans are so naturally inclined to stories that they can tell them with ease. Our imagination has no problem filling in the gaps between superficially distant events, like a tree and a plane. A single sentence is sufficient to connect them, and once the gap is closed, a narrative thread can run through it.

The compelling stories we mentioned at the start of this section probably didn’t come from story dice. But they did start small, with just one or two key events as the seed of the story. The authors then connected those events to others, refined the ideas, and ended up with a working narrative.

section.title: Ideas Are Cheap
section.para: Before moving on, we should note another lesson of the story dice: it is easy to generate ideas. A single roll of the dice could lead to a dozen stories in a single sitting. Similarly, a room of science-fiction fans could fill a blackboard with a hundred story ideas in ten minutes.

The point is that ideas are cheap. Sure, compelling stories have interesting ideas, but even interesting ideas are cheap—we can come up with many of them. The difference between a good story and a great story may not be in the quality of the original ideas but in how skillfully they were executed. Other topics in our course will cover the storytelling elements we need to turn narratives into living, breathing stories.

The cheapness of ideas isn’t scary but inspiring: it means that we don’t need to be creative geniuses to tell a good story. All we need is knowledge, effort, and time to turn a fledgling idea into something that other people want to hear.

section.title: Developing a Narrative: Why?
section.para: Let’s look again at “Story B” from section . We’ll focus on the events shown in from our previous narrative analysis.

figure.label: Figure 5.8
figure.title: A closer look at “Story B.”

imagedata.alt: A closer look at two main events in “Story B.” 1. Diamond smuggler boards plane. 2. Plane lands in sea.

section.para: The story doesn’t tell us whether these events are causally connected. That is, we don’t know whether the diamond smuggler boarding the plane had anything to do with the plane’s mechanical problems; maybe it was pure coincidence that the smuggler’s plane had troubles that day.

section.title: Coincidence? I Think Not
section.para: Then again, maybe it wasn’t a coincidence! If the arrow represented some causal connection between these events, then there would be a reason why the plane wasn’t working, and the reason would involve the smuggler: maybe a secret diamond cabal is out to get his gems, or the passengers found out about the smuggling. Going beyond a temporal connection between these events to link them causally opens up brand-new avenues for narrative development and storytelling.

More broadly, for each pair of events in our narrative analysis, we can ask, Why are these events connected? This question seeks a reason why one event follows another. Sometimes the answer to this question uncovers a mundane causal connection that doesn’t deepen the narrative—for example, the plane’s mechanical troubles cause it to land in the sea, but that connection only gives the background circumstances for the story rather than revealing a new aspect of it. The question above will uncover other connections, which will become part of the narrative we want to tell.
We can also ask this question of a single event in our narrative. shows the first event from “Story A” in section :

figure.label: Figure 5.9
figure.title: A closer look at “Story A.”

imagedata.alt: A closer look at “Story A.” 1. Airplane hits tree.

section.para: About this event, our story only said, “Unfortunately, an airplane crashed into the tree one day.” But why did the airplane crash into that particular tree, which just happened to overlook a village that just happened to lay at the base of a diamond mine? It can’t be just a coincidence, right? The event demands an explanation, and the explanation will deepen the story by connecting events in non-obvious or surprising ways.

section.title: Why Might These Events Be Connected?

figure.label: Figure 5.10
figure.title:
Event about the airplane.
Photo by Isabella Mendes via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: The underside of an airplane against a white background.

section.para: Asking, Why are these events connected? encourages us to develop connections between them that make sense. But we don’t want these connections only to make sense—we want them to make sense in an interesting and attention-grabbing way. Working toward interesting connections in our narrative makes our stories compelling and drives audiences to keep reading to find out what will happen next and why.

Now, as the story dice taught us, we can link up any two events in any way we want. Some connections make more sense than others, though, and lead to more interesting possibilities with a story. Take our event of the airplane hitting the tree. Here are two possible explanations for that event:
section.blockquote: Explanation 1: The pilot thought the tree was a mint-flavored icicle that had been placed upside-down on the hilltop. He loves mint, so he went for it.

Explanation 2: The plane was sabotaged by a secret diamond cabal that is working to monopolize diamond production throughout the world. The cabal also already knew about the diamond mine near the village.

section.title: Better, Richer Connections
section.para: What makes the second explanation better than the first? For one, it simply makes more sense than the first. Mint-flavored icicles aren’t likely to be very common, and ones large enough to sit atop a hill and be visible from a plane are probably even less likely. The first explanation raises several other questions that seem a little silly and don’t have anything to do with the rest of the story.

That’s another reason why the second explanation is better than the first: the second makes more meaningful connections to other events in the story. The story involves diamond mining and getting rich, and of the two explanations for the plane crashing into the tree, only the second one has obvious relationships to those other events. As a result, the second explanation raises many more narrative possibilities than the first.

Asking, Why? about the events in our narrative pushes us to consider the reasons why things are happening. Why did this event take place? Why were things set up that way? Who could have wanted that outcome, and why? Not all our answers to these questions will make it into our story. Many questions will just fill in the background details of our story. Plus, authors don’t need to share every detail. But the presence of the details in the mind of an author will drive narrative connections that have comprehensible, meaningful explanations. At least some of those explanations will have an impact on the story.

section.title: Narratives that Make Sense
section.para: In developing our stories, one of our primary goals is to see that the narrative makes sense. A narrative makes sense when the connections between its events make sense. We should note, though, that authors have no responsibility to make a narrative make sense from the beginning throughout an entire story. Some of the best stories make readers wait until the final page or even the final sentence before dropping the last piece to the puzzle. Authors can build all sorts of traps and false leads to trick readers into thinking they know what’s happening before finally revealing the crucial piece of information at a climactic moment.

Useful connections between events make a narrative coherent (everything fits together well) and consistent (there are no contradictions or inexplicable developments). Let’s consider an example of an event and an explanation that could go either way.

section.title: Another Example: The Lonesome Cowboy
section.para: Imagine that we’re writing a western about a cowboy and his search for his missing father. One of the key developments in our narrative involves the cowboy waking up late one night to shining lights outside his tent. He walks outside, passes the dying embers of his fire, and sees that an alien spaceship has landed. The alien then boards the ship and flies away.

figure.label: Figure 5.11
figure.title:
Lonesome cowboy.
Photo by Phinehas Adams via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A cowboy surrounded by a cloud of dust.

section.para: For most western-themed stories, an alien spaceship isn’t going to make much sense. It raises even more questions than the mint-flavored popsicle. Why are the aliens there? Where did they come from? Why do they have a map to the cowboy’s father?

When an author doesn’t at least try to answer some of these questions, the result is an incoherent narrative where things happen for no apparent reason. Continuing the story after the aliens as though nothing unusual had happened would have most readers wondering what’s going on.

On the other hand, the alien event could go another way entirely with the proper explanation and connection to other events. Maybe the aliens were the ones who kidnapped the cowboy’s father and are leading the cowboy into a trap. In this case, the aliens would be a more central part of the story, so the author would be able to give reasonable, if fantastical, explanations for their role in the story.

section.title: Unusual Events Require Greater Development
section.para: This example teaches us an important principle about narrative development. In most narratives, the more unusual an event is, the greater the role it must occupy in the story in order for the narrative to make sense. A completely random and never-revisited alien encounter in a western is totally out of place, but an alien encounter in a western involving aliens may make plenty of sense.

An event or event connection is incongruent if it doesn’t make much sense given the events preceding it in the narrative. In general, the more incongruent an event or connection is, the more central it must be to the overall story in order for everything to fit together.
All these points were prompted by taking a simple narrative and asking, Why? That’s a powerful question for developing and connecting the events in a story.

section.title: Narrative Failure

figure.label: figure 5.12
figure.title:
Narrative failure.
Photo by cottonbro via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman leans back in a chair with a book over her face.

section.para: To finish this section, let’s talk about a narrative failure—a failure of things to make sense. It’s an example that leaves viewers wondering why and even asking questions about other events in previous movies.

In Star Wars: The Last Jedi,Johnson, R. (Director). (2017, December 9). Star wars: The last Jedi [Film]. Lucasfilm Ltd. the heroic Resistance is fighting the evil First Order. At a key moment of the movie, the Resistance attacks a First Order stronghold by accelerating one of its spaceships to light speed and then slamming it into the structure. The structure is destroyed, and the Resistance lives to fight another day.

A ship ramming at light speed is somewhat incongruent in the context of this individual movie, and it’s a surprising moment for viewers. But the event is even more incomprehensible in light of previous Star Wars movies. Earlier films featured battles to defeat a large space station called the Death Star, and many soldiers died in siege attempts against the station. If it were possible to destroy an entire structure by simply accelerating an empty ship to light speed and ramming, why didn’t the previous heroes simply defeat the Death Star that way? But that exact event happened in The Last Jedi, raising questions about why so many soldiers needed to die earlier when the answer to the Death Star was so simple.

Narratives can fail when their events are incongruent and never explained. The more reasonable and interesting connections we make between events in our narrative, the more compelling our story will be. Developing a narrative involves asking, Why? and then filling in the answers with creative, coherent explanations.

section.title: Setting the Stage: Where?
section.para: Future topics will return to more specific issues in narrative development. For now, we’ll conclude this topic with a word on the setting of a narrative.

section.title: Setting

figure.label: Figure 5.13
figure.title:
A collection of maps.
Photo by Andrew Neel via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A pile of maps.

section.para: The settingThe place where an event happens. for an event is the place where the event happens. The setting is sometimes vague. For example, in our story about the smuggler’s plane crashing, the final setting is anywhere in the ocean. Our setting is only slightly more specific in the alien western. Other settings could be much more specific, like a certain town or even a single street in a town. A setting is as vague or as precise as it needs to be, depending on the story.

For the purposes of our course, the key to choosing and designing a setting is that the setting contributes to the narrative in a way that makes sense with the rest of the story. For example, the only proper setting for a Star Wars movie or book is some galaxy far, far away because nothing like the events in that series could happen in our actual galaxy. The correct setting for a western is usually the American West or someplace similar to it.

Having a setting that is coherent with the rest of the story does not mean that the setting doesn’t create conflicts for the characters living there. For example, suppose we’re developing a story about a free-spirited rebellious teenager living in Amish country in Pennsylvania. Such a setting doesn’t fit at all with the character, but that might be the point—the story could follow the teenager and her struggles against a traditional way of life. The tension between the setting and other aspects of the story drives the narrative.

Like any other aspect of a story, settings make much more sense given the rest of our narrative. It may help to consider a story’s setting as one of its events, or series of events, that we must keep coherent with everything else.

section.title: Your Brain on Narrative
section.para: Perhaps the most powerful aspect of narrative is that it taps into the ways that our brain is already organizing information. We understand ourselves as the central character in the story of our life—we are the main character, the hero, the villain, around whom everything else revolves. Our memories are stories that form the background for our lives and give us reference points to understand our current experiences, which are the plot points in an ongoing story. Likewise, our future is the pages we haven’t turned to yet, full of the unexplored possibilities of events that are still to come.

New research in neuroscience is urging the continued use of stories as ways of discovering how people understand and experience narratives of all kinds and sizes. Both this understanding and experience happen through the brain. As authors Lewis Mehl-Madrona and Barbara Mainguy put it, in their article “Neuroscience and Narrative”:

blockquote.para: A specific brain circuit exists to create and comprehend story. This circuit generates simulations or small stories, mostly about the important people in our lives and about ourselves. . . . People are fundamentally narrative, whether or not they are conscious of the stories they generate. Memory is fundamentally flawed with gaps that are filled at recall to fit the needs of the situation for which our story is being told. Life may be more fiction than we have previously realized.Mehl-Madrona, L., & Mainguy, B. (2021). Neuroscience and narrative. Anthropology of Consciousness, 33(1), 79–95.

section.para: To the extent that life is fiction, the stories we tell our audiences will be able to shape those fictions, as the narratives we create become part of the narratives that our audiences experience. Narratives “tap into the brain’s native machinery for representing the world.”Willems, R. M., Nastase, S. A., & Milivojevic, B. (2020). Narratives for neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences, 43(5), 271–273. Our narratives will have this power, when we learn to construct them correctly.

Although humans have been understanding their lives and their communities in terms of stories for longer than we have written records, we are just beginning to glimpse the powerful effects that stories have on our brains. This new knowledge can help us shape our stories to send the messages we want our audiences to receive in the form of narratives.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 5.14
figure.title:
Narrative.
Photo by Leah Kelley via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman holds a book in front of her face.

section.para: A narrative is a sequence of events that unfolds over the course of a story. We can use the method of narrative analysis to discover the structure of any story. In most stories, events are causally connected to each other, and the causes and effects in a story make up the narrative.

The best narratives feature events that make sense together—they are causally connected in interesting, comprehensible ways. To develop such narratives, we begin by figuring out what will happen in our stories. Then we begin connecting one event to another, creating a chain of interconnected developments.

section.title: Characters
section.para: Events aren’t the only things that matter for our narratives. Events happen to things—to people, animals, places, and other objects. Broadly speaking, the object in a narrative that makes events happen or that events happen to is called a characterThe entity in a narrative that makes events happen or that events happen to. .

The Cat and the HatDr. Seuss. (1957). The cat in the hat. Random House; Houghton Mifflin. involves characters like the two children, the fish, Thing One and Thing Two, and the children’s mother. In the movie The Lion King,Allens, R., & Minkoff, R. (Directors). (1994, June 15). The lion king [Film]. Walt Disney Pictures; Walt Disney Feature animation. characters include Simba, Simba’s parents, Nala, Scar, Timon, and Pumbaa. In Ernest Hemingway’s book The Old Man and the Sea,Hemingway, E. (1952). The old man and the sea. Charles Scribner’s Sons. the fisherman Santiago and the fish he catches are characters.

section.title: Characters Can Be Anything

figure.label: Figure 6.1
figure.title:
Settings as characters.
Photo by Emiliano Earano via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An ocean wave.

section.para: As we’ll see in the following sections, characters don’t even need to be living things; we could consider the ring in the fantasy series The Lord of the RingsTolkien, J. R. R. (1954–1955). The Lord of the Rings [Book series]. Allen & Unwin. to be a character because it drives so much of the plot through its interactions with other characters. Similarly, we might think of the sea in The Old Man and the Sea as a character as well. Many other settings could be characters—the arenas in The Hunger GamesCollins, S. (2008–2010). The hunger games [Book series]. Scholastic Press. actively cause events, and the human characters must work against the arenas to escape with their lives.

Events without characters are empty, stale descriptions of what happens in the world. Characters without events are vague images of objects that never act, change, or experience anything. Events and characters work together to fill out a narrative: through events, we understand what happens, and through characters, we understand why it matters.

This topic will cover the basics of characters as components in a narrative. We’ll discuss what characters are and how they should act, the points of view a story can take on a character, and how to build living characters that hop off the page and into real life.

section.title: Characters: Anyone and Anything
section.para: Anything can be a character in a narrative. The Emoji MovieLeondis, T. (Director). (2017, July 23). The emoji movie [Film]. Columbia pictures; Sony Pictures Animation. features emojis. In Inside Out,Doctor, P. (Director). (2015, May 18). Inside out [Film]. Walt Disney Pictures; Pixar Animation Studios. the main characters are different emotions, and Bee MovieSmith, S. J., & Hickner, S. (Directors). (2007, November 2). Bee movie [Film]. DreamWorks Animation; Columbus 81 Productions. focuses on bees.

figure.label: Figure 6.2
figure.title:
Anything can be a character.
iStock.com/Pogonici.

imagedata.alt: Many strings coming together to form a profile.

section.title: Characters: Objects in Stories
section.para: Of course, the movies we just named were aimed at children, but that doesn’t matter. Any object can be a character in a story, depending on how the author sees the events in the narrative unfolding. Those events may be happening to a character, or the character may be more actively causing those events to happen. Most characters experience a mix of both.

section.title: Characters Connect Emotionally with Audiences
section.para: Characters are the emotional link between a narrative and an audience. Audiences experience events in a narrative through the eyes and ears of the characters. As audience members, we imagine ourselves in the shoes of someone we are reading about or watching—we see what they see and feel what they feel, if only a little bit. This connection between characters and audiences allows a narrative to evoke powerful emotional responses even in relatively simple stories.

Characters also help a narrative answer questions about why certain events matter. The plane crash in our story matters because it happens to people, real people that we meet over the course of a story. We identify with the characters and their experiences and insert ourselves into the story, even if we are very different from the characters.
Let’s look at a brief example.

section.title: Characters and Emotion in The Lion King
section.para: The Lion King is an animated movie about a lion cub prince whose father is killed in an accident. The cub, Simba, abandons his family in order to escape his past and begin a new life elsewhere. But his old life catches up with him when he is discovered by his old friend Nala. Together, they return to face his father’s true killer so that Simba can take his rightful place as king.

figure.label: Figure 6.3
figure.title:
Lions.
Photo by Mariska De Beer via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Two lions in nature.

section.para: The events in The Lion King have such great emotional power because audiences identify with the characters. Simba loses a family member and seeks to run from his grief; his bereaved family searches for him without knowing whether he will return; he faces a choice between living the way he knows he should or forever escaping the real world in favor of a life full of triviality. The experiences Simba has are not unique to a particular sex, gender, race, or location. They are human experiences. Many people have had them, and many more know that they will. Simba and other characters become the lenses through which we live or relive these challenging aspects of human existence.

section.title: A Nature Documentary on Lions
section.para: Now compare The Lion King to a nature documentary about lions, filmed simply by setting up cameras in the African bush. The footage may show many events similar to those in The Lion King, such as the death of a lion, battles between different animals, and natural disasters. But the lions in a documentary are not depicted as characters; they are just nameless animals doing what animals do. Some people may have an emotional response to some events, but for most people, the absence of characters severs their emotional connection to the narrative.

The documentary about lions is a good example of an empty description because there are no characters. Things happen to the lions, and the lions cause other things to happen in turn. But unless the story treats them as characters, all the documentary will show is a chain of anonymous causes and effects.

section.title: From a Documentary to a Story
section.para: Now imagine that we wanted to turn the documentary into a story. Where would we begin? A great place would be to choose one or two lions as characters in the film. The new documentary might end up depicting very similar events, but by following a few characters in particular and describing events as they affect and matter to those particular lions, we’ve given audiences an emotional anchor in the story. Because the events in the documentary are happening to particular lions, audience members will have a more powerful way of connecting to the story.

There are many differences between The Lion King and a nature documentary about lions. But for storytelling purposes, the biggest difference is that the animated movie treats its lions as characters whose points of view and life experiences matter. Events take place, and the story describes them, but it does so by showing how those events affect the characters. The characters are a specific window to the chains of causes and effects in the narrative.

Treating lions, rocks, emojis, people, or anything else as characters involves less of what happens and more of how the story is told. The very same events can be part of a documentary or a story, depending on the way they are depicted.

section.title: Characters Establish a Point of View
section.para: There are many ways to treat objects in our stories like characters. The simplest one is to tell the story from a certain point of view. We can also give characters names, show what they are like, describe their background, and display their values, beliefs, and fears.
