Objects treated in this way become characters in our stories and transform a mere sequence of events into a meaningful narrative.

figure.label: Figure 6.4
figure.title:
Point of view.
Photo by Skitterphoto via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Binoculars sitting on a case.

section.para: There is no best way to depict characters. The choices we make depend on the story we want to tell and what messages our story communicates. In Cormac McCarthy’s book The Road,McCarthy, C. (2006, September 26). The road. Alfred A. Knopf. for example, the two primary characters are a father and a son. But McCarthy never gives them names—they remain nameless throughout the entire story. Nevertheless, the narrative is still gripping in its emotional impact, perhaps even more so because the characters are not named: they are anonymous people, so any one of us could easily have been them.

Depicting a narrative’s events through the lens of characters also helps link the events in believable ways. In , we discussed the importance of connecting events in reasonable and interesting ways. Cause and effect relationships do this, but so do characters. A single character’s experience of two seemingly random events may be enough for the events to make sense together.

section.title: Representing Characters as People
section.para: So far, we have observed that anything could be a character in a story, from an emoji to a lion to anything else. It is important to see that we can treat all these objects as characters because we represent them as people, or at least, we represent them as having certain humanlike abilities, thoughts, and reactions. Lions cannot talk, but they do in The Lion King, and bees feel no affection for others, but they do in Bee Movie. These objects become characters when authors make them human enough that humans can understand them. The technique of making nonhuman objects have humanlike qualities in order to treat them as humans in a story is called A literary technique in which a nonhuman object is portrayed as having humanlike qualities. personification .

section.title: Main and Secondary Characters
section.para: We can divide characters in a narrative into different groups. A main characterThe character or characters who figure most prominently in a story. figures most prominently in a story, and the story is primarily about them. A secondary characterThe character or characters who play minor or only incidental roles in a story. includes anyone or anything else that plays a role in the story.

section.title: Protagonist and Antagonist

figure.label: Figure 6.5
figure.title:
Protagonist and antagonist.
Photo by Anna Shvets via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Two women standing back to back.

section.para: Another name for the main character in a story is the protagonistThe main character or one of the main characters of a story. . The protagonist usually makes the key choices, experiences the key events, and deals with the key consequences once the dust has settled. In most narratives, the story is told from the protagonist’s point of view, and events are understood in terms of how they affect or change the protagonist.

Opposed to the protagonist is the antagonistThe character in a story who opposes or provides the chief conflict for the protagonist., the character against whom the protagonist struggles. The antagonist is the enemy and tries to destroy the protagonist or cause some other kind of harm. Although the antagonist is a central character in a story, they may not receive as much attention as the protagonist, and the antagonist’s own point of view may be entirely absent. Many stories include direct confrontations between the protagonist and the antagonist.

It is not the case that the protagonist is always “good” and the antagonist is always “bad.” These terms do not refer to moral evaluations of the characters’ actions but instead to the way the story is told and to the role the characters play in the narrative.

section.title: Active and Passive Characters
section.para: Other ways of thinking about characters include classifying them as active or passive. An active characterA character in a story who drives events forward by their actions or who causes events to happen. drives events forward by actions and is the cause of other events; a passive characterA character in a story who is more likely to let things happen or passively experience what is going on around them. is more likely to let things happen.
Characters are emotional anchor points for audiences. They transform mere sequences of events into meaningful narratives.

section.title: Point of View
section.para: Section hinted at different points of view that a story could take on based on its characters. Let’s discuss these points of view in greater detail.

No story can tell about every aspect of every event in the narrative. There would simply be too much information. Limiting a story to showing how events affect specific characters sets a limit on what information the story will contain.

section.title: Focusing on a Particular Character

figure.label: Figure 6.6
figure.title:
Focusing on a particular character.
Photo by Francis Suera via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man looking through binoculars.

section.para: Choosing to focus on particular characters also has the effect of telling the story through the eyes of those characters. A character becomes a main character when the author devotes more space to that character’s experiences and background. Though the audience doesn’t receive all the information that could possibly be given about the story, what they do receive shapes what they know and dictates what storytelling possibilities are open to the author.

An author can focus on particular characters by using a certain point of view. A point of viewThe position an author takes to describe the experiences of a character, determining such features of a story as the proper pronouns and the information available to the audience at a given time. is a position the author takes on a character. The position determines important features of the story, such as what pronouns the author will use and what information could be available to the audience at any given time.

section.title: An Example Point of View
section.para: Consider, for example, the difference between these two brief passages in a story:

blockquote.emphasis: I rose, pulling the mask off my face and staring the traitor in the eyes. “No, I am Spartacus,” I said.
Spartacus rose, pulling the mask off his face and staring his enemy in the eyes. “No, I am Spartacus,” he said.

section.para: The first passage is written as though Spartacus himself were the author. It uses pronouns like “I” and “my” and presents Spartacus’s take on the action. Spartacus notes, for instance, that he is staring down a “traitor,” but this term may merely reflect Spartacus’s opinion of the person and not an actual fact. This point of view is as though we are inside the head of Spartacus.

The second passage uses Spartacus’s name and pronouns like “he” and “his” to refer to him. The action is presented as a window on Spartacus’s actions but not directly from his own experience. The passage uses the term “enemy” instead of “traitor,” reflecting the fact that the person is a traitor in the eyes of Spartacus alone. This point of view is as though we are watching Spartacus through a camera or binoculars.

section.title: First and Third Person
section.para: These two points of view are called first-person point of viewA point of view in which the author tells a story from inside a character’s own experience, using “I” and “me” pronouns. and third-person point of viewA point of view in which an author tells a story as if the audience were watching that character from the outside, using “he,” “she,” “they,” and “it” pronouns. , respectively. The first-person point of view tells a story from inside a character’s head, as if that character were narrating his experiences to us personally. The third-person point of view tells us a story by following a particular character as if we were watching that character. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 6.7
figure.title: First-person vs. third-person point of view.

imagedata.alt: First-person point of view is an image of a brain with the words “I” and “we.” Third-person point of view shows someone looking through binoculars with the words “he,” “she,” “it,” and “they.”

section.para: First- and third-person points of view not only offer different perspectives on the events of a story but also determine what information the audience can have access to. A story told from a first-person point of view may contain more narration on a character’s thoughts and feelings.

section.title: Third-Person: Limited and Omniscient
section.para: The third-person point of view splits further into two other groups: third-person limitedA third-person point of view in which the author tells a story using only information available to the character whose point of view is being featured. and third-person omniscientA third-person point of view in which an author tells a story using any information the author wishes rather than only the information available to a particular character. points of view. A third-person limited point of view tells a story in the third person from the perspective of a particular character, but it does so by using only information available to that character.

“Omniscient” means “all-knowing,” so a third-person omniscient point of view tells a story in the third person using any and all information an author wishes to include, regardless of whether any particular character would have access to it. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 6.8
figure.title: Limited vs. omniscient.

imagedata.alt: The first panel shows third-person limited point of view. The view comes from one character and shines on other characters. The second panel shows third-person omniscient point of view. The view comes from an eye shining on all characters.

section.para: The difference in available information is more pronounced between third-person limited and third-person omniscient points of view. In the former, the audience experiences the story through a particular perspective without knowing everything about what is happening. In the latter, the only limit on what an audience knows is what the author chooses to share—in principle, the audience could have access to any person’s thoughts at any point of the story.

The three main points of view on characters are first person, third-person limited, and third-person omniscient. Most stories adopt one of these points of view and remain consistent as the narrative unfolds.

section.title: Consistent Points of View
section.para: For most stories, keeping a consistent point of view is better than switching. Switches may occur between chapters or even in the middle of scenes, but we should be careful if we find our points of view jumping around so quickly. Going from a third-person limited point of view on one character to the same point of view on a different character in the next chapter is normal, but a sudden switch to first person or an omniscient perspective is far more jarring and potentially confusing.

Readers normally assume that the narrator—the voice telling the story—is reliable. A reliable narratorA narrator who relates events in the story accurately. gives an audience reliable information—she tells the truth or at least tries to. In some stories, there is an unreliable narratorA narrator who may not be telling the truth about the story’s events; audiences may not be able to trust that an unreliable narrator is reporting what actually happens. —he may not relate the truth to the audience, so the audience cannot trust what he says. We are most likely to find unreliable narrators in literary fiction, but even there, the technique isn’t common.

section.title: Point-of-View Characters
section.para: Some stories depict events from the point of view of a single character the entire time, while others move from character to character across chapters or other sections in order to tell different aspects of the story. Any character whose perspective is adopted for at least part of the story is called a point-of-view characterAny character in a story whose perspective is adopted for at least part of the story. .
Stories may have one or more point-of-view characters, but not every important character needs to be one. The protagonist is usually a point-of-view character, and the antagonist sometimes is.

section.title: Stock Characters: Stereotypes
section.para: So far, we have discussed two important functions that characters play in stories. First, characters give audiences an emotional connection to a story. Second, characters allow the narrative to advance by having the audience experience the events of the story from the characters’ perspectives.

The second of these functions is more basic than the first. In other words, characters must show events from their own perspectives if authors wish to have a story at all, whether or not that character makes a strong emotional connection with the audience.

This means that a story can be successful and even compelling without having interesting, realistic, or well-developed characters. The most basic function of characters is to provide a means for the narrative to move forward. For an author to perform this function with her characters, she doesn't need to spend any energy creating memorable characters at all.

section.title: Stock Characters

figure.label: Figure 6.9
figure.title:
Stock superhero.
Photo by Roy Reyna via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A female superhero flying.

section.para: Stock characters are a common way of pushing a story forward without bothering to explain the characters’ identities or motivations. A stock characterA character who plays a well-defined stereotypical role in a story. is a stereotypical character who plays a well-defined, stereotypical role in a story. Stock characters receive little or no character development because their background and motivations are mostly irrelevant to the story. Stock characters fill certain roles in a narrative, and audiences recognize these characters and roles as soon as they see them.

A related term is “ flat characterA character the author doesn't develop; similar to stock characters. .” In a story, a flat character is one the author doesn’t develop much because there isn’t much to them. That’s why we call them “flat.” The opposite of a flat character is a round character, which we’ll discuss in section .

section.title: Stock Superheroes
section.para: Superheroes are frequently stock characters. In many depictions, Superman is a strong and morally virtuous person who would never do wrong—he’s always fighting crime, looking cool, and saving the day. He’s a stereotypical “good guy” that we can count on to fill a role in whatever situation he’s in. The same is true for Batman, Wonder Woman, and many others. Audiences don’t need to know very much about these characters because the details of their lives don’t matter—they’re there to defeat evil, and that’s what the story is all about.

section.title: Stock Science Fiction
section.para: Another genre with heavy use of stock characters is science fiction. Ideas are the centerpiece of many science fiction works, and events in the narrative are only a means to exhibit the ideas and their consequences. As a result, the characters are only incidental to the development of the ideas, so stock characters suffice. For example, the point of the Stephen Baxter novel RingBaxter, S. (1994, July 4). Ring. HarperCollins. is to develop interesting, scientifically motivated ideas about alternate universes and time travel. Baxter’s plot is secondary in importance to the ideas themselves, and the characters spend pages and pages in conversations that explore the implications of Baxter’s central ideas. The characters are as stock as they come.

section.title: Stock Romance
section.para: Romance movies also rely on stock characters. Most people won’t have trouble accurately envisioning the protagonist of a romantic comedy or drama: it’s the beautiful girl next door, fresh out of college, who’s trying to make it as a writer in New York. The details change from movie to movie, but the important parts are always the same—she’s unlucky in love but has so much to offer! Near the beginning of the movie, in sweeps another stock character, the strong man with alluring eyes who maybe, just maybe, will be the one for her. The details of his life don’t matter either. He’s there to play a role, and you could plug in any tall guy with nice hair, and the story wouldn’t lose anything.

figure.label: Figure 6.10
figure.title:
Stock romance.
Photo by Allef Vinicius via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A man kisses a woman's forehead.

section.para: Broadly speaking, audiences will have fewer emotional connections with stock characters and stereotypes. In other words, stock characters do a poor job of giving audiences an emotional window into a story. When stock characters do have an emotional impact, it is usually due to the role they fill rather than to unique aspects of their personality or individual experiences. Stock characters aren’t really living, breathing, full-blooded people; they’re more like cardboard cutouts with a job to do.

section.title: Advantages of Stock Characters
section.para: But the point of this discussion is not to condemn stock characters or to suggest that authors stay away from them entirely. There are advantages to using stock characters. They’re easy to use, for one, and immediately recognizable by audiences. When they encounter one in a book or movie, audience members will know right away what that character is like and what to expect from them. Authors can rely on an audience’s pre-existing collection of stereotypes in order to avoid the time-consuming work of developing a character, building a backstory, and designing the narrative in a way that allows the backstory to come through.

Stock characters are most useful in well-defined roles in genre-specific works. We drew our examples of stock characters from genres like comic books, romance, and science fiction. It isn’t really a coincidence that we find more stock characters in those domains compared to other genres. All three genres cater to specific audiences with certain expectations about how stories within that genre will develop. Stock characters allow an author to remain well within the audience’s expectations.

section.title: Disadvantages of Stock Characters
section.para: There are also disadvantages to using stock characters, both inside and outside of genre-specific fiction. The most obvious one is that authors lose the opportunity to emotionally connect with their audiences through powerful characters. Not every work will be able to or even want to have that kind of impact, but works of lasting value and acclaim usually have characters that go beyond stereotypes in some way.

Another disadvantage of using stock characters is that a story’s characters just aren’t that interesting. Audiences don’t have infinite patience for stereotypes, even when other parts of a story are promising. Most readers of Peter Hamilton’s The Reality Dysfunction,Hamilton, P. (1996, January 26). The reality dysfunction. Macmillan Publishers. for example, can only take so many girls throwing themselves at the annoying and dimwitted starship captain, Joshua Calvert, before they just put the book down and read something else. Stock characters may risk being not only uninteresting but also unbelievable.

Finally, the stereotypes inherent in stock characters may actually be offensive or harmful in the eyes of some audiences. Including token characters that could be described simply as “the Black man” or “the annoying female boss” plays into larger cultural stereotypes that can be perceived as harmful. It’s better to cut such characters entirely or to spend the time to turn them into real people.
But how do we do that? How do we create a living, breathing person from our imagination? That’s our subject in section .

section.title: Real Characters: Flaws and All
section.para: In section , we noted that stock characters often play roles in genre-specific fiction, like superhero movies. Stereotypical characters can be useful in those roles because the genre itself usually doesn’t demand much depth of characterization in order to tell a story.

But not all genre fiction works that way, and there are excellent examples of works whose characters go far beyond stereotypes. Some of these works take stock characters and flesh them out into real people, which gives the resulting narratives great power.

section.title: Batman, Then and Now

figure.label: Figure 6.11
figure.title:
Batman.
Photo by Lukas Denier via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Batman standing against a wall.

section.para: We will illustrate this point with Batman. In many comic book, television, and animated depictions, Batman is a standard hero fighting crime and saving the day in Gotham City. In particular, the 1960s television series BatmanDozier, W. (Executive Producer). (1966–1968). Batman [TV series]. Greenway Productions; 20th Century Fox Television. is known for its portrayal of the hero as a very basic character with no internal conflicts. In 1960, Batman romped through ridiculous situations to a soundtrack, and audiences knew exactly how to understand the show’s stock characters, including the villains.

But a more recent set of films, The Dark Knight Trilogy,Thomas, E., Franco, L. J., Roven, C., & Nolan, C. (Producers). (2005–2012). The dark knight trilogy [Film series]. DC Comics; Syncopy Films; Legendary Pictures. portrays Batman as much more than a stock superhero. In these movies, Bruce Wayne—the alter ego of Batman—is a tortured, emotional mess who turns to his life as Batman in order to work out personal issues of his own. Batman is no longer a basic hero doing basic things in the way the audience expects. He makes choices that harm himself and others, fails repeatedly, and is not able to resolve every conflict. The character is deeply flawed. His flaws are manifest throughout the films, and his actions as a flawed person have a real impact on the world.

section.title: The Dark Knight: Hero and Villain
section.para: The second movie of the trilogy, The Dark Knight,Nolan, C. (Director). (2008, July 14). The dark knight [Film]. Warner Bros. Pictures; DC Comics; Legendary Pictures; Syncopy. also pairs Batman with a villain whose character is even more tortured than Batman: the Joker. Although his backstory in the trilogy is unclear, the Joker is a psychopathic killer who relates disturbing stories from his childhood that make him, if not an object of sympathy, at least comprehensible.

The battle between Batman and the Joker in The Dark Knight is not a standard story of good against evil in which the roles of “good” and “evil” are played by stock characters that audiences already understand without the movie needing to characterize them. By turning the hero and his nemesis into real people with struggles, conflicts, and difficult feelings, the movie elevates the characters from stock stereotypes into memorable people.

Another term for the kind of character we’re talking about here is “ round characterA character the author spends time developing. .” We call a character “round” because the author has developed their personality and has made them real. There is more to a round character than to a flat one. In The Dark Knight, both Batman and the Joker are round characters.
For Batman, how did this transition take place? What did the movies do to go beyond stock characters? How can we turn flat, cardboard cutouts in our own stories into something more?
We’ll discuss three principles that help turn stock characters into living, breathing people who can make emotional connections with audiences. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 6.12
figure.title: Three principles to turn stock characters into people.

imagedata.alt: Three squares list the three principles to turn stock characters into people. 1. Build out a character's background. 2. Make Characters interesting. 3. Allow characters to grow.
imagedata.fileref: images/230 6.5 Three Principles to Turn Stock Characters into People.png

section.title: Principle 1: Build Out a Character’s Background
section.para: Stock characters can be human beings, but they aren’t really people. They don’t have a full set of life experiences that make them who they are, and since who they are hardly matters in their stories, they don’t need those life experiences either.

Real people, on the other hand—you, me, our friends and family, and everyone else we know—do have these life experiences, and what we’ve experienced makes us who we are. The accumulated experiences strongly, if not entirely, determine how we act and react, what we want and value, and how we relate to other people.

Think about your own life, for example: Have you been bullied? Have you had overbearing parents? Did you win an important competition? Did you face pressure to get good grades? Have you been in one or more harmful relationships? Did you meet the love of your life? Did you miss out on the career of your dreams? Have you had a near-death experience? Did you get that dream job? Have you lost someone close to you? Have you driven away a friend? Have you helped someone through a difficult time?

section.title: Experiences Leave Marks

figure.label: Figure 6.13
figure.title:
Character experiences.
Photo by Suzy Hazelwood via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A pile of black-and-white photos.

section.para: Experiences like these leave lasting impressions on the people who have them. They aren’t just memories, either—these experiences and others may shape a person’s beliefs and actions years or even decades after they happen. These experiences are part of our backgrounds; they contribute to who we are. Our backgrounds are full of both good and bad things that continue to influence our lives, even though we may not want them to.

Over time, the experiences of real people make them who they are. In order for the characters in our stories to go beyond stereotypes, then, our characters must also have experienced a lifetime of pain, joy, regret, and hope. Their experiences will all be in our imagination, but the way those experiences affect our characters will be as real as the way our experiences affect us.

The first principle of real characters is to give them a background. We must understand who our characters are by understanding where they came from. Just as we understand that a person with a troubled childhood thinks and acts in certain ways because of what they’ve been through, our characters will also think and act based on what they have been through.

section.title: Start with the Basics
section.para: Our first idea for a character may not be something about their past, but once we’re interested in designing a character for a story, we should work to fill in details about their life experiences. We can start with some basic questions: Where specifically is this character from? What was her childhood like? What things did she want, love, and fear? What relationships did she have with others?

As our answers to these questions become more detailed, the details will raise other questions that are more specific to the character we’re designing. Suppose we decide our character is from New York City and grew up in the 1990s. The place and time together suggest further questions. What part of the city did she live in? Did she take the subway to school? Did she want to go to college in the city or leave for somewhere else? How did she react to the events of September 11, 2001? The more specific the questions, the more life is injected into a character.

We will build out our character’s background by giving the character a history of realistic experiences. As authors, we tell the narrative of a character’s life, if only to ourselves or in our notes, so that we understand who they are. That narrative can then continue to play itself out as part of the story we want to tell.

section.title: Brainstorming Character Ideas
section.para: We can brainstorm ideas for characters just as rapidly as we can create ideas for plots. Start with a name: Ursula. Where is Ursula from? Indiana. Using Ursula from Indiana, we can then ask some “what if” questions to understand more about her. Basic questions and answers are fine, but strange or unusual ones are better because they make a character more likely to stand out. What if Ursula’s house was infested with spiders when she was growing up, and her parents just never could get rid of them? What if Ursula was a big fan of space but missed the great eclipse of 2017 because she was taking care of a sick sibling? What if her friend had been murdered when they were young, but the murderer was never caught?

Ursula could have experienced all or none of these things. As authors, it’s up to us. But by considering these possibilities and others, we’ll begin to create an actual person whose past influences how she sees the world and how she lives.

section.title: Characters Take Time to Develop

figure.label: Figure 6.14
figure.title:
Characters take time to develop.
Photo by Miguel Á. Padriñán via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A clock drawn in chalk on a chalkboard.

section.para: Like good ideas for plots, good ideas for characters take time to develop. We’ll probably run through dozens or even hundreds of ideas in order to develop fully fledged, fascinating people for our stories. Be patient, and don’t be afraid to move forward by leaving old ideas behind. Just because an idea is our first one doesn’t mean that we can’t discard it in favor of something better.

In our actual stories, not all the details of our characters’ backgrounds will be revealed. But the actions and feelings that do make it in will grow out of the background and will make sense in light of it. The ripples of cause and effect propagate from the past into the events a story actually describes. The audience won’t know everything about the past, but they’ll see the effects of the past in the present.

In building our characters and their backgrounds, we’ll want the causal relationships between events in their lives to make sense as well. It would be unusual, for example, for a person who experienced the loss of her entire family in a house fire to be unaffected by that event later in her life.

section.title: Principle 2: Make Characters Interesting
section.para: The second principle of real characters is to make them interesting. Stories are supposed to launch us into new lives and new worlds, not make us feel like we just spent a day at the office. Interesting characters with unusual features or experiences make for compelling stories.

To think of what would make a character interesting, we can start with interesting people we know in real life. What makes them cool? What parts of their past make us want to sit next to them at parties? Where are they going next week that makes us jealous? Interesting characters in stories can do the very same things or even more.

section.title: Interesting Characters Have Flaws
section.para: Interesting characters also have flaws. Some things are wrong with them—they make mistakes and have to live with the consequences, just like everyone else. Their limitations may also interact in interesting ways with a story’s plot. Suppose that our main character is trying to escape from prison, but he’s blind. That blindness is going to be a big problem and will probably play an important role in the story. But by giving the character an imperfection, we not only make that person more real but also open up narrative opportunities that we couldn’t have seen otherwise.

figure.label: Figure 6.15
figure.title:
Characters have flaws.
Photo by Thiago Matos via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A pile of broken glass that reflects an outstretched hand.

section.para: Perfect characters roll effortlessly through any obstacle, have an answer for any problem, and cause their friends to fall madly in love with them. Perfect characters are so common in some areas of fiction that they are referred to as “Mary Sue” and “Gary Stu.” But perfection is boring, both in real life and in fiction. No one wants to hang out with a Mary Sue or Gary Stu, much less read about one. Real people have flaws, and real characters do too.

section.title: Interesting Characters Have Goals
section.para: Real characters also have interesting goals. While many people in real life just want to survive the day long enough to put on comfy pants and watch Netflix until bedtime, interesting characters in our stories will probably want something more. Maybe Ursula wants to capture all the world’s starfish in order to make a genetically enhanced super-starfish. Maybe she wants to build a time machine to find out who Jack the Ripper really was. Or maybe she’s going to become the world champion in candlepin bowling. All of these are unusual goals that would make a character stand out in a crowd.

As before, the plot will interact with our character’s goals—usually by placing obstacles in their way. Our characters cannot just achieve their goals without any trouble! Interesting goals give us more material for designing compelling narratives because they lead to interesting conflicts.

Interesting things about a character grow at least partially out of their background as well. Their unusual features are part of who they’ve been and who they are now and will shape their future as well.
Readers and viewers want to encounter interesting characters. We should take the time to design them!

section.title: Principle 3: Allow Characters to Grow
section.para: The third principle of real characters is to allow them to grow. Since our characters aren’t perfect people, they will struggle to face their challenges and achieve their goals. That struggle will demand that they become something new and will leave its mark on their personality just like other aspects of their background.

figure.label: Figure 6.16
figure.title:
Allow characters to grow.
Photo by Zac Durant via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A man holding his arm's up in success in the sunlight.

section.para: A selfish, impatient character who is forced to care for sick family members may respond by becoming kinder and more understanding. The narrative may depict him making better choices at the end of the story than he would have made at the beginning. Other changes might be much smaller. Two people who are very different from each other may come to understand each other’s point of view by the end of a story.

Not all the ways our characters grow will be positive either. Dark or painful experiences can transform people in other ways, and a character’s descent toward evil may be the almost inevitable result of what they have lived through.

As always, characters will change in conjunction with events in the plot. Let’s say some event causes our character to become bitter and angry, which causes him to make choices he wouldn’t have made before, which causes new plot events to happen, which then makes him change even more. This example shows how the narrative of our character’s life unfolds just like the narrative of a story. Interesting, evolving characters with backgrounds and lives of their own create an emotional anchor for our stories and impact our audiences.

section.title: Show, Don’t Tell
section.para: So, by now, we’ve put in the time and vetted the ideas to develop interesting characters. Great news! But now what? How do we show our audiences the quality characters we’ve built?

section.title: Tell and Show

figure.label: Figure 6.17
figure.title:
Declan was quiet and shy.
Photo by Katerina Holmes via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A teacher stands at a table where two students are sitting.

section.para: Our story has to communicate information about our characters somehow, and there are many ways to do this. For example, if our main character, Declan, is quiet and shy, our story could contain the following line:

blockquote.emphasis: Declan was quiet and shy.

section.para: That line certainly does the job—it communicates information about Declan and what he’s like. Audiences now know something about him. But there are more effective and interesting ways of doing the same thing. A passage like this one might do it:

blockquote.emphasis: “Declan?” the teacher asked, her eyes burning a hole through his head as he tried to avoid her gaze. “Would you introduce yourself to the class?”

Cheeks flushed red, Declan shakily rose to his feet. “Uh . . . well . . . I . . . I’m Declan,” he said with a stutter. In the empty silence that followed, he risked a glance around the room. Everyone was staring at him, waiting to see if he would continue. He collapsed back to his chair and buried his face in his hands, fighting back tears.

section.para: This passage also communicates that Declan is quiet and shy, but it does so by putting Declan in a situation where these parts of his personality are forced to the surface. We learn about Declan by seeing him act and react to his experiences. We know what kind of person Declan is because we’ve seen him behave in certain ways.

section.title: Showing vs. Telling
section.para: The difference between these two ways of communicating about Declan is the difference between tellingA technique for communicating information about a character by giving descriptions of what that character is like. what our characters are like and showingA technique for communicating information about a character by putting that character in events that bring different aspects of their personality to the forefront. what they are like. We tell what our characters are like by including bare statements of their features, like “Declan was quiet and shy.” We show what our characters are like by creating events where they reveal that information themselves through their own actions.

When our characters show what they are like, the audience experiences their personality, their flaws, and their goals. They come to understand our characters just as they understand people in real life: by coming to know their behaviors.

In communicating information about our characters, we should make an effort to show rather than tell. At a minimum, showing is much more interesting for audiences than telling. But showing also provides a much richer picture of who a person is.

section.title: Showing Shows More
section.para: If we read that “Declan was quiet and shy,” we’ll wonder in what specific ways he is quiet and shy. There are many possibilities. But the passage about Declan’s introduction in class creates a much fuller picture in our minds of what he is like. We also understand much more clearly how Declan will probably react to other experiences he has. Because we were shown something about him, we know much more about what he is like than we would have if we had read sentences just listing his attributes.

Now, telling is sometimes appropriate. Sometimes we learn things about a character by being told in a conversation or in a monologue from the narrator. Telling may not always be bad. It may be more helpful to compare how frequently we are telling or showing in our narrative. If all our story does is tell, it may be time to revisit the ways we communicate information about our characters.

Unfortunately, showing about a character is also much harder than just telling about one. Giving a list of a character’s attributes is easy—we can do it in a single paragraph and move on with the narrative. But showing requires us to set up the narrative in such a way that the events not only push the plot forward but also reveal who the characters are. Designing such a narrative calls for careful thought and practice.

But the payoff is worth it. Audiences learn about the most interesting characters by seeing them live their lives. When our audiences are shown who our characters are, our audiences come to know our characters just as they do real people because the characters are real people.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 6.18
figure.title:
Characters tie the events in a narrative together.
Photo by Francesco Ungaro via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Many knots in many ropes.

section.para: Without characters, events in a narrative are just arbitrary strings of causes and effects. Characters give audiences a perspective on those events, and characters become emotional anchor points in our stories by tying events together through their experiences.

We can take different points of view on our characters, and characters can be stock stereotypes or more like real people. Better-developed characters are more interesting and have a greater chance of connecting with audiences. We develop our characters by building out their backgrounds, giving them interesting strengths and weaknesses, and allowing them to grow. We then communicate this information about them by showing our audience what they are like.

section.title: Using Stories to Communicate
section.para: Authors communicate in many different ways. An office memo, a novel, a tweet, and a movie are all pieces of communication, and in each case, an author hopes to express a message that an audience will understand. An author conveys information in words or other forms with the intention of sending that information to others.

section.title: Communication about Donuts

figure.label: Figure 7.1
figure.title:
New donut policy.
Photo by Sharon McCutcheon via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A close-up of donuts with bright colors and sprinkles.

section.para: In many pieces of communication, the message the author intends to send is right on the surface; the piece wears its meaning on its sleeve, so to speak. If the HR director at our company wants to inform everyone of the new one-donut-only policy, she can send a company-wide email with the subject line “New donut policy.” After a salutation at the beginning, the message can then frankly state the new policy and give the consequences for breaking it. Then the message can end, and nothing else is necessary.

For us, as receivers of that message, there’s no mystery about its meaning. We don’t need to read it over multiple times, wondering about the symbolism or the true goals the author had in mind when she wrote it. We don’t need a degree in literary analysis to decipher it. The message is intended to communicate a new policy and does so by stating the policy. The information the HR director wants to convey is on the surface.

section.title: Other Kinds of Communications
section.para: But not all pieces of communication are like office memos. Sometimes authors wish to communicate a message that goes beyond the literal or apparent meaning of the words. The writer of a movie, for example, may create a narrative that depicts events inside a prison, while in reality, they are using those events to communicate a broader message about injustices in many areas of society. If that were the writer’s true intention, the events in the narrative would be vehicles for a deeper meaning that the film does not spell out explicitly. The film would use elements of a story as a frame for something else.

In other words, storytellers can use the components of stories to communicate something beyond simply the events in their narrative. Stories can be the frame for messages about anything the author likes. More importantly, stories may actually be a more effective way of conveying certain kinds of messages and may have particular power among certain audiences.

section.title: Using Stories to Share Messages
section.para: Using stories to share messages is the subject of this topic. Even though not all stories have underlying messages, we will treat such messages here as important elements of a story. In many professional and organizational settings, we create stories to share a message that is integral to the story and could even be the reason for its existence in the first place. A story can be the frame with which we convey some other piece of information. That information is the message. Its content drives some or all of the narrative, characters, and other elements of the story.

section.title: Messages and Frame
section.para: Any story, message, or other piece of communication is given within a certain frame. Generally, the frame for a communication is how it is presented, pitched, or delivered to its audience. When we say that the frame is how a message is presented, we should understand the “how” to include all of the author’s decisions about packaging the message.

section.title: Frame and Communication

figure.label: Figure 7.2
figure.title:
Ketchup.
Photo by Vova Krasilnikov via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Squirting ketchup on a hamburger.

section.para: Here is a simple example. Let’s suppose that our partner has a habit of making lunch in the kitchen but leaving out all the ingredients and utensils used to make it. This behavior bothers us, and we’d like to do something about it so that it stops.
There are various ways we could approach a conversation with our partner. Here are three different things we could say:

listitem.para: “If you ever leave out the ketchup again, there will be consequences.”
“Please don’t leave out the ketchup again.”
“I feel frustrated when the ketchup is left out in the kitchen. I enjoy the room more when it’s clean and tidy, and ingredients staying out for a while makes it difficult to keep that way.”

section.para: All three of these possibilities communicate the same fundamental message: “I don’t want you to leave out the ketchup any longer.” What’s changed between them is the frame, or the way that the fundamental message is packaged and delivered to its audience.

section.title: Same Message, Different Frames
section.para: The first possibility is dark and a bit of an overreaction. This is a conflict frame. Our partner will receive the message, but the way we’ve delivered it will either intimidate them into compliance or start a fight.

figure.label: Figure 7.3
figure.title:
Different frames.
Photo by Jessica Ruscello via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Many empty colorful picture frames.

section.para: The second possibility is a simple command presented as a request. This is a transparent frame in that we have just stated the content of the message outright without adopting a certain way of communicating it. In many situations, this sort of frame would probably be appropriate.

Note how the frame of the third possibility differs—the fundamental message is the same, but we have presented it with extreme delicacy. We’ve removed all “you” pronouns so that the message doesn’t even directly reference our partner; we’ve spoken only in terms of how a certain situation makes us feel. We haven’t passed any judgment and have issued no condemnation. We might call this approach the therapist frame, for lack of a better description.

section.title: Frame Can Determine How Our Messages Are Received
section.para: In this example, we have packaged a single message in three different ways, or three different frames. Clearly, the frame we choose will have an enormous impact on the way our partner receives the message. In fact, if our partner is already disposed to comply with what we want, then the frame not only influences how our partner will respond but also determines that response. The conflict frame escalates immediately and almost guarantees they will ignore our request or fight back; the transparent frame might be the best bet for success in most relationships, while the therapist frame may have our partner looking at us strangely and wondering why we’re talking like that. These different reactions result from the same core message, presented in three different ways.

Thus, in this situation and in many others, it is not the content of the message that accomplishes the goal of our communication but the frame. It is the method of delivery that causes the message to succeed or fail, not the message itself. In communication, the frame for a message is as important as the message itself and sometimes is all that matters.

section.title: Frame Is Unavoidable

figure.label: Figure 7.4
figure.title:
Story frame.
Photo by Tim Gouw via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Four picture frames with text and images of giraffes.

section.para: We cannot avoid questions of frame in communication. Even the conscious rejection of a frame for a message is itself a frame; the lack of deliberate choice in how to tell someone something is a method of delivery in its own right. Trying to avoid a frame is a frame.

What does all this have to do with stories? The key is that stories can be frames. The story frame is one choice in deciding how to convey a message. Adopting this frame is a live option for our own communications.

Within the story frame, there are many more possibilities, just as there are many ways of communicating a message within the therapist frame. The story frame will shape our message in certain ways, perhaps by highlighting some things and leaving others in the background. Adopting the frame doesn’t automatically give us a clear path for telling a story, but it’s a legitimate method of delivery.
Every message has a frame, but the choice of frame is not always straightforward. Focusing on our audience will help, and we’ll discuss that next.

section.title: Audience and the Story Frame
section.para: The story frame is a possibility for delivering a message. Let’s look at two examples of a message delivered within the story frame, and then we'll discuss how to decide whether this frame is appropriate.

section.title: The Correct Frame

figure.label: Figure 7.5
figure.title:
More of those toys.
Photo by cottonbro via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A child plays with wooden dinosuars.

section.para: Earlier, we imagined an HR director communicating a new donut policy in an email. Normally we’d give that message directly with the meaning on the surface. But what about a story frame? Suppose the director sent an email whose subject was “A cautionary tale,” with the following story:

blockquote.emphasis: Once upon a time, there was a young man who wanted a certain kind of toy. He wanted it so much that he decided to steal it. Later, even though he already had one of those toys, his desire for it grew. He decided to steal more of those toys. And more! When his thievery was through, he possessed all such toys in the land. The townspeople loathed him for his selfishness.

section.para: Anyone receiving this message from the HR director would probably just be confused. It’s clearly a caution about something, but what? What do the toys represent? And is it really that bad to be loathed by all the townspeople if we’ve got all the toys?

section.title: Another Example
section.para: We could also use the story frame to deliver a message to our partner about putting away the ketchup in the kitchen. Imagine saying the following to the person you live with:

blockquote.emphasis: May I tell you the tale of Tina the tidy tilefish? She loved to clean up after herself. After eating, she would dispose of her waste and sweep stray sand particles away. What a special fish!

section.para: Captivating. Who wouldn’t be enthralled by Tina’s adventures? Probably our partner. The story frame isn’t the only one at work here; sarcasm and condescension are shaping this message as well.

As a frame for certain kinds of messages, storytelling can be silly and out of place. The story frame isn’t always appropriate, especially when the message we want to send is short or about a small issue that we could just state directly. But not all messages are like that, and a story frame has the power to expand and deepen a message.

section.title: Religious Writings and Stories

figure.label: Figure 7.6
figure.title:
Religious writing.
Photo by Fatemah Khaled via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An open book next to a candle and a plant.

section.para: Religious writings offer many examples of a story frame used effectively. Jewish traditions recount the experience of a man named Abraham, who late in life became a father to a son, Isaac. God commanded Abraham to kill his son as a test of loyalty. Just as Abraham was about to kill his son, God instructed Abraham not to kill him. Abraham fulfilled God’s commandment because he would have killed his son if God had not told him to spare his life.

The most obvious message of this story involves loyalty to God—even in difficult circumstances. The Jewish author uses the story frame to convey that message. But by using the story frame, the author allows for dimensions of meaning that go beyond a simple statement of what the story seems to be about. Instructing someone to “be loyal to God” makes the same point, but the bare commandment does not allow the depth of interpretation we find in the story frame.
The story-frame strategy can therefore fail completely or powerfully succeed. What makes the difference? How do we decide the appropriate frame for our messages?

section.title: Choosing the Story Frame
section.para: Part of our choice depends on the message itself—the meaning or idea that we want our audience to receive. In the case of donuts and ketchup, the messages are simple and pertain to very limited circumstances. But the message of Abraham’s story deals with an entire way of life and perspective on the world. For a much broader message, the story frame offers possibilities that other frames do not.

There are no perfect rules to match a message and its content to the right frame. Sometimes simple messages may do better with more sophisticated frames, while broader messages could succeed outside of stories. The correct frame for a message is simply whichever one will help the audience best understand our message or best experience the emotional and intellectual impact we want to share.

section.title: Audience and the Proper Frame

figure.label: Figure 7.7
figure.title:
Proper frame for an audience.
Photo by Zhanna Leontyeva via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Many images in many picture frames.

section.para: The audience for our message consists of anyone who will or may receive our message. Our goal is to get those people to receive, understand, accept, and maybe even act on our message. Since they’re the targets, it is the audience and their needs that we must consider when selecting the frame for our communications.

To illustrate the importance of the audience, let’s revisit the donut and ketchup examples from earlier in this section. Let’s suppose that our audience for those messages consists not of one or more adults but of one or more children. All of a sudden, the story frame doesn’t seem so silly or out of place. Stories are effective ways to communicate with children, and in some cases, may be the only way to deliver certain messages. Sure, we’d probably have to revise the stories about the toys and Tina the tilefish, but delivering a message in a story would be a great way to communicate with children.

The only difference between this imaginary scenario and our previous examples is the audience. When the audience changed, a new set of possibilities became viable for the frame. The frame that seemed odd or even condescending for one audience may be perfect for another.

section.title: Learning about Our Audiences
section.para: There is much more to an audience than its age or stage in life. If we’re going to consider audience members in deciding a frame for our message, then the more we know about them, the better. In defining our audience, we’ll want to be as specific as possible. A message about hot vampires in high school will probably target mostly female teenagers, so the needs and wants of female teenagers would be important in determining the message’s exact frame. We will write other messages to far more limited audiences: to a working group at our company, for example, or to a close friend and no one else.

After defining our audience, we must try to understand them and their needs. This subject is important enough that we will cover it in later in this course. For now, we’ll merely offer a few questions that can push us in the right direction as we determine the frame appropriate for our communications:

figure.label: Figure 7.8
figure.title:
Our audiences.
Photo by Daria Lisovtsova via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A crowd of people.

section.blockquote: What are the needs of our audience?
What is the background of our audience?
What are the expectations of our audience with respect to the kind of message we wish to send them?
Does our audience already know us? If they do, what do they think of us?
What interactions have we had with our audience in the past, if any? How might those past interactions influence future ones?
section.para: We won’t always have access to answers for all these questions, but whatever information we have will help us decide the frame for what we want to say. The more information we have, the better chance we have of making a good decision.

Some of the principles we’ve discussed here will help decide whether an audience might be receptive to a story frame. Broader or more sweeping messages, messages with moral importance, and messages to children are good candidates for delivery via story. But it takes careful consideration of the audience in light of the message we hope to send to determine which frame is best.

For the remainder of our topic, we will set aside the question of how to determine whether a story frame is appropriate for some message or some audience. We’ll proceed as though we’ve already made that choice and are deciding how to deliver our message in a story.

section.title: Communicating Messages with Stories
section.para: After we’ve decided on a frame for our message, we must actually cast that message into the frame: we have to write the message according to the rules dictated by the frame. This process isn’t different in principle from the way we construct a message within any other frame. In an earlier example, we considered delivering a message about cleaning the kitchen in a therapist frame. Casting the message in this frame required us to use only first-person pronouns, focus on feelings, and avoid judgment. These techniques kept us within the rules of the therapist frame and shaped our message for a certain purpose.

section.title: Casting a Message into a Story
section.para: The process of castingThe process of creating a story to tell a message beyond the events of the story; involves creating a mapping between parts of the message and elements of the story. a message into a story frame is no different, but it may be more complicated. The rules of the story frame are the elements of storytelling that we learn about in this course: narrative, causal relations, characters, point of view, and more that we’ll learn later. We design a story that uses these elements, but we build the story in such a way that the message we really want to convey—the point of telling the story in the first place—is readily discernible as a natural interpretation of the story.

section.title: Mappings: Connecting Sets

figure.label: Figure 7.9
figure.title:
Connecting two sets.
Viktoriya Kuzmenkova © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Someone draws a line between Point A and Point B.

section.para: We can think of this process as creating a mapping. A mappingA series of correspondences or relations between two sets of things. For the purposes of storytelling, a mapping connects parts of a message and elements of a story so that a story can communicate a message beyond the events in the story. is a series of correspondences or relations between two sets of things. Say we have five friends, for example. A mapping between our friends and their favorite ice cream flavors would be a list of all five people followed by their preferred flavor. We could create a mapping of our friends and their cars, which would pair each person with their vehicle. We could come up with further mappings between our friends and their addresses, their professors, or their other friends.

section.title: Mappings between Messages and Stories
section.para: In the same way, we can begin to cast a message into a story frame by creating a mapping between parts of the message and elements of the story. We can map the main character of our story, for example, to members of our audience. This mapping would mean that the main character represents our audience or that we intend the audience members to understand that they are the main character in the story. The mapping would suggest that actions taken by the main character are actions our audience could take, that consequences faced by the character might also threaten our audience, and so on.

Even simple messages cast into stories will have various parts, so we should begin by considering what is the most important part of our message, or the most fundamental thing we want our audience to understand. We should map that part of the message into elements of a story in a way that allows those elements to be prominent. We don’t want to bury our message in a part of the story that people will ignore or that seems irrelevant. If the message is about warning audiences away from some negative course of action, then we probably don’t want to represent members of the audience as minor characters in the story. The audience probably won’t notice such characters or at least won’t focus on them, so we would fail to convey the message behind the story.

section.title: Examples of Mappings
section.para: Mapping will connect parts of our message to events, characters, and other aspects of our stories. The narrative will unfold in a way that allows the message we’re sending to become prominent. Let’s look at a few examples of how authors have created mappings between messages and stories.

figure.label: Figure 7.10
figure.title:
Grasshopper.
Photo by Pixabay via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A grasshopper clinging to a plant.

section.para: The first story is about ants and a grasshopper, attributed to the Greek storyteller Aesop.Aesop. (1995) The ants and the grasshopper. American Teaching Aids. (Original work published in 1894) A grasshopper spends his summer dancing and singing in the beautiful weather while the ants gather food for the winter. At times, the grasshopper even makes fun of the ants for their work. But when the winter comes, the tables turn because the grasshopper has nothing to eat. The grasshopper begs the ants for food, but the ants refuse and chastise the grasshopper for its irresponsible behavior.

The message behind this story is fairly clear: hard work and planning are important and may even save our lives. The story needs a way of communicating that, so it sets up a series of events in which hard work ends up paying off. The correct attitude about work is mapped to the ant, who experiences the reward at the end; the incorrect attitude is mapped to the grasshopper, who gets a punishment. The story urges the audience members to map themselves to the ants as well in an effort to produce the desired behavior.
The mapping for this story is fairly simple, and so is the moral. The story is as simple as it needs to be to communicate the point.

Our second story is the novel Howards EndForster, E. M. (1910, October 18). Howards end. Edward Arnold. by E. M. Forster. The novel is set in the early 1900s and follows a cast of characters from various parts of English society, including the wealthy Wilcoxes, the cultured Schlegels, and indigent Leonard Bast and Jacky.

The message communicated by Howards End is far more complex than that of Aesop’s ants-and-grasshopper tale, and we cannot summarize it in a single sentence or paragraph. One aspect of it, though, is about the possibility of relationships between people of different wealth classes. Leonard, from the bottom of society, sees himself as a man of fashion and ideas and tries to prove it in various interactions with the Schlegels. His successes and failures and the resulting attitudes toward him held by different members of the Schlegel family send the message that such inter-class relationships are fraught with prejudice and misunderstanding.

Given the more complex message, the mapping between Forster’s message and elements of his novel is correspondingly more complex. Leonard represents poorer classes of people in England and the Schlegels represent wealthier ones. Events in the narrative are designed to explore the different ways in which these classes experience art and high society. In one memorable interaction, Leonard and the Schlegels attend a concert. While the Schlegels enjoy the music, Leonard loses his umbrella, and distress from thoughts of his missing possession distract him from the concert. Forster begins the following chapter by reflecting on the novel’s message and on the mapping he has created to carry it out: “We are not concerned with the very poor. They are unthinkable, and only to be approached by the statistician or the poet. This story deals with gentlefolk, or with those who are obliged to pretend that they are gentlefolk.”Forester, E. M. (1921). Howards end. Vintage Books, 45. (Original work published in 1910)

figure.label: Figure 7.11
figure.title:
Gulliver’s Travels.
Photo by Daan Mooij via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A model village on rocks.

section.para: The final example we’ll discuss here is the book Gulliver’s Travels,Swift, J. (1726, October 28). Gulliver’s travels. Benjamin Motte. written by Irish author Jonathan Swift in 1726. The main character of the book is Lemuel Gulliver. Swift uses the first-person point of view to write as Gulliver and to recount his “travels” in such places as Lilliput, Brobdingnag, and the Land of Houyhnhnms.

Gulliver’s destinations and his interactions with the locals are all imaginary, and the audience easily understands them to be so: Lilliput is inhabited by people less than six inches tall, the Brobdingnagians are giants, and the Houyhnhnm characters are talking horses. All this silliness is intentional because Swift’s book is a satire of English society, government, and philosophy.

Besides being an interesting example of storytelling, Gulliver’s Travels teaches us a lesson about the importance of the audience in sending messages. Both Aesop’s fable and Howards End represent aspects of their messages in fairly straightforward ways, such that even now the mapping is comprehensible for most readers. That isn’t true for Gulliver’s Travels, however, which most readers would now find impenetrable. Most of Swift’s message is so specific to early eighteenth-century England that only a person very familiar with that era would understand the message.
For Swift’s audience, however, the message was received, and the book was a huge success. The background, knowledge, and needs of the audience are key.

In all three examples, important parts of the author’s message were mapped to key characters and events in the story. As an audience, we experience these storytelling elements on the level of the story, but we can also discern the message the author wants to communicate on another level that would relate the story to our own lives.

section.title: Designing a Narrative to Communicate a Message
section.para: In this section, we will create our own mapping between a message we want to share and a story. Our mapping will be simple, nothing like that in Howards End or Gulliver’s Travels. But we will see how to use narrative, character, and other story elements to communicate a message.

figure.label: Figure 7.12
figure.title:
Cars.
Photo by Life of Pix via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Cars on a road.

section.title: A Message about Self-Driving Cars
section.para: Suppose that our message is about self-driving cars. Self-driving cars are becoming more common and more accessible for lower-income buyers, but some people believe they are morally problematic. Let’s see why.

section.title: A Moral Dilemma
section.para: In an accident involving vehicles driven by people, the drivers themselves are responsible for the accident. Even if only one driver caused the accident, we could still assign blame to that driver and to no one else. The situation seems to be different for self-driving cars, however, because there is no human driver and no immediate target for blame.

section.title: Framing the Message
section.para: This imaginary situation offers one possible moral problem for self-driving cars, but there are others. Let’s suppose that these problems have convinced us that self-driving cars ought to be illegal. We believe that they are dangerous and that no one should be able to own one, and we wish to convey this message to others.

We need a frame for our message, and a few possibilities come immediately to mind: We could write an academic article giving formal arguments for our position. We could also write a letter to the editor of a local newspaper listing the reasons for our concerns. We might even write a blog post to reach a different audience but include much of the same information as an academic article or letter.

We could also consider the story frame. A moral issue like self-driving cars is a pressing and interesting one, and these issues lend themselves to expression through stories. Let’s try out the story frame.

section.title: A Message’s Most Important Part
section.para: We begin by determining the most important aspect of our message. Unlike the deep and wide-ranging societal messages of Forster or Swift, ours is a discrete moral issue without many dimensions. The message is just that self-driving cars should be illegal because they are morally problematic. The most important parts of our story will need to map in some way to this message.

section.title: Charcters

figure.label: Figure 7.13
figure.title:
Robot.
Photo by Rock'n Roll Monkey via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A blue robot with multiple cogs and buttons.

section.para: Next, we need a way of representing self-driving cars in our story. We’ll probably want to do so by means of a character. Using a robot character might be a good choice, with the obvious connection between robots and cars. We’ll make the robot a street-cleaning robot to give it something to do.

Our robot character will have to interact with others. Why not make one a child? Using a child will help our story have an emotional impact and may lead to a more favorable response from some audiences. We’ll also include the robot’s designer—to represent the software developers—and other people who know the child.

section.title: Events in the Narrative
section.para: Now we need to create events for the narrative. The events and their causal relations to each other should depict a moral problem analogous in some way to the problems we perceive with self-driving cars.

In designing this narrative, we are limited only by our creativity. We could generate dozens of possibilities if we thought hard enough, so let’s just go with a situation where a robot is performing its duties but harms a child. The robot is cleaning the streets when its path is blocked by a bundle of blankets in the gutter. The bundle is trembling, and any person who saw it would know it hid a lost child. But the robot doesn’t realize this and injures the child as it tries to move past.

The events of this narrative include the robot finding the child, deciding what to do, and injuring the child. We could fill out the story with additional events, including a discussion between the robot and its creator and a confrontation between the creator and the child’s parents.

section.title: A Mapping between Message and Story
section.para: Using these events and characters, we’ve created a simple mapping between the important aspects of our message and a story. The story presents a moral problem, and the mapping encourages audiences to interpret the story in a way that goes beyond the story itself. If we execute our story well, our audiences will reflect on moral problems involving intelligent machines and may come to adopt our belief that self-driving cars are morally problematic.

section.title: A Possible Passage
section.para: Perhaps our story will contain a passage like this one, to drive home the point:

figure.label: Figure 7.14
figure.title:
Victor and the woman.
iStock.com/anyaberkut.

imagedata.alt: A man and woman argue outside.

blockquote.emphasis: Victor, the robot’s creator, stood aghast. The child’s arm was definitely broken, he saw, as she wept into the blankets. The robot chirped behind him, ready to continue its cleaning. Victor flipped a switch on its back to put it in standby mode.

“My baby!” a woman yelled as she ran out a door from a nearby house. “What’s wrong? My baby!” The child cried harder now that her mother had arrived. The woman looked to Victor in shock and then to the robot. The blank look on Victor’s face was all she needed to know what happened.
She turned back to him with venom in her eyes. “That dangerous robot hurt my child! It could have killed her!”
Victor felt speechless. “I don’t know what happened. It’s not supposed to do that. I didn’t make it that way. . . .”
“What do you mean, ‘It’s not supposed to do that’?” the woman shrieked again, cuddling the child against her chest. “You programmed it, didn’t you?”
“Yes,” Victor admitted.
“It just does whatever it’s told! I guess you must have told it that its job was more important than a person!”

Victor’s lips trembled. “No, of course not!” he said meekly. “It’s not supposed to harm people!” The woman glared. “But it’s impossible to predict everything that it will do. Even I don’t always know how it will react.”
“So, you let a murderous robot roam the streets without even knowing how it would behave?” the woman accused.
Victor kept silent, rooted to the ground between the people and his creation. The robot chirped again, reminding him that it was ready to resume its duty.

section.para: Even with the specific decisions we made above, the story could still have gone in many different directions. This attempt is just an example. The important thing is the discernible mapping between the message we want to send about the moral problems of self-driving cars and the elements of the story. The events in the story create a moral dilemma analogous to those involving cars, and the confrontation between Victor and the mother underscores the concern about assigning responsibility. The story may be a bit heavy-handed, but it could do the job.

The story frame is a powerful one for many messages. We cast our messages into stories by using storytelling elements to map to different aspects of our message. The most important aspects map to prominent elements of the story, including characters and settings. We then design the events of the narrative in a way that reveals the features and importance of the message.

section.title: Literary Devices
section.para: A story frame is a powerful way to share a message. This frame relies on characters, narrative, and the cause-and-effect relations between events to make a message clear.

Stories told with a message in mind often achieve their goals by relying on techniques called literary devicesAny techniques used in literature to convey meaning beyond what words and phrases mean literally. . A literary device is just a way of conveying some bit of meaning without needing to state it directly. In this section, we will discuss three useful literary devices and mention some others that may be worth studying.

section.title: Symbolism
section.para: The first is symbolism. SymbolismA literary device involving the use of symbols, or the representation of one thing by another, to convey meaning. is the use of symbols in a story, and a symbol is anything that represents something else. Symbols are an important part of sending messages through stories because a story can use symbols to appear to be about one thing while really being about another.

We’ve already seen a number of symbols in our discussion during this topic. One obvious one is the robot in our imaginary story. The robot was a symbol for self-driving cars. Although the robot has some features in common with those cars, it’s also pretty different. But it’s similar enough that it can represent cars, other machines, or something else entirely.

Symbols are most effective when they’re similar to but not the same as the object they want to represent. Our imaginary story, whose message was about self-driving cars, could have actually featured self-driving cars. But then we would just be making up a fictional story about the cars in order to prove they are bad. By using a symbol to represent the cars—something that isn’t a car but is similar enough—we can make the point we want while allowing readers to interpret the events of the story for themselves.

Symbols that aren’t similar enough to what they represent probably won’t be successful. To successfully represent something, a symbol has to have something in common with what it is representing. We will be able to send powerful messages through stories by using good symbols.

section.title: Metaphor and Simile

figure.label: Figure 7.15
figure.title:
Life is a highway.
Photo by Sebastian Palomino via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An empty road against the mountains.

section.para: The next literary device is a metaphor. A metaphorA literary device in which one object is affirmed to be another, thereby illuminating some aspect of the first object in a new or unusual way. is like a symbol in that it refers to something else but has fewer restrictions on how similar it must be. In fact, a metaphor doesn’t need to require that the compared objects be very similar because the metaphor may seek to highlight a single feature of an object.

One famous and catchy metaphor comes from the Rascal Flatts song “Life is a Highway.”Flatts, R. (1991). Life is a highway [Song]. On Mad mad world [Album]. Capitol. Life is what humans experience, and a highway is a place where cars travel, so the two things don’t seem to have much in common. But we can think of life as a highway: we have a destination and fellow passengers, and we must take time and use resources to reach our destination. The metaphor draws attention to these features of life by comparing it to a highway.

Stories often state metaphors outright. In our self-driving car story, for example, the robot’s designer Victor might say, “The robot is Frankenstein’s monster.” Obviously, the robot isn’t really Frankenstein’s monster, but making the comparison draws attention to certain features of the robot, like that the inventors never expected what they created to cause harm.

We sometimes use the term “metaphor” more broadly as well—to refer to multiple objects or a series of events that represent something else. In this use of the literary device, a metaphor is more like a set of symbols and their relations to each other. So, we might say that our story of Victor’s robot is a metaphor for the dangers of self-driving cars.
Metaphors can be powerful figures of speech that draw unusual comparisons. They are useful tools for making our story do more than just present a narrative.

The term “metaphor” is often discussed in conjunction with another literary device, the simileA literary device in which one object is affirmed to be like another by using “like” or “as,” thereby illuminating some aspect of the first object in a new or unusual way. . The explanation for the difference is usually that while a metaphor says that one thing is another thing, a simile only says that one thing is like another thing. Take the following sentences:

listitem.para: Life is a highway.
