Life is like a highway.

section.para: The first of these sentences is a metaphor, while the second is a simile. But since no one takes the first sentence as literally saying that life is, in fact, a highway, we will let the reader decide how different these two sentences are.

section.title: Juxtaposition
section.para: The third of our literary devices is juxtaposition. A juxtapositionA literary technique in which two objects are deliberately brought together in order to emphasize their similarities or, more commonly, their differences. is just the position of two or more objects in relation to each other. Usually, though, the juxtaposed objects contrast with each other in some way. If I bring a Big Mac to an extremely expensive restaurant and set it on the tablecloth, then I’ve juxtaposed the burger with upscale dining in an unusual way.

figure.label: Figure 7.16
figure.title:
Expensive restaurant.
Photo by Zakaria Zayane via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A fancy restaurant with folded napkins on each table.

section.para: Our imaginary story showed an example of juxtaposition. At the end of the passage in which Victor confronts the child’s mother, he stands forebodingly between the robot and the two people. The juxtaposition of the man and the man-made was striking.

We use the technique of juxtaposition to contrast two different things, or to emphasize their differences. Since stories usually don’t call explicit attention to a juxtaposition but merely set it up, it is up to the audience to notice how objects in the story relate to each other.

section.title: Literary Devices and Audiences
section.para: The literary devices we’ve covered here, as well as many others, can help make our stories more powerful. They can also deepen the messages we want to send through them. But not everyone has a degree in literary analysis, so some literary techniques risk going completely unnoticed. As in the case of the frame and other issues, we should carefully consider our audience in deciding how to use literary devices.

section.title: Stories Can Frame Any Message
section.para: In this topic, we’ve focused on using stories to send messages that go beyond the events of the story. We’ve learned to determine whether a story frame is appropriate and to develop a narrative that maps important parts of the message to elements of the story.
With a few exceptions, our examples have dealt with messages that have a moral component. This is because such messages are easy to understand and because they are well-suited to a story frame.

section.title: Not Just Moral Messages
section.para: However, it isn’t just moral messages that stories tell well. Stories can frame any message we want if we’re careful to consider our audience and the events in our narrative. We saw an example in , where we read the opening passages of a groundbreaking scientific paper on DNA. The authors of that paper, Watson and Crick, used a story frame to establish a few characters and set the stage for their discoveries. Their story subtly positions them as the heroes who stumbled across a great secret.

section.title: Journalism and Stories

figure.label: Figure 7.17
figure.title:
Nurse.
Photo by Jonathan Borba via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A nurse sits on a bench wearing a mask.

section.para: The story frame is especially common in investigative journalism from publications like The Atlantic and The New Yorker. For example, a recent article from The Atlantic about the COVID-19 pandemic began this way:

para.emphasis: Nick Klein knew the man wasn’t going to make it through the night. So the 31-year-old nurse at the University of Iowa ICU put on his gown, his gloves, his mask, and his face shield. He went into the patient’s room, held a phone to his ear, and tried hard not to cry while he listened to the man’s loved ones take turns saying goodbye. When they were finished, Klein put on some music, a muted melody like you might hear in an elevator. He pulled up a chair and took the man’s hand. For two hours that summer night, there were no sounds but soft piano and the gentle beep beep beep of the monitors. Klein thought about how he would feel if the person in the bed were his own father, and he squeezed his hand tighter. Around midnight, Klein watched as the man took one last, ragged breath and died.
para.footnote: Godfrey, E. (2020, December 3). Iowa is what happens when government does nothing. The Atlantic. Politics. https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/archive/2020/12/how-iowa-mishandled-coronavirus-pandemic/617252/.

section.para: Here we see the story frame in action. The article is about the pandemic’s effects in Iowa, but it doesn’t just launch into reporting facts or citing statistics. It begins by telling a story: establishing characters, describing a setting, and putting key events into motion. Readers are immediately immersed in the story frame before encountering the facts about the outbreak, which is the primary purpose of the article.

We can use the story frame for any communication we wish. The story frame won’t always be appropriate, but by paying close attention to our audience, its expectations, and the content of our message, we will find opportunities to send powerful messages through stories.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 7.18
figure.title:
Stories convey messages.
Photo by Diana Akhmetianova via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Many manila envelopes.

section.para: Prior to this topic, we had learned about narrative () and character (), two of the most important elements of stories. Following this topic, we’ll learn about other parts of stories and how to use them.

Here, though, we dealt with the ability of stories to convey messages beyond their narratives. Using a story frame gives us access to a story’s communicative power, and we can deliver messages of great emotional weight through stories. We do so by mapping the most important parts of our message to elements of a story and then designing a narrative that will make those parts prominent.
Moving forward, we’ll learn more about stories, and we’ll be better able to use them to send messages of all kinds to our audiences.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 4. This week, you will read the following topics:

listitem.para: : The Hook—Capturing an Audience
: The Stakes—Why It Matters
: The Conflict—A Struggle with Purpose

section.para: We’ll concentrate on the nuts and bolts of telling compelling stories. We’ll learn about how to grab an audience with an interesting hook and how to keep them in their seats by raising the stakes and intensifying the conflicts.

section.title: Capturing an Audience
section.para: So far, we’ve been discussing elements of stories. We have focused on narrative, or the events in a story, and characters, or the entities that experience the events in a story. Without these two elements, a piece of creative work doesn’t really have a story at all. They are essential; they make a story a story.

section.title: Genres of Stories

figure.label: Figure 8.1
figure.title:
Many genres.
Photo by Polina Zimmerman via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Many books on several shelves.

section.para: Beyond these very basic requirements, however, stories can be extremely different from each other. Some differences are more obvious than others, such as genreThe storytelling category a story belongs to, such as romance, historical fiction, western, science fiction, and so on. Works belonging to the same genre are likely to share general features such as subject matter and style. —a western, a romance, and works of science fiction and historical fiction all differ from each other in the basic conventions of their genre. The focus of a romance is the romance, and focusing on that requires elevating particular aspects of the story, such as the relationships between the main characters. Those relationships may be optional in a work of science fiction, where the focus is usually the ideas or the strangeness of the world. Different focuses in each genre will make the narrative structure and characters different.

section.title: Making Audiences Like the Story
section.para: But there’s another group of storytelling elements that, while not necessary for a story like narrative or character, are usually found in good or interesting stories. These other elements are not dictated by any particular genre and will be found in all kinds of stories. In conjunction with the events in the narrative and the characters, these elements make audiences want to continue the story. They glue audiences to their seats and compel them to find out what happens because they are so invested in what they have experienced.

Such elements of stories include hooks, conflicts, and stakes. For the next few topics, we’ll be discussing these elements: what they are, why they’re important, and how to use them. We’ll see the role they play in stories and how they connect with both narrative and characters in order to make our stories something worth paying attention to.

section.title: Capture an Audience

figure.label: Figure 8.2
figure.title:
Captured audience.
Photo by Min An via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman reading a book while walking outside.

section.para: The purpose of things like hooks and conflicts is not to turn something into a story but to capture an audience. Countless stories fill bookshelves and the queues of our streaming services—there are more good stories in novels, movies, and television shows than we could possibly experience in a lifetime. How will our contributions to these piles of tales stand out among the rest? How do we convince busy audiences with short attention spans that our work deserves their time?

If we want audiences to read or watch our work, then we must answer those questions. It isn’t just about designing riveting plots or groundbreaking characters; it’s about communicating those things to audiences in ways that will convince them to pay attention. If we bury our good ideas and don’t give even a hint of them to our audiences, then why would anyone pay attention to the stories we write? No one would believe our stories would deserve their time because we’ve given them no reason to believe.

The next few topics are about giving our audiences these reasons to pay attention to our stories. In this topic, we’ll discuss hooks, which have to do with an audience’s very first impressions of our work. Hooks help create the right impressions, which then lead audiences to want more.

figure.label: Figure 8.3
figure.title:
Grab people’s attention.
Photo by Andrea Piacquadio via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman looks at her phone in surprise.

section.title: Hooks
section.para: A hookAnything used to capture someone’s attention. is anything we use to grab people’s attention. It’s an interesting line, catchy phrase, powerful image, or something else designed to get an audience to look our way. We may know little about something, but a good hook can make us want to know more.

section.title: Many Communications Have Hooks
section.para: In this topic, we’ll speak of hooks in relation to stories, but hooks aren’t unique to stories or even to novels or movies more generally. Advertisers want good hooks so that we’ll pay attention long enough to buy something; salespeople need hooks, companies need hooks for investors, and radio hits are full of vocal and instrumental hooks that get stuck in our heads. Even institutions like governments and churches need hooks to engage and keep an audience.

section.title: Hooks Come at the Beginning
section.para: Most hooks appear at the beginning of a work. They are the opening line of a book, the opening scene of a movie, or the opening paragraph of an essay. The hook is an audience’s first taste of what’s to come, and it leaves them wanting more.

section.title: A Sample Hook
section.para: Let’s see some examples of hooks. Here are the opening lines of Dan Brown’s 2003 novel The Da Vinci Code:

para.emphasis: “Renowned curator Jacques Saunière staggered through the vaulted archway of the museum’s Grand Gallery. He lunged for the nearest painting he could see, a Caravaggio. Grabbing the gilded frame, the seventy-six-year-old man heaved the masterpiece toward himself until it tore from the wall and Saunière collapsed backward in a heap beneath the canvas.”Brown, D. (2009). The da Vinci code. Anchor Books, 3. (Original work published in 2003)

section.para: Imagine someone handed you a book manuscript with no title, author, or anything else to indicate what the manuscript was about. All you read is this short paragraph about Jacques Saunière’s apparent demise. Would you be interested? Would you keep reading? Many people were and did because Brown’s book sold over 80 million copies.Reuters. (2009, September 16). Dan Brown novel breaks one-day sales records. https://www.reuters.com/article/us-books-danbrown/dan-brown-novel-breaks-one-day-sales-records-idUSTRE58E5Q720090917. The unusual circumstances in the hook—a museum curator’s near-death experience, damaging priceless art inside his museum as he dies—get eyes onto the page and hook them for more.

section.title: Another Hook
section.para: Here’s an even better-known hook, from the Jane Austen novel Pride and Prejudice:

para.emphasis: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.”Austen, J. (2008, February 12). Pride and prejudice. C. Scribner’s Sons, 1. (Original work published in 1813)

section.para: This hook works in a very different way from the one at the front of The Da Vinci Code. There’s no murder here and not even any action; there’s no mention of any specific character or circumstance at all. Instead, the hook is a humorous remark presented almost as a law of physics, setting the tone for the entire book. After reading the hook, we as readers wonder who could acknowledge such a silly idea as a universal truth—and then we meet Mrs. Bennett.

section.title: A Hook in a Movie

figure.label: Figure 8.4
figure.title:
Indiana Jones.
Nikolay Antonov © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A whip, a hat, a compass, and a pair of boots.

section.para: For novels such as Brown’s and Austen’s, the hook often appears on the opening page or in the opening lines themselves. Hooks in movies appear early too, though they take a bit more time to play out. Consider the opening scene of the 1981 film Raiders of the Lost Ark.Spielberg, S. (Director). (1981) Raiders of the Lost Ark [Film]. Paramount Pictures. (Watch the scene here.)

From the exotic setting and heroic Dr. Jones to the death-defying stunts and ancient mythology, everything about these first few minutes makes us want to keep watching. The hook works by introducing the style and themes of the movie in a way that grabs audiences and doesn’t let them go.

These examples of hooks from books and a movie show what this story element is all about: giving audiences something captivating right from the very start to make a work stand out among everything else they could be reading or watching. That’s the purpose of a hook. The best narratives and characters in the world can’t unfold unless audiences read past the first page or watch past the first scene.

In the end, a hook is exactly what it says: it’s what we use to capture the audience. Audiences have an unlimited amount of ways to spend their time. So, why would they spend it with our stories? Because we’ve hooked them.

section.title: Audiences and Effective Hooks
section.para: So just how do we attract audiences with a hook? How do we get them to drop everything else they’re doing to pay attention to us? What makes for an effective hook?

section.title: Effective Hooks
section.para: We can begin to analyze hooks by thinking of the things that capture our attention. Let’s look at another hook, this one from author John Grisham in the 1992 legal thriller The Pelican Brief:

figure.label: Figure 8.5
figure.title:
Abraham Rosenberg character.
Photo by Alexandre Saraiva Carniato via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man sits in a wheelchair looking outside.

para.emphasis: “He seemed incapable of creating such chaos, but much of what he saw below could be blamed on him. And that was fine. He was ninety-one, paralyzed, strapped in a wheelchair, and hooked to oxygen. His second stroke seven years ago had almost finished him off, but Abraham Rosenberg was still alive and even with tubes in his nose his legal stick was bigger than the other eight. He was the only legend remaining on the Court, and the fact that he was still breathing irritated most of the mob below.”
para.footnote: Grisham, J. (1992) The pelican brief. Doubleday, 1.

section.para: This hook is just a description of a character, but the character is unusual: a ninety-one-year-old Supreme Court justice who’s had two strokes and whose continued existence alone is enough to make everyone mad. With his age and his health conditions, the character seems lucky to be alive. What has he done to make everyone so angry? We know Supreme Court justices are powerful—but description given makes the character seem physically weak. Can the audience trust him to make decisions of national importance?

section.title: Something Needs Resolution
section.para: Grisham’s hook in The Pelican Brief creates a series of unanswered questions that cry out for resolution. The questions involve a bit of mystery, but they also may get us going emotionally. “Rosenberg is too old and frail to make national decisions!” we may say to ourselves. “He should have retired a long time ago!” Maybe Grisham agrees, and maybe not; it doesn’t really matter. If we’re asking those questions and feeling those ways, then the hook has already worked. We’re invested in the story and primed to keep reading.

section.title: Hooks Make People Feel and Think
section.para: An effective hook is one that makes people feel or think in interesting, unusual, or powerful ways. Authors can provoke these feelings and thoughts with all kinds of material, but a strong emotional or intellectual investment from an audience will hook them and motivate them to keep experiencing the work.

section.title: Creating Emotional Investment
section.para: The best way to get a feel for hooks is through examples. Here’s another one from the early career of suspense author Mary Higgins Clark. These are the last three paragraphs of the prologue to Where Are the Children? and they tell of a disturbed man who’s spying on a woman named Nancy:

figure.label: Figure 8.6
figure.title:
Telescope.
Photo by Félix Besombes via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A telescope against a dark sky.

para.emphasis: “He swallowed nervously. He could feel the feverish dryness of his mouth, even while his hands and armpits were wet and warm. He gulped, then swallowed again, and the sound evolved into a deep chuckle. His whole body began to shake with mirth and jarred the telescope. Nancy’s image blurred, but he didn’t bother refocusing the lens. He wasn’t interested in watching her any more today.

“Tomorrow! He could just see the expression she’d have at this time tomorrow. Exposed to the world for what she was; numbed with worry and fear; trying to answer the question . . . the same question the police had thrown at her over and over seven years ago.

“‘Come on, Nancy,’ the police would be saying again. ‘Come clean with us. Tell us the truth. You should know you can’t get away with this. Tell us, Nancy—where are the children?’”Higgins Clark, M. (1975). Where are the children?. Simon & Schuster, prologue.

section.para: The feelings overflow here, but they aren’t positive: they’re unsettling, uncomfortable, and creepy. The final question, “Where are the children?” only deepens our discomfort. Through the entire prologue, we’re assuming that the stalker following Nancy must be the bad guy, but if the police are asking Nancy where the children are, then they must have some reason to think that she knows or had something to do with what happened to them. We’ve got a psychotic stalker using a telescope to spy on a woman who may be responsible for the disappearance of children. What happened? Who can we trust? And where are the children, anyway?
Obviously, the only way to answer any of these questions is to read on. Our feelings are demanding it—our mind won’t relax until we do. Higgins Clark’s hook has succeeded.

section.title: When Hooks Fail
section.para: Another way of thinking about effective hooks is to consider what happens when our stories don’t have one. Imagine being handed a manuscript with no title or author and reading the following opening paragraph:

figure.label: Figure 8.7
figure.title:
Cereal.
Photo by freestocks.org via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Cheerios in a green bowl.

para.emphasis: Smack, smack, smack went the cereal against the brown bowl. Henry poured the milk in and took a bite. Then he took another one. After a few more bites, he became full of cereal and washed the bowl. Then he gathered his things and went to work. Work was fine, and when he finished, he came home and warmed up some leftovers for dinner. After a bit of TV, it was time for bed. The next day and the day after that he did the same thing.

section.para: Spellbinding? Enthralling? Definitely not. It’s a boring paragraph about a boring man. Nothing interesting happens, nothing interesting is hinted at, nothing interesting appears to even be possible in this man’s world. A manuscript that started like this probably isn’t going to be read long.

section.title: Bad Hooks Bore
section.para: A hook like this one—if we can even call it a hook—fails to capture an audience. It doesn’t make the audience members feel, and it doesn’t make them think. It passes through a reader’s mind in the same way that Henry passes through his day: completely unremarkably. It makes no impact on the audience and gives them no reason to continue.

section.title: Never Bore the Audience

figure.label: Figure 8.8
figure.title:
Bored audience.
Photo by Andrea Piacquadio via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman sleeping on an open book.

section.para: Whatever the goals of our stories, the one thing they cannot do is bore the audience. If we make the audience excited, scared, entranced, angry, or horrified, we’ve got them. If we make them bored we’ve lost them, and we probably won’t get a second chance.

A good hook will make people feel and think and will set them up to experience the full story we want to give them. In this way, a hook does more than just catch someone’s attention—it also serves as the frame for the opening part of the story and even for the whole story taken together.

If a hook is mysterious and exciting, like Brown’s in The Da Vinci Code, then it promises that we’ll get more mystery and excitement by reading on. A museum curator’s unusual death leaves a lot of questions unanswered, and readers go on past the prologue to answer those questions and experience more of what the hook made them feel. Here, the hook frames the story as a thriller, and the rest of the story delivers.

The opening line of Austen’s Pride and Prejudice plays the same role by doing something completely different. The sarcastic point about rich single men looking for wives sets a tone of sophisticated irreverence that Austen maintains throughout the book. Readers keep going not only to learn more about the alleged “universal truth” of romance but also to laugh out loud at the oblivious and buffoonish characters. The hook frames the story as a romance and a comedy, and the remainder never deviates.

Hooks capture an audience’s attention by making them think and feel. Along the way, they frame the tone of a work and set an audience’s expectation. Failing to do these things or doing them boringly leaves a potential audience with no reason to keep experiencing our work. If we care about what’s happening in our audience’s heads, we’ll want to craft hooks that convince them to keep going.

section.title: Titles, Subtitles, and Elevator Pitches
section.para: So far, we’ve seen many examples of hooks. These examples all came from the beginning or near the beginning of stories, designed to catch and keep an audience.

In section , we’ll group hooks into different categories to analyze the ways that they make people feel and think. In this section, though, we want to look beyond opening lines or scenes to other parts of a work where thinking in terms of hooks can be beneficial.

section.title: Titles

figure.label: Figure 8.9
figure.title:
Titles.
Photo by Anastasia Zhenina via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A book showing the title page lies next to a plant and a teacup.

section.para: The title of a work is the main way we refer to the work, and we use the title to find more information about it. A title tells us something about the work, serving as a very brief description. But a good title is also a hook in and of itself and can be a way of attracting attention.

Some titles hook by stating exactly what the work is about, like Snakes on a Plane.Ellis, D. R. (Director). (2006, August 17). Snakes on a plane [Film]. Mutual Film Company. Since watching people deal with snakes while on a plane sounds exciting, this title works. Good Will HuntingVan Sant, G. (Director). (1997, December 2). Good will hunting [Film]. Be Gentlemen. names the main character of the movie but is also a pun, communicating the idea that the characters are hunting for or seeking someone of goodwill. To All the Boys I’ve Loved BeforeHan, J. (2014, April 15). To all the boys I’ve loved before. Simon & Schuster. is an even more descriptive title, made interesting by its reference to more than one boy and its hint at different feelings in the present.
A catchy title isn’t necessary for a story to succeed, but it helps. Even things that aren’t strictly part of the story can still hook audiences.

section.title: Subtitles
section.para: Another example is a subtitle. A subtitle is a further description of a work that sometimes accompanies the actual title and supplements it in some way. Although less important and usually less known than the title, subtitles can still provide interesting information to a potential audience. One example is the subtitle of Roots,Haley, A. (1976, August 17). Roots: The saga of an American family. Doubleday. a novel about African Americans and slavery in the United States. The subtitle of Roots is The Saga of an American Family. This subtitle works with the image created by Roots to describe a family and juxtaposes the traditional idea of an “American family”—not usually considered to be a Black family—with the fact that the near ancestors of the family come from Africa.

section.title: The Elevator Pitch

figure.label: Figure 8.10
figure.title:
Send one boy and one girl.
Photo by Henri Pham via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A teenage boy and girl stand against a wall.

section.para: A third important part of a story is the elevator pitchA short description of something intended to generate interest in it. Unlike a hook, an elevator pitch does not actually appear inside a work. , named after the description we might give of our story to someone while riding with them in an elevator. An elevator pitch is short, to the point, and contains a hook or two in order to interest the audience and make it remember what we said.
Many books contain a version of an elevator pitch, usually on the back cover or on the inside flaps of the dust jacket. Here is one such pitch for the novel The Hunger Games:

para.emphasis: “In the ruins of a place once known as North America lies the nation of Panem, a shining Capitol surrounded by twelve outlying districts. The Capitol is harsh and cruel and keeps the districts in line by forcing them all to send one boy and one girl between the ages of twelve and eighteen to participate in the annual Hunger Games, a fight to the death on live TV. Sixteen-year-old Katniss Everdeen, who lives alone with her mother and younger sister, regards it as a death sentence when she is forced to represent her district in the Games. But Katniss has been close to dead before—and survival, for her, is second nature. Without really meaning to, she becomes a contender. But if she is to win, she will have to start making choices that weigh survival against humanity and life against love.”
para.footnote: Collins, S. (2010). The hunger games. Scholastic Inc, synopsis. (Original work published in 2008)

section.para: This synopsis is longer than a title and a subtitle but doesn’t begin a story. It gives a few crucial points of the plot and tells a little about the setting and the looming conflicts. The purpose of the pitch is to describe enough to get the reader interested without giving away the best ideas and spoiling the story. This synopsis does a good job of that.

In addition to titles, subtitles, and elevator pitches, there may be other things that aren’t technically part of a story but that can still be seen as hooks. The purpose of all of them is to attract audiences and convince them to stay. Many aspects of our story, both inside and out, can do this.

section.title: Kinds of Hooks
section.para: We’ve seen many examples of hooks from different stories. We’ve also discussed what makes a hook effective. Hooks attract audiences by making them feel and think in interesting, unusual, or powerful ways.

section.title: Categories of Hooks
section.para: But since there are many approaches to get people to feel and think like that, we need some guidance. In this section, we’ll discuss nine different categories of hooks. We’ll discuss each category and talk about when an author might prefer one category to another. The points we’ll make here aren’t ironclad rules but will help us brainstorm and find a hook that piques an audience while framing our story in the way we want.
Remember, the purpose of all these is to grab an audience’s attention. Think about how you would react to each hook and whether it could convey a message about your story.

Note that the term “hook” in writing usually refers to the first part of a book, but it can also refer to just the opening lines or even to the opening sentence by itself. Our examples will be longer than just a single sentence to show how an opening passage taken as a whole works to interest an audience.

Here are the nine categories of hooks we’ll cover, with examples of each: the drop-into-the-action hook, the surprising statement hook, the mystery hook, the fear hook, the funny hook, the flashback hook, the flashforward hook, the question hook, and the character hook. (See .)

figure.label: Figure 8.11
figure.title: Hooks.

imagedata.alt: Nine circles label hooks. 1. Drop-into-the-Action 2. Surprising Statement 3. Mystery 4. Fear 5. Funny 6. Flashback 7. Flashforward 8. Question 9. Character.

section.title: Drop-into-the-Action Hook

figure.label: Figure 8.12
figure.title:
Shanique Saturn.
Photo by uncoveredlens via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A black and white profile of a woman.

section.para: This one is all in the name. The drop-into-the-action hookA hook in which a story’s action begins immediately with little or no explanation of why it is taking place. drops the readers right into the action with no background or explanation. They don’t know why, but something exciting is happening. The “why” is for later—this hook just gets on with the action to get the reader going.
This hook might read like the following:

para.emphasis: Shanique Saturn dumped the empty shells from her gun and reloaded. The rain continued to pour and lightning crashed above her, knocking over her companions. But Shanique was unmoved. She was a Saturn, after all. And when death calls, Saturns answer.

section.para: Who’s Shanique Saturn? Who has she been shooting at and why? What have members of the Saturn family done in the past to merit such a reputation? This hook answers none of these questions, and it’s a good bet that the pages following it wouldn’t either. The emphasis is on the action. The action does raise all those questions, but there will be plenty of time to settle them later because the audience is already invested in what Saturn is doing.

This hook works by accelerating the story to escape velocity right from the very start. Fights and escapes are the kinds of high-stakes situations that work with this hook. The action has to matter and generate a lot of excitement.

The drop-into-the-action hook works best with thrillers and other action stories because of the frame it gives for everything else. Such an opening sets readers’ expectations high, and the book will need to continue to deliver on the promise made in the opening sentences. Genres with lots of action are best at that.

section.title: Surprising Statement Hook
section.para: The surprising statement hookA hook in which a story begins with a surprising or bizarre statement; intended to puzzle the reader and entice them to keep reading. has another self-explanatory name. It says something unexpected or even bizarre without drawing much attention to it. This hook puts us off-guard: the surprising statement is seemingly normal in the story world, but for us, it may be anything but.

Here’s an example of this hook in action from the opening sentences of the Orson Scott Card novel Ender’s Game. Note the first sentence in particular, in which we hear about something very unusual, which is passed over as if it were just a comment about the weather:

figure.label: Figure 8.13
figure.title:
I’ve seen through his eyes.
Photo by Arvind shakya via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A young boy wrapped in a blanket peers out.

para.emphasis: “‘I’ve watched through his eyes, I’ve listened through his ears, and I tell you he’s the one. Or at least as close as we’re going to get.”
“‘That’s what you said about the brother.’
“‘The brother tested out impossible. For other reasons. Nothing to do with his ability.’
“‘Same with the sister. And there are doubts about him. He’s too malleable. Too willing to submerge himself in someone else’s will.’
“‘Not if the other person is his enemy.’
“‘So what do we do? Surround him with enemies all the time?’
“‘If we have to.’
“‘I thought you said you liked this kid.’
“‘If the buggers get him, they’ll make me look like his favorite uncle.’
“‘All right. We’re saving the world, after all. Take him.’”Card, O. S. (1985, January 15). Ender’s game. Tor Books, 1.

section.para: The whole passage is a conversation between two characters, but a careful read of the first sentence tells us that one of them has “watched through his eyes” and “listened through his ears.” Whose eyes and ears? And how is it possible to do that? We don’t know yet, but the speaker intends his words literally here. We soon find out that this character really has felt the experiences of another, and through those experiences, the speaker is able to declare that “he’s the one.”

The surprising statement hook is a technique useful in many genres. Ender’s Game is a work of science fiction, so the frame communicated by the surprising statement is that the world readers are stepping into is not like the real world. They’ll need to pay attention to the details because their expectations of how things normally work are going to be violated.
This hook communicates a similar frame in other works: things aren’t normal here. As readers, we want to move forward to find out why.

section.title: Mystery Hook
section.para: Using a mystery hookA hook in which a story begins with a mysterious or unexplained event. is like using a surprising statement, but the mystery hook calls attention not to an unexpected detail but to some larger unexplained event. The hook frames the event as a focal point for the book rather than just setting or upending our expectations for the story world.

figure.label: Figure 8.14
figure.title:
Empty desks.
Photo by Dids via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A classroom full of empty desks.

section.para: We already saw an example of the mystery hook in the Mary Higgins Clark novel Where Are the Children? The end of the prologue asks the titular question, establishing the children’s disappearance as the central event in the narrative.
Another mystery hook used in a very similar place occurs in the novel Thirteen Reasons Why. Here are the final two paragraphs from the prologue:

para.emphasis: “At the front of the room, facing the students, will be the desk of Mr. Porter. He’ll be the last to receive a package with no return address. And in the middle of the room, one desk to the left, will be the desk of Hannah Baker.
“Empty.”
para.footnote: Asher, J. (2016) Thirteen reasons why. Razorbill, 4. (Original work published in 2007)

section.para: These paragraphs come after some description of the package and its purpose. Hannah’s relation to the package isn’t clear, and now, we’ve discovered that her desk is empty. She’s disappeared! The mystery hook brings together several important elements of the story and sets a course toward resolving the mystery one step at a time.
Neither of the hooks we’ve mentioned here occurs at the very beginning of their books. Here are the opening lines of the prologue in Thirteen Reasons Why:

para.emphasis: “‘Sir?” she repeats. ‘How soon do you want it to get there?’
“I rub two fingers, hard, over my left eyebrow. The throbbing has become intense. ‘It doesn’t matter,’ I say.

“The clerk takes the package. The same shoebox that sat on my porch less than twenty-four hours ago; rewrapped in a brown paper bag, sealed with clear packing tape, exactly as I had received it. But now addressed with a new name. The next name on Hannah Baker’s list.”
para.footnote: Asher, J. (2016) Thirteen reasons why. Razorbill, 1. (Original work published in 2007)

section.para: There are unanswered questions here: Why the throbbing? What’s in the package? And what about that list? But these questions don’t mean much to us until we get to the end of the prologue—when we discover that Hannah is gone. The opening lines of the book present an apparently normal situation that we then reinterpret in light of what we read just a few pages later.

The important parts of these mystery hooks don’t come right at the beginning of the story, but they don’t necessarily need to. What we read a few pages in changes how we interpret the opening lines and frames the story as one whose goal is to explain a mystery.

It’s obviously common for mystery novels to use the mystery hook, but other stories can use it as well. Any story of any genre that relies on an unexplained event can begin with a mystery. In most cases, that mystery will be central to the story, but mysteries can be set as science fiction, fantasy, historical fiction, and many other genres.

section.title: Fear Hook

figure.label: Figure 8.15
figure.title:
Watching you.
Photo by Анна Хазова via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man peeks out behind sunglasses.

section.para: A good hook makes us feel or think things in interesting ways. Fear is a feeling, a strong one, and we can use a fear hookA hook in which a story begins with a scary scene. to get an audience invested.

Below is the second paragraph from the Caroline Kepnes novel You. The novel is written from a first-person point of view, and the narrator has just noticed a girl enter his bookstore. Here is how he describes her:

para.emphasis: “You are classic and compact, my own little Natalie Portman circa the end of the movie Closer, when she’s fresh-faced and done with the bad British guys and going home to America. You’ve come home to me, delivered at last, on a Tuesday, 10:06 A.M. Every day I commute to this shop on the Lower East Side from my place in Bed-Stuy. Every day I close up without finding anyone like you. Look at you, born into my world today. I’m shaking and I’d pop an Ativan but they’re downstairs and I don’t want to pop an Ativan. I don’t want to come down. I want to be here, fully, watching you bite your unpainted nails and turn your head to the left, no, bite that pinky, widen those eyes, to the right, no, reject biographies, self-help (thank God), and slow down when you make it to fiction.”
para.footnote: Kepnes, C. (2014). You. Atria/Emily Bestler Books, 1.

section.para: The narrator, presumably a man, has been watching the girl since she entered the store. He notices the way she bites her nails, turns her head, and widens her eyes. No one would want to be watched by a stranger like that, so the mood has been set. The girl should be scared but doesn’t know it yet. But we know it, as readers, and the disquieting fear we feel pushes us to keep going.
The fear hook is an opener for thrillers, mysteries, and other stories. It sets an anxious mood and signals to readers that their anxiety will only increase.

section.title: Funny Hook
section.para: Audiences will accept pretty much anything that makes them laugh, so using the funny hookA hook in which a story begins with something humorous. can be very effective. A movie might begin with a joke or a funny line, but stories may also use a bit more setup to cash in for something funnier.
Amy Poehler’s book Yes Please takes both approaches. Here are some of her opening passages:

figure.label: Figure 8.16
figure.title:
Amy Poehler.
Photo from Peabody Awards, May 21, 2012, flickr, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons.

imagedata.alt: Amy Poehler.

para.emphasis: “It’s clear to me now that I had no business agreeing to write this book. I have a job that keeps me shooting twelve hours a day, plus two children under six. I am going through a divorce and producing many projects and falling in love and trying to make appointments for cranial massage. All of these things are equally wonderful and horrible and keep me just off balance and busy enough to make spending hours alone writing seem like a terrible idea. Plus, I am forty-two, which is smack-dab in the middle. I haven’t lived a full enough life to look back on, but I am too old to get by on being pithy and cute. I know enough now to know I know nothing. I am slugging away every day, just like you. But nonetheless, here we are. I’ve written a book. You have it.

“Everyone lies about writing. They lie about how easy it is or how hard it was. They perpetuate a romantic idea that writing is some beautiful experience that takes place in an architectural room filled with leather novels and chai teas. They talk about their ‘morning ritual’ and how they ‘dress for writing’ and the cabin in Big Sur where they go to ‘be alone’—blah blah blah. No one tells the truth about writing a book. Authors pretend their stories were always shiny and perfect and just waiting to be written. The truth is, writing is this: hard and boring and occasionally great but usually not. Even I have lied about writing. I have told people that writing this book has been like brushing away dirt from a fossil. What a load of [crap]. It has been like hacking away at a freezer with a screwdriver.”
para.footnote: Poehler, A. (2014, October 28). Yes Please. Day Street Books, preface.

section.para: Many people will be able to relate to Poehler’s experiences, and they’ll also be laughing. The frame communicated by a funny hook is obvious: the reader expects to laugh hard and often and will gladly pay for the privilege of doing so. Many genres can use a funny hook because humor is a great thing to add to almost anything. But a funny opener promises more funny material later on, so make sure to follow up on the hook with more of the same.

section.title: Flashback Hook
section.para: Many stories begin with a flashback hookA hook in which a story begins with events set sometime before the story’s primary timeline. , or an event that falls outside of the primary timeline for a story. A movie set in Las Vegas in 2020, for example, might begin with a character’s experience on September 11, 2001. That experience would then give us a frame for understanding what is happening to her now, nineteen years later.

figure.label: Figure 8.17
figure.title:
Rocky ridge.
Photo by Julia Volk via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A rocky landscape.

section.para: Brandon Sanderson’s epic fantasy novel The Way of Kings begins with a flashback. In fact, the flashback scene serves as a prologue for the entire series that The Way of Kings belongs to, giving us information that we don’t understand yet but that we can revisit later.

para.emphasis: “Kalak rounded a rocky stone ridge and stumbled to a stop before the body of a dying thunderclast. The enormous stone beast lay on its side, riblike protrusions from its chest broken and cracked. The monstrosity was vaguely skeletal in shape, with unnaturally long limbs that sprouted from granite shoulders. The eyes were deep red spots on the arrowhead face, as if created by a fire burning deep within the stone. They faded.

“Even after all these centuries, seeing a thunderclast up close made Kalak shiver. The beast’s hand was as long as a man was tall. He’d been killed by hands like those before, and it hadn’t been pleasant.
“Of course, dying rarely was.”
para.footnote: Sanderson, B. (2010, August 31). The way of kings. Tom Doherty Associates, 15.

section.para: We notice elements of other hooks in this passage, especially the surprising statement hook. Having been killed before is as unexpected an idea as any, and Sanderson’s description of the thunderclast invites us into a new world that is nothing like our own.

The surprising statement hook gets readers to go on, but the flashback hook delivers a payoff later when readers are able to digest the events in the flashback given what they find out about the world. When the events in the flashback begin to make sense later on, the flashback scene becomes a kind of second hook, driving readers to find out what those events were so important as to appear at the very beginning of the book.
Depending on its use, the flashback hook may require a bit more setup, as Sanderson’s clearly does. But the flashback continues to pay dividends even after readers have moved far past it.

section.title: Flashforward Hook

figure.label: Figure 8.18
figure.title:
The life of a mother and her child.
Photo by August de Richelieu via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A mother and daughter cooking together.

section.para: A flashforward hookA hook in which a story begins with events set sometime after the story’s primary timeline. is the opposite of a flashback: rather than seeing an event that happened before the primary timeline for the story, we see an event that happens in the future. We, therefore, know something about what is coming, and we use that to frame our understanding of what happens now, wondering how the story will get us from here to there.

We see an example of a flashforward in the movie Arrival.Villeneuve, D. (Director). (2016, September 1). Arrival [Film]. FilmNation Entertainment; Lava Bear Films; 21 Laps Entertainment. Watch the scene here. The scene presents events in the life of a mother and her child, but we soon realize that these events are happening in the future and are not the focus of the movie’s story. Louise Banks narrates the scene, and her monologue about the nature of time gives us a clue about the mind-bending developments to come.
At first, the flashforward seems to spoil the story—we already know something important about the ending! But the focus shifts from the ending to the events required to get there.
Genres of all kinds can use both the flashback and flashforward hooks. The only thing to remember is that the rest of the narrative should eventually intersect with the material in the hook.

section.title: Question Hook
section.para: Stories may also begin with a question hookA hook in which a story begins with an important question; the question usually frames the rest of the story. . The question may be deep, such as something religious or psychological, or maybe it’s simply unexpected—more like a surprising statement.

figure.label: Figure 8.19
figure.title:
Lady Justice.
Photo by Tingey Injury Law Firm via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Lady Justice holds scales in one hand and a sword in the other.

section.para: Our example will be a one-word question, from the very first line of the William Gaddis novel A Frolic of His Own:

para.emphasis: “Justice? —You get justice in the next world, in this world you have the law.”
para.footnote: Gaddis, W. (2013, June 18), A frolic of his own. Scribner, 1. (Original work published in 1994)

section.para: The question is a single word: “Justice?” But that word reverberates through the readers’ minds as they reflect on times they have or haven’t received justice. The question is philosophical, too, identifying a concept that philosophers have discussed for thousands of years.

Some stories may leave the hook question unanswered, but that isn’t what Gaddis does. Gaddis offers a character’s own answer, a cynical philosophical take: “You get justice in the next world, in this world you have the law.” Normally we associate justice with the law or see the law as the instrument of justice. This passage challenges that association and pushes us to consider the ways that the law falls short of actual justice in real life.

The question and its answer frame the rest of the story as an investigation into justice and its imperfect, real-world manifestations. A question hook can do the same for other stories by drawing attention to concepts or objects occupying a central place in the story. As such, this hook is appropriate for many genres.

section.title: Character Hook
section.para: The final hook we’ll discuss is the character hookA hook in which a story begins with an interesting or unusual character. , which works by describing an interesting or unusual character. This hook may involve more description than action, making it less likely to have a strong impact on audiences. But it’s still a viable option for some stories.

figure.label: Figure 8.20
figure.title:
Miss Brooke.
Photo by Suzy Hazelwood via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman from the Victorian era holding a teacup.

section.para: Here is an example of the character hook. It’s from the very beginning of the George EliotGeorge Eliot is Mary Anne Evans’s pen name. novel Middlemarch:

para.emphasis: “Miss Brooke had that kind of beauty which seems to be thrown into relief by poor dress. Her hand and wrist were so finely formed that she could wear sleeves not less bare of style than those in which the Blessed Virgin appeared to Italian painters; and her profile as well as her stature and bearing seemed to gain the more dignity from her plain garments, which by the side of provincial fashion gave her the impressiveness of a fine quotation from the Bible, — or from one of our elder poets,—in a paragraph of to-day’s newspaper.”
para.footnote: Eliot, G. (1994). Middlemarch: A study of provincial life. Wordsworth Classics, 5. (Original work published in 1871)

section.para: The character is Miss Brooke, and the opening sentence describes her as having the kind of beauty that’s emphasized by bad clothes. She has delicate features and is as impressive as a quote from the Bible or from a poet, but only if that poet were writing in a newspaper.
Those are all unusual ways to describe someone, suggesting that Miss Brooke herself is an unusual person. The only way to get to know her is to read on.

As we see in Eliot’s opener to Middlemarch, the character hook has a lot of description. But if the person is interesting enough, it may convince readers to stick around. Interesting people can populate any story, so any genre can begin with the character hook.

section.title: Varieties of Hooks
section.para: In this section, we’ve discussed nine different categories of hooks. They all work to attract an audience’s attention, and they do so in different ways. Some induce strong feelings; others rely on the unexpected or striking.

Each category of hook works best in certain genres of storytelling, but we’re always free to adapt a hook or change it for our own purposes. Whatever we use to get an audience interested in our story, the hook will frame everything else, setting an audience’s expectations for what they’ll get from our tale.

section.title: Designing a Hook
section.para: Now that we’ve seen different kinds of hooks, let’s try our hand at designing one of our own.

If we’re looking to write a hook, we probably already have some story ideas and maybe even a plot. In this case, our story will be about action heroine Shanique Saturn, the world’s best sharpshooter and the protector of Arcylla. Shanique is escaping from the henchmen of her archnemesis, Captain Opnyh, sworn enemy of the kingdom.

section.title: Generate Lots of Ideas

figure.label: Figure 8.21
figure.title:
Generate ideas.
Photo by Luca Nardone via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A cupped hand beneath a lightbulb.

section.para: The first step is to generate a lot of ideas. The more possibilities we have, the more we’ll be able to separate the good ideas from the boring ones to find the best one. Remember that ideas are cheap, and our first ones probably won’t be our best.

All we know about our story so far is that Saturn is escaping from some devious henchmen. An escape can happen in many ways, which means that we have a lot of room for being creative about how we open the story. Earlier, we saw our first draft of a hook for this story. Here it is again:

para.emphasis: Shanique Saturn dumped the empty shells from her gun and reloaded. The rain continued to pour and lightning crashed above her, knocking over her companions. But Shanique was unmoved. She was a Saturn, after all. And when death calls, Saturns answer.

section.para: The first half of these lines are standard action fare. The second half is stronger and has more potential, so we might want to build around that. The hook is overall is fine, but we can definitely do better.

section.title: Make a Hook More Interesting
section.para: The second half of our hook has Shanique responding to a scary situation, but it’s only rain and lightning so far. If we up the stakes and put her life in actual danger, then we’ll increase the excitement as well, and the part about answering when death calls will punch harder. Maybe we have her surrounded by Opnyh’s henchmen, facing certain doom, and her only resort is to go down in a blaze of glory. That’s a lot more interesting than rain. Here, then, is another try at a hook for Shanique:

blockquote.emphasis: Shanique Saturn dumped the empty shells from her gun and reloaded. Black-hooded soldiers surrounded her, their guns glistening in the rain. Lightning illuminated their faces: all eager to kill. Thunder crashed, the roar of bloodthirsty gods shaking the earth. She checked her magazine—a single bullet left. That was enough to face certain death.
Shanique was a Saturn, after all. And when death calls, a Saturn answers.

section.para: We’ve set the powerful part of our original hook as a separate paragraph for emphasis. We’ve also rewritten the material prior to that to put Shanique in more serious danger, which better sets up the bit about how a Saturn answers.

section.title: Revise a Hook Further

figure.label: Figure 8.22
figure.title:
Lightning.
Photo by takenbytablo via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Lightning in a dark sky.

section.para: This drop-into-the-action hook is definitely better than our first one, but it’s still just an early draft. We can build on it further and draw from other kinds of hooks to make the scene even more striking:

blockquote.emphasis: Shanique Saturn dumped the empty shells from her gun and reloaded. Black-hooded soldiers surrounded her, their guns glistening in the rain. Lightning illuminated their faces: all eager to kill. Thunder crashed, the roar of bloodthirsty gods shaking the earth. They would drink their fill before the day was through. She checked her magazine—a single bullet. That would be enough to take down four or five, six if she were lucky. That still left dozens. Death was near, all but certain.
But Shanique was a Saturn. And when death calls, a Saturn answers.

section.para: We’ve added more material to this new opening passage, referencing the coming fight and underscoring Shanique’s dire situation. We’ve also included a surprising statement: Shanique’s got only a single bullet, but apparently, she’ll be able to eliminate up to six henchmen with it. How can she do that? She must be awesome, and awesome characters make us want to read on.

section.title: Hooks Convince Audiences to Continue
section.para: Obviously, our audience knows that Shanique will survive the encounter, but they read on to find out how. This hook sets up a life-or-death struggle for our heroine and forces her to escape by the slimmest of margins. The frame for the rest of the story is action, action, action—and the stakes couldn’t be higher. The way this hook is written suggests that we’ll learn more about the Saturn family and what makes them so special.

figure.label: Figure 8.23
figure.title:
Hooks convince audiences to continue.
Photo by Josh Hild via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man sits under a tree in the dark reading a book with a flashlight.

section.para: We could no doubt improve this hook more if we kept brainstorming to refine it. Coming up with more and more ideas will help us vet the boring to get to the exciting and find the things that will make our audience feel something. That’s what makes for an effective hook.

As we think about our other stories, we will want to ask ourselves, what is new? What is fresh? How can we emphasize those parts? How can we draw from different categories of hooks to capture our audience and compel them to stay involved in our story?

Answering these questions well will take time. The opening parts of our stories will especially take a long time to refine. Not all parts of our story are created equal—the hook comes at the beginning for a reason. If we can interest an audience with a hook, then we’ve bought some time to describe a setting and to develop some characters. But if we lose them at the beginning, then our hard work elsewhere will mean nothing.
Let’s be ruthless in our search for the most interesting, powerful, and emotionally impactful ideas.

section.title: Reeling in the Hook
section.para: The image of “hooking an audience” tells us something about what a hook is supposed to do: capture an audience so that they’ll experience not just the first part of our story but the entire thing.

figure.label: Figure 8.24
figure.title:
Hooking an audience.
Photo by Lisa Fotios via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man lies on the couch reading a book.

section.para: But after the capture, the work isn’t over. We have to follow up on the promise of the hook with more interesting material to come. The rush isn’t as great—not every part of our story can be a hook—but boring the audiences in the third chapter is only marginally better than boring them on the first page.

section.title: Following Up Immediately
section.para: Our follow-up to the hook occurs in at least two different ways. First, we follow up on it immediately in the lines and pages that follow the opening. If it’s a hook in an action or mystery novel, we’ll want to sustain the suspense until the opening scene is completely finished. For other genres, we’ll want to maintain whatever tone we set by the hook. Once the opening is done, our plot will advance, and we can begin introducing other elements of the story.

section.title: Following Up Later
section.para: Second, the hook must also occur later in the story by fulfilling the promise of the hook and maintaining the tone and frame we established early on. The early parts of our story will set our audience’s expectations for what comes next, and we fill those expectations by delivering more of our good ideas. Once again, the need to capture an audience isn’t as urgent—the original hook has already done the capturing. But we also want to keep the audience around until they reach the end.
In later topics, we’ll discuss how other elements of stories work to generate audience interest until a story is finished.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 8.25
figure.title:
Hook.
Przemyslaw Koch © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A fishing hook against a white background.

section.para: This topic has built on previous topics by introducing the idea of a hook. A hook is anything designed to capture an audience, and most stories we’ll create will have hooks. The hooks are our way of standing out among a crowded world of stories.

There are many kinds of hooks, and we divided them into nine different categories. These hooks have different ways of working and don’t always appear at the very beginning of a story. But they all seek to get an audience invested in the characters and events of the story by making them feel and think in interesting, unusual, or powerful ways.

We design hooks by generating as many ideas as we can and then refining them into whatever is best. The openings of our stories, and the hooks, in particular, are some of the most important parts. Spending time to get them right will help our stories succeed in attracting and keeping audiences.

section.title: Something Finally Happens
section.para: At their most basic, stories involve characters experiencing events. Characters without experiences are static—they do nothing, cause nothing, and feel nothing. Events without characters are just causes and effects, empty of the kind of meaning we want our stories to have.

In , we added to our understanding of stories by introducing the idea of a hook. A hook is anything that interests an audience, and many stories, in many types of media, use hooks to capture an audience’s attention. A hook is less necessary to a story than characters and their experiences in the narrative. Although a hook at the beginning of a story does frame the material that follows it, a story can get by without a good hook and may even succeed without having one at all, depending on the audience.

section.title: Absence of Conflict

figure.label: Figure 9.1
figure.title:
Time to write.
Photo by picjumbo.com via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man writes in a notebook.

section.para: In this topic, we’ll discuss another element of stories: conflict. For stories, conflicts are more important than hooks but not as essential as characters and events. We can easily tell a story without a conflict—here’s one about me before I sat down to write this morning:

para.emphasis: The alarm rang. I shut it off and grabbed a towel. After a shower, I ate some breakfast. I read a bit of news, saw some sports scores, and laughed at a funny joke I remembered someone saying back in high school. Then I entered my office and shut the door. Pulling out my chair, I sat. It was time to write.

section.para: Let’s take a look at what we have here. There’s a character: me. And there’s a sequence of events, some of which have clear causal relationships to each other. There isn’t a hook, at least not in this passage. If we read these sentences, we might expect them to be the start of the story, but there are enough story elements here to consider the passage a story in its own right. It’s a boring story, and no one would want to read it, but it’s still a story.

Though my sentences count as a story, the narrative they tell lacks any kind of conflict, and that’s the main reason why the story is so boring. Who wants to read about someone getting ready for work and having breakfast when that’s all there is to the story? Not many people. Like a hook, conflict isn’t strictly necessary to a story, but a story without conflict is just someone’s boring life. There’s a character who’s living out a narrative but not much else.

section.title: Conflicts Make Things Interesting

figure.label: Figrue 9.2
figure.title:
Cucaracha Montoya.
Photo by David Clode via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: A cockroach.

section.para: Add some conflict and the story of my morning suddenly gets a bit more interesting:

para.emphasis: Pulling out my chair, I sat. It was time to write. But then a giant cockroach holding maracas leapt from my closet and spoke: “My name is Cucaracha Montoya. You killed my father. Prepare to die!”These lines have been adapted from The Princess Bride. Reiner, R. (1987, September 25). Act III Communications; Buttercup Films; The Princess Bride Ltd. The cockroach raised his maracas high. I scanned my desk, looking for a weapon. All I had was a broken pencil. I picked it up and kicked aside my chair. “I’ve been waiting,” I replied.

section.para: We’ve added some conflict, and the story is shaping up. The Pulitzer awaits!

section.title: Conflicts: Something Happens
section.para: Ok, not really. But the story is more interesting. We’ve gone from a boring list of things in my daily routine to a fight to the death between me and a giant insect. The story still has limited appeal since the market for stories recounting giant insect battles probably isn’t very large. But at least something happens.

And that’s the difference between a story that has conflicts and a story that doesn’t. Even though the original story of my morning had a narrative with a few events, nothing really happened. By “nothing,” we mean nothing meaningful or interesting or important from a human perspective. No one needs to experience that story because many people live it most mornings. Not everyone lives the conflict with Cucaracha Montoya, however, and that conflict gives life to the story.

section.title: Characters Have Goals
section.para: In our stories, we’ll want our characters to have goals. A goalSomething a character wants to achieve in a story. for a character in a story is the same as a goal we have in real life—it’s just something we want to achieve. The Joker’s goal in The Dark KnightNolan, C. (Director). (2008, July 18). The dark knight [Film]. Warner Bros. Pictures; DC Comics; Legendary Pictures; Syncopy. is to cause mayhem and panic; Batman’s goal in that story is to stop him. In section , my goal was to survive the cockroach battle, while the cockroach’s goal was to avenge his dead father. Each character in these stories wants to accomplish something.

figure.label: Figure 9.3
figure.title:
Characters have goals.
Photo by Julia M Cameron via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man sits at a desk. A schedule is written on a chalkboard above his head.

section.title: Goals Motivate Characters
section.para: The goals that characters have motivate them to act in certain ways and further their goals. Cucaracha Montoya’s lust for vengeance motivates him to wait in my closet until the time is right to strike; the Joker’s desire for chaos and pain motivates him to rig boats with explosives and to threaten the passengers. Goals are causes, and the actions are effects. Goals, therefore, have a natural place in the structure of a narrative as things that make other things happen.

section.title: Anything Can Be a Goal
section.para: Anything can be a goal: small or large, simple or complex. Wanting a newspaper, saving the world, designing a building, finding a child, and writing a book are all goals, and these and other goals could drive characters to do almost anything.

The goals our characters have will partly be determined by the kind of story we’re writing and what genre we’re writing in—saving the world is usually a goal in fantasy, science fiction, comic books, and related works, while a story about someone wanting a newspaper would probably be something out of literary fiction. But goals are also born out of what a character is like, their background and their circumstances. The fit of a goal with a character’s experiences, beliefs, and circumstances makes the goal comprehensible to the audience and allows for an easier fit between the character and the events in the narrative.

section.title: Goals Fit into the Story
section.para: Goals can be less comprehensible if we wish, but they may require suitable adjustments to the story. To make sense, a story about a man who wanted to be a bird would probably have to tell us a lot about who that man is and why he holds that goal. The goal falls so far outside normal human experience that it borders on the irrational, so the story would have some explaining to do. As we noted in section , the more unusual an event is, the greater the role it must occupy in the story in order for the narrative to make sense. The same goes for a character’s goals. The stranger they are, the more central a role they will probably play in a story.

Goals are a major way in which audiences identify with our characters. Audiences can see themselves in the characters as they fight and struggle to achieve what they want. Our morning routine may be easy, but a great deal of real life is spent pushing back against things we don’t control in order to produce the right results. Stories dramatize those struggles, and the characters who experience them can give audiences insight into themselves and their own struggles toward their goals.

section.title: What Are Conflicts?

figure.label: Figure 9.4
figure.title:
Conflict.
lightwise © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Two men walk on lines toward a cloud of many tangled lines.

section.para: Now that we’ve talked about goals, we’re ready for conflicts. In the context of story and narrative, a conflictAny obstacle in a story that blocks a character or characters from achieving their goals. is an obstacle of any kind that prevents a character from achieving some goal. In section , we’ll look at different types of conflict. For now, we’ll see some examples of conflicts and talk about the roles that these conflicts play in different stories.

section.title: Conflicts and Obstacles
section.para: The sample story we’ve been following involved me and a spiteful cockroach named Cucaracha. Cucaracha’s goal is to avenge his dead father, whom I apparently killed. He’ll get revenge when he puts an end to my existence. What’s the obstacle stopping Cucaracha from achieving this goal—in other words, what’s the conflict? The obstacle is my continued existence: as long as I am alive, Cucaracha’s goal cannot be achieved. The conflict is against me. Any struggle in an effort to destroy me is a struggle toward achieving Cucaracha’s goal.

The story of Cucaracha is an example of a goal that produces a somewhat one-sided narrative. What would be my goal in that story, after all? I definitely want to survive, which is why I pick up the broken pencil to fight. Cucaracha threatens my life and so becomes an obstacle to me, but I actually have many ways of achieving my goal of surviving: I can win the fight, run out of the house, or grab a can of Raid. Cucaracha, on the other hand, has a more specific goal and a narrower avenue to achieve it. The one-sidedness of the narrative gives a deeper motivation to Cucaracha, so the story might be better served by focusing on him.

section.title: Broader Conflicts, Broader Obstacles

figure.label: Figure 9.5
figure.title:
Avengers.
Anton Ivanov © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Iron Man, Hulk, Captain America, Scarlet Witch, and Thor.

section.para: Other stories feature goals and conflicts that aren’t so focused on a single character. In the Avengers: Infinity WarRusso, A. & Russo, J. (Directors). (2018, April 23). Avengers: Infinity war [Film]. Marvel Studios. and Avengers: EndgameRusso, A. & Russo, J. (Directors). (2019, April 26). Avengers: Endgame [Film]. Marvel Studios. movies, the villain Thanos wishes to eliminate half the living creatures in the universe. This goal motivates him to seek out the Infinity Gauntlet and Infinity Stones, the weapons capable of doing the job. The Avengers, a group of superheroes, are working against Thanos. They recognize the problems that Thanos wants to resolve by killing, but they wish to deal with those problems in other ways. Their goals put them in opposition to Thanos, and the conflict arises from the motivations of both sides.

section.title: Smaller Conflicts, Smaller Obstacles
section.para: The Avengers moviesWhedon, J., Russo, A. & Russo, J. (Directors). (2012–2019). The avengers [Film series]. Marvel Studios. take place on a grand scale, with the fate of the universe at stake. But conflicts don't need to be this large. In the Dr. Seuss book Green Eggs and Ham,Dr. Seuss. (1960, August 12). Green eggs and ham. Random House; The Living Books Company. the unnamed main character faces an onslaught of offers to try a plate of green eggs and ham. This character’s motivation is a conservative one: he wants to keep his life comfortable and familiar and isn’t interested in anything new. Consequently, he refuses all offers of the food. Opposed to him is adventurous foodie Sam-I-Am, who wants nothing more than to get his friend to try the dish. The conflict between “what is the same” and “what is new” escalates throughout the book. Here, nothing is at stake but one part of a single person’s lifestyle. Nothing more is needed for the story, however. Everyone in the audience can relate to the conflict, and it’s sufficient to drive the zany events in the story.

We’ve described the conflicts we’ve seen so far at a very high level as the overarching clash that underlies an entire book or movie. But in many cases these larger conflicts consist of smaller ones that take place in single chapters or scenes, contributing to the story as a whole. Let’s take a look at such a conflict next.

section.title: Breaking Conflicts Down

figure.label: Figure 9.6
figure.title:
The Empire.
Photo by Brian McGowan via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Many empire soldiers lined up.

section.para: In Star Wars: A New Hope,Lucas, G. (Director). (1977, May 25). Star wars: A new hope [Film]. Lucasfilm Ltd. the Rebel Alliance is at war with the Empire. From a high level, the conflict is easy to discern because the goals of the Alliance and the Empire are in direct conflict: the Alliance wants to break the Empire’s authoritarian stranglehold on much of the galaxy, while the Empire wants to consolidate and increase its power. This conflict provides the backdrop for the movie and its sequels.

The high-level conflict then plays out in the various events of the narrative. For example, when Obi-Wan, Luke Skywalker, and Han Solo try to rescue Princess Leia, Obi-Wan has a lightsaber battle with Darth Vader. In that scene, Darth Vader’s goal is to destroy Obi-Wan, while Obi-Wan’s goal is to buy time for everyone else to escape. This conflict is much more specific than “Alliance vs. Empire,” but it clearly relates to the larger conflict with Obi-Wan representing the Alliance and Darth Vader the empire.

In this example, the local conflict between Obi-Wan and Darth Vader drives a particular scene, while the global conflict between the Alliance and the Empire drives the entire movie. The local conflict provides motivations for character actions in the short term, while the global conflict provides motivations for characters and groups of characters in the long term. The smaller conflict is nested inside the larger, being a particular instance of a much more general goal.

section.title: Nesting Conflicts
section.para: This nested relationship between conflicts, in which a smaller conflict represents the larger in some way, isn’t always necessary. In a later Star Wars movie, Return of the Jedi,Marquand, R. (Director). (1983, May 25). Star wars: Return of the Jedi [Film]. Lucasfilm Ltd. the characters try to rescue Han from the bounty hunter Jabba the Hutt. The primary conflict is still the global one between the Alliance and the Empire, but Jabba doesn’t represent the Empire and bears no relation to it, at least as presented in the movie. The particular conflicts with Jabba occur outside of the ongoing main one, but the narrative soon returns to the Alliance’s battle against the Empire.

Smaller conflicts occurring outside of the main one can serve various purposes, including developing characters, creating tension, or setting up some other important event. In our stories, there’s nothing wrong with having minor conflicts that don’t follow the main sequence of events. We should be clear about the purpose of these conflicts, however, or else our story will begin to wander as we lose the thread of the narrative.

In Star Wars, the Empire places obstacles in the way of the Alliance getting the freedom they seek—in other words, the Empire creates conflicts. These conflicts are the centerpiece for the movies, just as Thanos’s struggle to kill half of all living things is the centerpiece of several Avengers films. The conflict involves two sides, both fighting to achieve their goals and prevent the other side from achieving theirs. Smaller conflicts are smaller obstacles that occur along the way, contributing to the global conflict or other aspects of the story.

section.title: Types of Conflicts
section.para: In previous sections, we saw various examples of conflicts, from children’s stories to epic universe-spanning adventures. In each case, the characters had goals, and something was stopping them from achieving those goals.

In this section, we’ll learn about three different types of conflict: character-to-character, character-to-world, and world-to-world. (See .) Each type involves different conflicting entities, so the obstacles differ as well.

figure.label: Figure 9.7
figure.title: Types of conflict.

imagedata.alt: Three types of conflict labeled in circles. 1. Character-to-character conflict. 2. Character-to-world conflict. 3. World-to-world conflict.

section.title: Character-to-Character Conflicts

figure.label: Figure 9.8
figure.title: Character-to-character conflict.

imagedata.alt: Two stick figures fighting each other with swords.

section.para: All the examples we’ve seen so far involve a conflict between two or more characters. This is the first type: a character-to-character conflictA conflict in a story occurring between two or more characters. . (See .) Character-to-character conflicts are the most common in all genres of fiction. They make up stereotypical battles between good and evil and also describe more mundane interactions, such as the friction between an employee and a boss when the former asks for a raise.

In a character-to-character conflict, the characters have their own goals, and the goals are incompatible—they cannot both be satisfied at the same time. In Green Eggs and Ham, the unnamed character’s goal is to lead a comfortable life with familiar experiences, but Sam-I-Am’s goal is to get him to try the new dish. The goals themselves are in conflict; achieving or trying to achieve one is an obstacle to achieving the other. The goals cannot coexist, so something has to give.

This feature that both goals cannot be achieved is why character-to-character conflict is so common in many stories. Characters are essential to stories, and when the goals of two characters are incompatible, a natural conflict arises. If those characters are really committed to their goals, then they will be motivated to act to achieve them. The actions they take will be events in the narrative. They’ll push against each other as they place obstacles in the other’s path. Their interactions will continue to escalate until a climactic moment arises, and—boom!—we’ve got a story. And it all came from conflicts between characters.

section.title: Multiple Conflicting Characters
section.para: A character-to-character conflict can involve more than two characters. In the animated film Toy Story,Lasseter, J. (Director). (1995, November 19). Toy Story [Film]. Walt Disney Pictures; Pixar Animation Studios. there’s an initial conflict between the toys Woody and Buzz Lightyear because the former doesn’t want to share his relationship with their owner, Andy. But as Woody fights against Buzz, their conflict grows to engulf the other toys, who align themselves with Buzz.
