A one-character-to-one-character conflict becomes a one-character-to-many-characters conflict, and Woody must work to restore his good name not only with Buzz but also with everyone else.

It isn’t really possible to have an important conflict between a main character and a secondary character. If there is a large conflict between two characters, then both are main characters. They both need to have a large impact on the story in order for the conflict to play itself out across the narrative. There may be subordinate conflicts between main characters and secondary ones, but these tend to occupy less space in the story or be resolved quickly in order to contribute to larger conflicts.

The key is that the characters in a story’s most important character-to-character conflicts will figure prominently in the story. They may not be point-of-view characters—the antagonist, or enemy of the main character, isn’t always a point-of-view character, for example—but we still know who these characters are and what their goals and motivations are. We know that they are playing an active role in putting up obstacles for other characters.

section.title: Character-to-World Conflicts

figure.label: Figure 9.9
figure.title: Character-to-world conflict.

imagedata.alt: A stick figure with a sword with a graphic of earth.

section.para: The second type of conflict is a character-to-world conflictA conflict in a story occurring between characters and the world or setting in which the story is based. . (See .) In a character-to-world conflict, characters are not struggling against other characters, or at least not exclusively. Rather, they are fighting against obstacles coming from the world or the setting where they live. In most cases, these obstacles are naturally occurring events that no character chooses to create or cause; they just happen in the world and provide the conflicts for characters.

Stories of survival usually feature character-to-world conflicts, and a classic example is the novel Robinson Crusoe.Defoe, D. (1719, April 25). Robinson Crusoe. William Taylor. Published in 1719, the story follows the struggles of the titular character, who ends up stranded on a remote island and must fight to survive for more than twenty years. Crusoe has interactions with other characters at times, but the main conflict in the story is character-to-world. His goal is to survive, and the obstacles are natural dangers that anyone would face in such a situation.

Other survival stories, such as the Tom Hanks film Cast AwayZemeckis, R. (Director). (2000, December 22). Cast away [Film]. ImageMovers; Playtone. or the Jurassic Park movies,Spielberg, S., Johnston, J., Trevorrow, C., & Bayona, J.A. (Directors). (1993–2018). Jurassic park [Film series]. Amblin Entertainment; Universal Pictures; Legendary Entertainment; The Kennedy/Marshall Company; Perfect World Pictures. involve similar conflicts. A character-to-world conflict plays a smaller role in many other stories as well. In The Hunger Games,Collins, S. (2008, September 14). The hunger games [Book series]. Scholastic Press. the overarching conflict driving the story is that between poorer and wealthier citizens of Panem. That’s a character-to-character conflict. But a major part of the book sees the characters in a struggle against the obstacles in the arena, where they face traps and other dangers. Those conflicts and obstacles are character-to-world.

Character-to-world conflicts are not as common as character-to-character conflicts and are usually more specific to particular genres of fiction. Other branches of survivalism use character-to-world conflicts, including many stories with apocalyptic or post-apocalyptic events.

section.title: World-to-World Conflicts

figure.label: Figure 9.10
figure.title: World-to-world conflict.

imagedata.alt: Two graphics of earth.

section.para: The third type of conflict is a world-to-world conflictA conflict in a story occurring between two aspects of the world or setting in which the story is based. , the least common. (See .) In a world-to-world conflict, forces beyond the control of the characters struggle against each other to achieve their goals. Such stories often feature passive characters who experience or merely observe and report on events because they are not able or powerful enough to cause anything meaningful to happen.

One genre where we see world-to-world conflicts is far-future science fiction. Some authors imagine alien races whose scientific knowledge so far outpaces that of humanity that they are effectively omnipotent. The conflicts between races that powerful are sometimes depicted as beyond human comprehension, so the characters merely observe what is happening to them rather than taking an active role in the narrative. An example of a story like this is the novel RingBaxter, S. (1994, July 4). Ring. HarperCollins. by Stephen Baxter. Novels from author Olaf Stapledon, like Star Maker,Stapledon, O. (1937). Star maker. Methuen. also use world-to-world conflicts.

Most of the stories we write will involve character-to-character conflicts. The most common deviation from that pattern will use character-to-world conflicts to put characters in danger or transition from one part of the narrative to another.

section.title: Conflict and Narrative Tension
section.para: In stories with conflicts, things actually happen. Characters act to achieve their goals, which stops other characters from achieving their goals, and interactions between all characters drive a narrative forward to its conclusion.

section.title: Keeping an Audience’s Attention
section.para: Conflict in stories also plays an important role for audiences. The hook captures an audience’s attention, but conflict helps keep that attention over time. Audiences invest themselves in the conflicts, take sides, and keep reading or watching a story to find out what happens. Their investment may be emotional, intellectual, or both, but at its root, the conflict keeps them going.

section.title: Narrative Tension
section.para: Conflict makes this happen by creating narrative tensionThe uncertainty an audience feels about what will happen in a story; narrative tension motivates an audience to find out what comes next. . Narrative tension is the uncertainty felt by an audience about what is going to happen in a story; audience members desire to resolve that uncertainty by finding out what comes next. That desire keeps them turning pages. At its root, narrative tension is what makes audiences go on in a story. It’s what stops them from putting the book down, changing the channel, or walking out of the theater.

figure.label: Figure 9.11
figure.title:
Narrative tension.
Prudencio Alvarez © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man looks astonished as he holds a book.

section.para: Some writers speak of narrative tension as the uncertainty that a story’s characters feel toward the events within the story. Characters do often feel uncertain about what to do or about what will happen to them. But from the perspective of authors trying to write stories themselves, it is much more useful to think of narrative tension as something an audience feels rather than as what the characters are feeling.

section.title: Narrative Tension in the Audience
section.para: Here is an example to illustrate the difference and to emphasize the importance of narrative tension on the audience’s part. Suppose we’re writing a story about a stalker, and in our story, the stalker is currently hiding out in a man’s house. The man who’s being stalked has no idea that there’s someone else in his place—he comes home from work and makes dinner, totally oblivious to the woman watching him. This man feels no uncertainty about anything; for him, it’s just a normal weeknight. But the audience for our story knows that the stalker is there, and so they feel completely differently! The audiencs feels the narrative tension because they know something that the character doesn’t. The audience’s uncertainty and even dread about what will happen next keeps their attention and compels them to go on. It is the audience’s feelings that matter, not the character’s feelings.

As authors, our job is to create that tension. If we want audiences to care about our stories, we have to craft them in ways that create narrative tension. We have to put characters in difficult situations and let them struggle. We have to bring together events imaginatively so that they interact in unexpected ways, creating conflicts that the audience can’t see coming. The surprise and tension our audiences feel in themselves will glue them to their seats.

section.title: Creating Narrative Tension
section.para: In the remainder of this section, we will suggest one way to generate this narrative tension: nesting conflicts. This method is a suggestion, not a rule. There are many different ways of crafting stories and the tension that makes them interesting. Different authors write in different ways and have different workflows. It’s important to give many methods a try, but most importantly, find what works for you and what leads you to the most interesting characters and conflicts.

section.title: Nesting Conflicts

figure.label: Figure 9.12
figure.title:
Harry Potter.
Photo by Vinícius Vieira ft via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A red and gold scarf on a desk next to glasses.

section.para: One way to think about building this narrative tension is by starting with the overarching conflict. In the Harry Potter novels,Rowling, J.K. (1997–2007). Harry Potter [Book series]. Bloomsbury; Arthur A. Levine/Scholastic; Raincoast. the overarching conflict is Harry against Voldemort. In Star Wars,Lucas, G., Kershner, I., Marquand, R., Johnson, R., & Abrams J. J. (Directors). (1977–2019). Star wars [Film series]. Lucasfilm Ltd.; 20th Century Fox; Bad Robot Productions. it’s the Rebel Alliance against the Empire. In The Old Man and the Sea,Hemingway, E. (1952). The old man and the sea. Charles Scribner’s Sons. it is Santiago against the fish and everything the fish represents. With these overarching conflicts comes a fairly natural division into sides of the conflict. Harry and all his friends are on one side, facing off against Voldemort and the Death Eaters. Luke, Han, and Leia are on one side, while Darth Vader, the Emperor, and the Storm Troopers are on another. Santiago is battling old age, a dying way of life, and past failures, which are all represented in the form of a fish.

The conflicts we have identified are too large to be entirely resolved in an individual scene or event—that is, unless we want our story to be pretty short. Take the conflict between Harry and Voldemort in the Harry Potter series as an example. The series’ author, J. K. Rowling, could have boiled the seven-book series down to a short story by having Harry and Voldemort face off immediately for the final battle. But the story is bigger than that, and the conflict goes beyond those two characters as well, enveloping thousands of people across the world. Rowling couldn’t share her vision with so little space.

It follows that we must break down the overarching conflict into smaller conflicts, nested inside the larger one. We create smaller conflicts by looking at our characters, their goals, and the setting. We then ask ourselves, What do these characters want? How will they act to get it? Then we design events in which they must overcome obstacles to get what they want. Each event and obstacle is a small contribution to the narrative tension the audience feels.

section.title: Conflicts Build toward a Climax
section.para: Let’s use Harry Potter as an example again. In the large-scale conflict, Harry wants to overcome Voldemort and the evil he represents. But Harry also wants to attend school at Hogwarts, go to Hogsmeade, play quidditch, and do other normal things. The narrative of each Harry Potter book follows a similar pattern, placing Harry in events where he is able to achieve his goals by overcoming various obstacles. He wants to attend school but misses the train in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets,Rowling, J. K. (1998, July 2). Harry Potter and the chamber of secrets. Bloomsbury; Arthur A. Levine; Scholastic; Raincoast. so he and Ron have to overcome that obstacle by taking the flying car. Harry wants to help his team win quidditch but has to outrun a rogue bludger.

The Harry Potter books are filled with small conflicts or minor obstacles in the way of smaller goals. But these smaller conflicts and events lead inexorably toward a much larger conflict, one that is more directly a part of the fundamental struggle of the entire series.

Harry’s various school experiences in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets eventually land him in the Chamber of Secrets, where he has a showdown with Voldemort’s forces. The scene in the Chamber is the climaxThe point at which a story’s conflicts reach their breaking point and the stakes and excitement are highest. of the book—everything previous has combined to force Harry to go there and confront his antagonist. The narrative tension is at its highest. In fact, it couldn’t be higher because the confrontation between them is the major conflict of the book. Its outcome has major ramifications for the direction of the overall plot. But it is the smaller events that lead these characters to the confrontation, one step at a time.

section.title: Aligning Conflicts toward the Climax

figure.label: Figure 9.13
figure.title:
Climax in a story.
iStock.com/pick-uppath.

imagedata.alt: An open book with mountains coming out of it. A character stands on top of the mountain with a flag.

section.para: As we break down the overarching conflict into smaller ones, we align the conflicts so that they lead toward the larger conflict or climax at the end. This clash between the two sides of the conflict will bring together all the characters and all their goals into a crisis whose resolution cannot end well for everyone. Not everyone’s goals will be achieved; even characters who have experienced small successes in previous events may end up disappointed. Those small events were merely waypoints to the culmination of the narrative in which the plot conflict is resolved.

Usually, the smaller conflicts escalate in size and stakes as the narrative progresses. The narrative tension increases in a corresponding way. When the conflicts can’t get any bigger, then suddenly everything comes to a head—the smaller conflicts have come together to form the largest possible conflict between all the characters, and the narrative tension created by the story reaches its peak. At that point, many in the audience will be feeling an overwhelming desire to find out how everything is resolved, no matter the cost. That’s the desire that keeps people up at night finishing a book or movie because they can’t bear to go to bed without knowing what happens.

section.title: The Slow-Burn Narrative
section.para: Narrative tension like that is built over time in a slow burn of smaller events that push characters toward the climax. The final conflict might be like an explosion, but it’s not a bomb that goes off spontaneously without explanation. Each minor conflict lights the next part of the fuse and builds the tension to a point where the incompatibility of the characters’ goals forces them to face each other once and for all.

With planning and patience, we can create that narrative tension in our stories. Conflicts do it, but it usually isn’t just one. We break down our largest conflict into smaller ones, and then the smaller ones grow and grow until they inevitably lead back to the largest. Narrative tension grows along with the conflicts. As the characters put more and more on the line, audiences do too.

section.title: Conflict, Character Action, and Struggle
section.para: In the examples and suggestions we’ve given so far, we’ve been treating every story as though it’s a high-stakes affair where the fate of the entire world hangs in the balance. For some stories, like Star Wars or Harry Potter, that is actually true. However, many other stories don’t occur on that scale, and they deal with conflicts that are limited to a particular place, community, or individual.

The principles we’ve discussed will still apply to more limited conflicts. Character-to-character conflicts can be local and even intimate, involving few characters and seemingly routine events. But even in smaller conflicts, storytellers can still create narrative tension, and that tension can be just as agonizing for the audience as it is when the universe is at stake.

section.title: A More Intimate Conflict
section.para: A good example of such a story is the 2019 film Marriage Story.Baumbach, N. (Director). (2019, August 29), Marriage story [Film]. Heyday Films. Marriage Story focuses on the relationship between a husband and wife. The conflicts between them do not extend far outside their immediate family, but they still carry great emotional power and create enormous narrative tension for the audience. The principles of conflict apply to conflicts of all kinds, regardless of scale.

Likewise, conflicts are for all genres of storytelling. As long as characters have goals and face obstacles, then our stories will have conflicts. Comedies, action stories, thrillers, science fiction, romance, and other works have features determined by conventions unique to their genre, but they’ll all have characters who want to accomplish things and struggle to get there.

section.title: Conflict and Character Action

figure.label: Figure 9.14
figure.title:
Character actions make chains of cause and effect.
Scott Betts © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A link in a chain formed by groups of people.

section.para: Conflicts push characters to act. Their actions are part of the chain of causes and effects in the narrative. A character’s actions cause other things to happen and may place obstacles in the way of other characters. Those characters will then respond by acting to achieve their goals, which will cause other things to happen, which will place obstacles in the path of the first character, and on and on.

We’re familiar with this feedback loop from real life, where we experience it every day. We might start our day with the goal of getting our daughter ready for preschool, while she wakes up with the goal of ruining everything we want to do. We pick an outfit, and she throws it downstairs; we respond by picking another, and she does the same. This back-and-forth of character action, in which an action produces an effect and feeds back into a sequence to influence other things, is what real life is made of.

Stories are made of the same elements: causes and effects, actions and reactions, goals and efforts, and failures and successes. We comprehend stories so easily because they’re our lives on a screen or on a page.

section.title: Making Characters Struggle
section.para: We’ll finish this section with a note on struggle. Many people spend much of their lives trying to achieve their goals and thereby minimize conflict in one way or another. Whether their goals are big or small, characters in stories try to do the same thing. They’ll act to overcome conflicts and obstacles, and they dissolve the conflicts by reaching their goals.

As the authors of stories, however, we get to decide the conflicts our characters face. Having that control, sometimes we’ll feel the temptation to let our characters off easy or to rescue them from their conflicts and spare them real struggle. There are at least two good reasons not to let our characters off easy, though, and to instead make them struggle.

The first reason is that storytelling is about dramatizing real life, not necessarily depicting what is strictly real. Authors get to choose which aspects of life they will present in their stories. Those choices reveal something about what an author believes to be important. By choosing to involve our characters in difficult struggles, we emphasize their humanity and the importance of the human struggle for success in a difficult world.

figure.label: Figure 9.15
figure.title:
Characters struggle.
Photo by Vera Arsic via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Two people looking upset sit on a bench next to each other.

section.para: The second reason is that emphasizing our character’s humanity can have a powerful effect on audiences. Audiences are drawn to stories of accomplishment against difficult odds. No one wants to watch a character battle to write an office memo, but they may want to watch a character struggle to provide for his family after losing his job and being evicted from his home. The latter conflict is far more difficult, which gives it much greater power to impact audiences. With difficult challenges for characters, authors choose to emphasize the human ability to push back against what is truly tough to deal with.
We may love our characters, but that doesn’t mean we have to make life easy for them. Their triumph will be all the sweeter when they face down the biggest conflicts we can provide for them.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 9.16
figure.title:
Conflicts are necessary for good stories.
Michal Bednarek © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man pushes a boulder up a hill.

section.para: Conflicts aren’t strictly necessary for stories, but they do make stories interesting. Any story worth paying attention to will feature many conflicts. They can be small or large and can occur between characters or the world they live in.

Conflicts fit into the natural network of causes and effects in our stories: an obstacle in one character’s path causes them to react, which puts an obstacle in a different character’s path. This process occurs many times in different ways over the course of a story.

Conflicts also produce narrative tension, or the audience’s uncertainty about what will happen next. Narrative tension is a key part of keeping an audience after getting them interested in the first place. This tension grows as the conflicts do and motivates audiences to keep experiencing the story in order to find out what happens.
Conflicts may not be necessary for stories, but they are necessary for good stories.

section.title: Upping the Ante
section.para: We’ve now covered narrative, characters, messages, hooks, and conflicts. In this topic, we’ll add a new weapon to our storytelling arsenal: stakes.

As we noted earlier, the two elements most essential to a story are narrative and character. Even a very boring group of sentences can count as a story as long as we’ve got events happening in someone or something’s existence. A sequence of events and someone experiencing those events is all it takes to make a story.

section.title: Good Stories
section.para: However, we’re interested in making good stories, so we’ve gone beyond narrative and character to add things like hooks and conflicts. Hooks capture the audience’s attention; conflicts create narrative tension, or the anticipation an audience feels when wanting to know what happens next. Anyone who’s binged a book or a TV show before knows that blending interesting conflicts together can keep an audience reading or watching for hours at a time—even if it means missing food or sleep.

section.title: What’s On the Line

figure.label: Figure 10.1
figure.title:
Stakes.
iuphotos © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A chalk drawing showing a scale with “risk” on one side and “reward” on the other.

section.para: The concept of stakesWhat is on the line in a particular situation, or what a story’s characters stand to gain or lose. complements hooks and conflicts in creating narrative tension. The stakes are what’s on the line in a particular situation, or what the characters stand to gain or lose as a result of what they do. We’re familiar with this idea from many areas of life. For two high school basketball teams in the state championship game, the stakes are the state championship—the winning team takes the prize; the losing team goes home empty-handed. The stakes of a poker game are the amount of money that a player will lose or gain. A stake in a legal battle over a deceased relative’s inheritance is the control of money and property.

Stakes complement hooks and conflicts by helping create and increase narrative tension. As a rule of thumb, we can say the higher the stakes, the higher the narrative tension. When more is on the line, audiences will generally be more interested in finding out what happens. If all that a character stands to lose in a conflict with his adversary is a nickel or a sandwich, then audiences will probably not be too invested in the outcome of the conflict. For many people, the normal events in a day are low-stakes affairs, not the kind of thing that an external audience would want to engage with.

section.title: Characters Experiencing Stakes
section.para: That doesn’t mean that a story where the fate of the universe is at stake is automatically more interesting than one whose conflicts and stakes are much smaller. We don’t need to threaten all existence or someone’s life in order for the stakes to be high. What we mean by “high stakes” has more to do with how characters experience the stakes than it does with the scale or quantity of the stakes. In a story about a woman’s choice to give a baby up for adoption, for example, the stakes are objectively low, in that her decision affects almost nothing outside her own life. But for her personally, nothing could be more important, so the stakes couldn’t be higher—in her own experience, absolutely everything could ride on that one choice. A good story can help an audience feel those stakes as keenly as any other event.

Ultimately, stakes work like hooks and conflicts to keep audiences interested. If what’s on the line in a conflict is something of real value to a character, no matter how objectively valuable it might be, then audiences will feel that narrative tension. They’ll experience increasing amounts of conflict as the outcome of the stakes becomes more and more uncertain. The readers’ desire to resolve the tension will keep them invested in the story until the very end.

section.title: Conflict and Loss
section.para: In section , we suggested that it can be a bad idea to let our characters off easy in our stories. We made this suggestion for at least two reasons: One, storytelling is a dramatization of real life, exploring unfamiliar conflicts in unfamiliar ways. Two, audiences are more likely to be interested in characters who overcome long odds or who really struggle to achieve something.

One way we let characters off easy is by allowing them to experience only minor conflicts. If our characters never deal with anything difficult, then they never face any tests and don’t have to fight for what they want. Audiences may have a hard time relating to our characters when they get everything for free or when doors are always open for them.

section.title: The Possibility of Real Loss
section.para: Adding conflicts to our story is one way of helping us to avoid going easy on our characters. But there’s also another way—stakes. We would also be taking it too easy on our story’s characters if we never made them face any consequences for their mistakes or bad decisions. If making the wrong choice or losing a conflict doesn’t produce any real loss—if it doesn’t take away or deprive a character of something with real value—then there’s nothing really at stake. The conflict could be as broad as the universe, but if losing it means a character walks away unscathed, then the conflict couldn’t have been very great after all.

section.title: An Illustration of Stakes: Two Children’s Games
section.para: Great conflicts require great stakes. The conflicts might be physical, as in actual battles or wars, or they could be psychological, as in a character’s struggle to forge or maintain a certain identity. Whatever the conflicts are, there must be a real possibility of loss.

section.title: Candy Land

figure.label: Figure 10.2
figure.title:
Candy Land.
Aleksei Sysoev © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A gingerbread house surrounded by candy and sweets.

section.para: Let’s illustrate the importance of stakes by considering some children’s games. Candy Land is a game in which players advance on the board by drawing cards. Most cards have one or two colored squares. A blue square means that the player advances to the next blue square on the board; a double purple means that she moves to the second purple square ahead of her current position. Players take turns drawing cards and moving their pieces until they reach the goal of meeting King Candy in Candy Land.

Even in this simple setup, there are unique features that increase the stakes of the game. There are three spaces on the board that require players to lose a turn or draw a certain card before continuing their progress. Additionally, some of the cards in the deck (or on the spinner in modern editions of the game) correspond to special character spaces in fixed positions on the track. These special cards can make players surge forward on the board or drop back along the track.

section.title: Chutes and Ladders

figure.label: Figure 10.3
figure.title:
Chutes and Ladders.
Erin Cadigan © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A board game with multiple squares that have either chutes or ladders.

section.para: Chutes and Ladders is another children’s game that utilizes stakes and chance. The game board is a 10 x 10 grid of squares that players traverse by spinning a number and then moving that many squares. A number of chutes, or slides, and ladders connect the various squares. Players who land on a square with a ladder leap ahead by climbing the ladder to a new square, while those who land on a chute square lose progress by sliding back to a previous square.

Chutes and Ladders and Candy Land are interesting because the game boards and cards are full of danger, uncertainty, and meaningful obstacles. With Chutes and Ladders, most versions of the game increase the number of chutes near the goal so that getting to the end is a real accomplishment. A player who makes one unlucky spin can lose everything, falling back by more than fifty or sixty squares in a single turn. Conversely, hitting the right ladder launches a player forward and can turn the tables on players who are farther ahead. In Candy Land, a player can draw a character card at any point and get suddenly whisked away to a different area of the board, often to the detriment of the player’s progress. These games are interesting until the very end because the stakes are real, and the final outcome is always unknown.

section.title: Stakes
section.para: Even these simple games made for preschoolers are engaging because of how the games utilize stakes. You would be hard-pressed to find a game of chance that only utilizes positive chance; low or no-stakes games likely aren’t as fun or successful and would not survive in the market. The same is true of low or no-stake stories. Good stories have conflicts and real stakes. Sliding down a long chute or being sent back to the first character space is a real loss that jeopardizes a player’s goal and threatens to nullify the entire journey. Likewise, a protagonist’s struggle toward what he wants may all be for nothing if he makes a wrong choice or fails to overcome an obstacle in time.

section.title: Loss and Narrative Tension
section.para: The possibility of real loss helps create the narrative tension that pushes audiences to move forward in a story. Part of the anticipation to find out what happens next is knowing that it might be something bad. But if a narrative is just an uninterrupted string of lucky coincidences that always turn out well, then the tension can’t rise nearly as high.

Now, some audiences do want everything to turn out all right all the time. There isn’t anything wrong with writing those stories, especially if we write them in a way that the outcome really does seem unknown. But if the stakes are high and our characters never lose, then we’ll be missing out on domains of experience that are just as characteristic of human life as winning, if not more so. Consequently, we’ll put artificial limits on the depth and emotional impact our stories can have.

section.title: Stakes: What’s in Play?
section.para: Earlier, we defined “stakes” as what’s on the line in a particular situation. Let’s discuss the general idea of stakes in more detail and give some specific examples of stakes in stories.

section.title: What Are Stakes?
section.para: The stakes in a story are what’s on the line: what is disputed, what will be gained or lost, or what will be understood, learned, forgotten, remembered, or otherwise changed in any way. We usually talk about stakes in terms of gaining and losing, but we aren’t just referring to physical objects. As we’ll see later, some of the most important stakes are mental or psychological objects, like a character’s self-image or self-understanding.

figure.label: Figure 10.4
figure.title:
Stakes in a story.
Photo by Dariusz Grosa via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A wooden fence with many stakes.

section.title: Stakes Are Important to Characters
section.para: Anything can be at stake in a story as long as it’s important. By “important,” though, we don’t mean “objectively important,” as in, “everyone on earth believes that this thing is important.” All we mean is that the stakes must be important to a particular character. Even if the stakes are something the audience doesn’t care about, audience members can still care about the character’s pursuit of those stakes because they recognize that what the character feels for her goal is what they feel for their own goals. Audiences relate not to the specific object at stake but to what a character feels about that object.

section.title: Examples of Stakes
section.para: Let’s see some specific examples of stakes in stories. In larger, multi-part works, like Star WarsLucas, G., Kershner, I., Marquand, R., Johnson, R., & Abrams J. J. (Directors). (1977–2019). Star wars [Film series]. Lucasfilm Ltd.; 20th Century Fox; Bad Robot Productions. and Harry Potter,Rowling, J.K. (1997–2007). Harry Potter [Book series]. Bloomsbury; Arthur A. Levine/Scholastic; Raincoast. the stakes are usually large and affect many people. In Star Wars, the lives of the main characters are at stake, but they are also fighting for something much larger than themselves. They are part of the Rebel Alliance, which fights for freedom from oppression and a return to representative government. Opposite them stands the Empire, fighting for power and what they perceive as a superior way to run the galaxy. Characters’ lives are at stake but so are their values, ideas, hopes, and ways of life.

Note that while the characters in Star Wars have a deep personal investment in the stakes of the story, that investment doesn’t have much to do with self-preservation. Of course, the characters would like to survive, if possible, but many are willing to give their lives to achieve their goals and win the stakes. The stakes are high partly because the characters’ lives are of secondary importance compared to their ideals. Accordingly, audiences are invested because the conflict and the stakes go beyond life and death; they are worth living and dying for.

The novels in the Harry Potter series have similar stakes. The scale is a bit smaller—Voldemort is after power over the world, not the galaxy—but the lines between good and evil are drawn like those in Star Wars. The characters also fight for similar values and are willing to die for their goals rather than be subject to the tyranny of the opposition. The escalating conflicts over the course of the books, some marked with blood, manifest the reality of the stakes and clarify that no character will escape from the battle unscathed.

section.title: Stakes on a Smaller Scale

figure.label: Figure 10.5
figure.title:
Okonkwo.
Photo by Dazzle Jam via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An African man with markings on his face dressed in colorful cloth.

section.para: Let’s look at some stakes that take place on a smaller scale but are no less real in the lives of the story’s inhabitants. In the novel Things Fall ApartAchebe, C. (1958) Things fall apart. William Heinemann Ltd. by Chinua Achebe, the main character Okonkwo strives to develop his own identity in the face of his father’s failures and the rapid political and religious changes occurring in his society. These internal and external conflicts intertwine at various places in the novel, including the accidental killing of a village elder’s son and Okonkwo’s son’s conversion to Christianity. The forces of imperialism, religion, and traditional tribal life come together at the end of the novel to force Okonkwo to make an impossible choice about his own future.

Like the novel’s conflicts, the stakes of Things Fall Apart are both internal and external. Okonkwo’s own actions first build and then threaten his identity as a man and a regional leader. His self-image and character, especially given his father’s failures, are on the line throughout the book. But the external conflicts also give rise to external stakes, including the direction of traditional tribal beliefs and government.

At no time in Things Fall Apart is the fate of the world at stake; nothing of what Okonkwo does will have an effect outside his small area of Nigeria. But the stakes are so important to him personally and to other Africans in the book that the audience interprets the stakes to be just as large as those in Star Wars or Harry Potter. We do not need an objective measure of which story has greater stakes or which character has more on the line in a particular conflict to determine which story is written better; that is the wrong way of thinking about stakes. What matters is how the characters within the story are invested in the stakes. Stakes that the characters care about don’t need to be large to have a psychological impact on both the characters and the audience.

section.title: Internal Stakes
section.para: A novel whose conflicts and stakes are almost entirely internal is Crime and PunishmentDostoevsky. F. (1866). Crime and punishment. (Garnett, C., Trans.). The Russian Messenger. by Fyodor Dostoevsky. Near the beginning of the story, Raskolnikov, the protagonist, performs an act of brutality and anxious desperation. The rest of the work follows his slow descent into confusion, guilt, and madness. The conflicts are local to Raskolnikov’s community and even to his own mind. The galaxy, the world, or a part of a country are not at stake, but the sanity of a single man is. Audiences feel those stakes acutely as the loss of sanity leaves only paranoia and remorse.

Our last example of stakes in a story is from a children’s book entitled Knuffle Bunny.Willems, M. (2004, October 2). Knuffle bunny. Hyperion Books Toddler Trixie loves her stuffed rabbit, Knuffle Bunny, but loses it at the laundromat. She is inconsolable until her parents get it back. The stakes are as small as an author could make them—a child and a play rabbit—but Trixie’s reaction makes audiences, especially other children, feel that much more is on the line. Author Mo Willems’s depiction of Trixie’s desperation mirrors our own feelings of regret and defeat at the loss of a personal possession that may have little objective value—but value doesn’t need to be objective in order to have a psychological impact.

These examples make clear that good stories can put anything on the line and still be interesting. The right measure is not the size or scale of the stakes but how crucial the stakes are to the well-being of our characters.

section.title: Stakes Get Characters Personally Invested
section.para: In figuring out the stakes of our stories, then, we should choose something in which our characters can be personally invested. If a character’s life is on the line, then the personal investment he has in preserving it will be obvious. But other stakes might require a bit more setup. For example, if a character’s dream is to be a pilot, then whether she passes her flying exam is very important to her. By showing her studying, being nervous, and agonizing over the test, we communicate her personal investment, and the stakes become meaningful not only for her but also for those reading the story.

figure.label: Figure 10.6
figure.title:
Sample questions.
Comaniciu Dan Dumitru © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man surrounded by question marks.

section.para: We can test our stories for what’s at stake in their conflicts. Here are a few sample questions we could ask:

listitem.para: Does my character face situations in which she experiences the real possibility of loss?
Will anything bad happen to my character if he makes a wrong choice?
How will my character change if she doesn’t achieve her goal?

section.para: If the answer to these questions is “no,” “no,” and “they won’t,” then the stakes in our stories are probably not high enough. In other words, we aren’t compelling our characters to encounter trouble and make difficult situations—they are not tested, and they stand to lose nothing valuable if they fail.

section.title: Playing a Risky Game
section.para: Such characters may appear on the outside to face external conflicts, but the obstacles in their path will be illusions. When it’s impossible to lose, victory is inevitable, and it’s only a matter of time before resistance fades away. Our characters need to be able to lose and sometimes must actually lose in order to have played a risky game.

In our stories, we should make sure that the outcome of the stakes is unknown. Our characters’ paths to success shouldn’t be cheery and easy jaunts but strenuous and difficult climbs in which one wrong step could cause them to lose everything.

section.title: Raising the Stakes
section.para: Given the importance of stakes for narrative tension, a good general way to improve a story is to raise the stakes. When more is on the line, characters will have to risk more, and the importance of the conflicts will become even more apparent.

section.title: Raising the Stakes Naturally
section.para: Of course, raising the stakes doesn’t mean we have to force awkward conflicts into stories where they don’t belong. If we’re writing a meditative piece about an aging woman and her daughter with disabilities, then landing aliens on their front lawn to threaten the earth’s existence is not a way of raising the stakes. Introducing such an event into that story would ruin the entire thing—the story isn’t about aliens, and even a conflict beyond the woman’s struggle to raise her daughter may be out of place.

As with everything we put into our stories, the stakes must make sense in light of everything else going on. What’s on the line has to fit into the network of causes and effects in the narrative. The universe isn’t at stake in a story about a boy’s feelings for his dog, and a story about galactic civilizations battling it out should probably have greater stakes than a baloney sandwich. The stakes have to cohere with and be proportional to the characters, their goals, their conflicts, and the world they live in. When we raise the stakes, we may have to make other adjustments in our stories as well.

Raising the stakes will also introduce a greater possibility of loss for our characters. Characters who can lose are characters with weaknesses. Full-blooded, real characters of the kind we discussed in section and section will face loss and trials. Sometimes they will actually lose, and they will not always react in the best ways.

For the rest of this section, we’ll discuss six ways of raising the stakes in our stories: irretrievable loss of something important, irreversible change in a life, physical danger, loss of personal identity, drop-dead point, and two bad choices. (See .) As always, these are suggestions and ideas to consider using. Try them out and see what higher stakes can do.

figure.label: Figure 10.7
figure.title: Six ways to raise the stakes.

imagedata.alt: Six circles labeleing the six ways to raise the stakes in a story. 1. Irretrievable loss of something important. 2. Irreversible change in life. 3. Physical danger. 4. Loss of personal identity. 5. Drop-dead point. 6. Two bad choices.

section.title: 1. Irretrievable Loss of Something Important
section.para: Conflicts introduce the possibility of loss, but not every loss is permanent. Sometimes a possession is just lost for a time—a relationship might be broken off only to be healed later on.

But other losses are forever, and we can up the stakes in our stories by making it clear that a character is facing a permanent loss. For example, a man giving his spouse an ultimatum about her behavior puts her in a difficult position: should she change or continue living the way she’s used to? If she doesn’t change and the ultimatum is real, she’ll lose her husband forever. If she doesn’t want that, then she has a difficult road ahead.

If such an ultimatum is nothing but words, however, and the woman doesn’t believe that her husband will follow up on it, then the stakes are actually very low. She has no reason to change because she has no reason to believe he will actually leave her. In that situation, the stakes are low for her behavior because she doesn’t actually stand to lose anything. Her behavior makes no lasting difference in her husband’s actions.
When a loss is irretrievable, there’s much more on the line. Audiences will take note, even if our characters choose not to accept that they might lose everything for good.

section.title: 2. Irreversible Change in Life

figure.label: Figure 10.8
figure.title:
Propelled on a path.
Photo by Tobi via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Someone's feet walking down a wooden path.

section.para: The next suggestion is similar to the previous one but puts more emphasis on a change in circumstances. An irreversible change in someone’s life propels that person on a path that he cannot change—he cannot go back and make a different choice. There may be good things about the path he chose, but he’ll have to accept any bad things that come along with it because the change is irreversible.

An example would be a character facing a choice between two different jobs in different parts of the United States. If the jobs and places are different enough from each other, then taking one will provide opportunities and a lifestyle that the other one will not. The stakes are high in such a choice, especially when characters, like real people, often make these decisions based on very little available information.

A story can portray this situation early on as well and then follow the consequences of the character’s choice. As long as the choice is irreversible, then the character can’t go back on what he’s decided. Any regret or negative experience reminds the character and the audience of the stakes.

section.title: 3. Physical Danger
section.para: The easiest way to up the stakes in any story is simply to put the characters in physical danger. The stakes are automatically high when someone can be injured or worse.

We should use this suggestion with care, however. Not every story or situation will benefit from an element of danger. We can increase the tension when a character visits the post office by having ninjas flood the building, but that doesn’t mean we should. As always, the more unusual an element of our story is, the more central a role it must play in the narrative in order for the story to make sense.

More subtle ways of increasing physical danger may be more effective. For example, in an argument between two people, we can have one get close enough to the other to physically harm them. In this way, we introduce the mere threat of physical danger, which is often enough to do the trick. No one needs to actually get hit in order for an audience to feel the tension of a conflict.

section.title: 4. Loss of Personal Identity
section.para: In stories like Crime and Punishment, what’s at stake is almost totally mental or psychological: a character’s sense of self, her identity as a member of a certain group, or even her own sanity. We can raise the stakes by testing the mettle of our characters and threatening them not with the loss of a possession but with the loss of their identity.

figure.label: Figure 10.9
figure.title:
Personal identity.
melpomen © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A woman analyzes a digital image of a thumbprint.

section.para: If we reflect on our own lives for a moment, we’ll see many aspects of our identity that are essential to who we are. I am a father, a husband, and a writer, to take just three of the categories that describe me. All three of these aspects of my life are important to my identity. Compromising any of them would change not only the opportunities available to me but also the way I understand myself and the way I relate to other people.
The same is true for our characters. Sometimes they will be forced to make choices that reveal who they really are instead of who they believe they are.

Let’s say that we’re writing a story about a religious family that describes itself as strongly committed to values like tolerance, diversity, and inclusion. These values are an important part of the family’s identity. But imagine that a few new people move into the neighborhood. If those people aren’t of the same faith as the family or come from a different part of the world with very different beliefs and traditions, then the family’s commitment to inclusive values will be tested. When faced with events that test its values, the family may discover that it is not as committed to those values as it originally supposed.

In this sample story, we have raised the stakes by introducing the possibility of a loss of personal identity. Commitments to core values make us who we are, and losing that picture of ourselves can be a serious threat.

section.title: 5. Drop-Dead Point
section.para: Another good way to up the stakes of our stories is by adding a drop-dead point, or a deadline. At some moment in the near future, action will become impossible, so our characters have to act quickly. When there’s a drop-dead point, there’s a countdown, and the stakes will grow as the timer gets closer to zero.

An example of a drop-dead point is when a bomb is going to go off at City Hall, and our characters must race to disarm it. The audience could visualize the clock attached to the bomb, ticking closer to zero in red numbers. The countdown on that clock creates enormous narrative tension and makes it impossible for audiences to look away. The stakes couldn’t be higher.

We can use drop-dead points in less obvious ways as well. An impending court date can be a countdown for characters who are rushing to gather evidence to exonerate a client. They know the evidence is out there—the question is, can they get to it in time? The client’s whole life may be on the line. The timer here isn’t a bomb, but the countdown plays the same role in creating narrative tension.

section.title: 6. Two Bad Choices

figure.label: Figure 10.10
figure.title:
Two bad choices.
Photo by Pixabay via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A road sign with arrows pointing two directions.

section.para: Our final suggestion for raising the stakes in a story is to give a character two bad choices. Many choices characters make are between two good things or one good thing and one bad thing, and the tension springs from a character’s ignorance of which is which. An alternative is to make clear that both choices a character has are bad or have seemingly unacceptable consequences.

This technique creates narrative tension through the character’s knowledge that both choices are bad. The tension tends to dissipate when only the audience knows that; the stakes are higher when we experience the character’s agony at being unable to choose. We don’t feel much when a character is unknowingly choosing between a surgical operation that will eventually leave her blind and a surgical operation that will eventually leave her legs paralyzed. However, when that character has full knowledge of her options and must decide, then we experience the choice with much more anticipation and emotion.

In this section, we’ve reviewed six ways of raising the stakes in our stories. All six techniques boil down to putting more on the line so that our characters have a greater personal investment in the narrative events. Whether that be physical, psychological, or even imaginary, audiences will respond.

section.title: Pacing: Think Fast or Lose
section.para: The final subject in our discussion of stakes is the idea of pacingThe speed with which events occur in a story. . The pacing of a story is how fast the events occur. In a thriller novel like Angels and Demons,Brown, D. (2000). Angels and demons. Pocket Books. events go by at a blistering rate, and almost every chapter brings some new or unexpected development. In a longer epic like Middlemarch,Eliot, G. (1871). Middlemarch: A study of provincial life. William Blackwood and Sons. events happen much more slowly, and conflicts are sometimes left to fester for hundreds of pages before reaching their breaking point.

figure.label: Figure 10.11
figure.title:
How quickly the stakes are put in place.
Photo by Any Lane via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A wooden fence with the stakes placed far apart.

section.title: What Is Pacing?
section.para: The pacing of a story affects how quickly the stakes are put in place and allowed to grow. In a detective story or superhero movie with a lot of action, the stakes are established quickly and develop quickly as one event follows another. In other stories, especially those with an emphasis on character development, a moderate pace will be better. Characters need time to act, reflect on their actions, and then act again in order to move the plot along.

Poor pacing is a major contributor to making audiences feel as though a story doesn’t make sense. When a story gives the impression that an important event is far down the road but then jolts the audience forward with no explanation to the resolution of that event, then the comprehensible causal relations between events in the story are lost. When this happens, it seems as though things are happening for no reason, and characters have little reason to be personally invested in the events of the narrative.

section.title: Determining Correct Pacing
section.para: We determine the proper pacing for a story based on a number of different factors, including genre, the length of the narrative, the characters and their goals, the size of the conflicts, and the stakes involved. Genre and the audience expectations it generates is perhaps the largest factor, at least initially.

If we’re writing a detailed character study, but major events are happening every other chapter as conflicts rise and fall, then we probably have a mismatch between the genre and what we’ve actually created. In this case, we’ll need to slow things down to match the expectations of the genre or keep the pace while pushing the genre in another direction. Some of the lighter genres we’ve mentioned so far, like superhero and detective stories, will probably have a faster pace and will whisk audiences from one important event to another rather quickly. In general, faster paces are appropriate for those stories because the focus is on action and external conflicts.

In contrast, many stories of literary fiction and historical fiction have a slower pace and so unfold much more slowly. Works such as these tend to be contemplative, focusing on internal developments in characters. Even the most climactic moments of these genres may occur at a slow pace as characters make crucial discoveries about themselves.

Perhaps the simplest way to slow down the pace at a particular point is to use longer sentences. Though we’ve cautioned against writing too many long, complex sentences, they do have a use in forcing the reader to slow down and take time to get through a passage. And the opposite of that is true as well: shorter sentences will speed up the pacing. Readers will be able to get through shorter, simpler sentences much more quickly, so writing simple sentences will increase the pace.

Beyond remarks like those, it is difficult to provide advice about how to weigh each factor in setting up a narrative. Plot, character, conflicts, and stakes all interact with each other, and an adjustment in one place may require adjustments in other places. Perhaps the most important general point is to include all and only those storytelling elements—events, conflicts, stakes, and so on—that are necessary for a story to be told in the way its author intends. Let’s take a moment to discuss this point in a bit more detail.

section.title: What is Necessary

figure.label: Figure 10.12
figure.title:
Include what is necessary for a narrative and not more.
Sergey Nivens © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A chalk drawing of a lightbub surrounded by other drawings.

section.para: Among the myriad problems faced by new authors are the temptations to write too little or too much. Here we don’t refer to how much actual time the authors spend writing per day but to how much information and how many events they write into a narrative. On the one hand, some authors don’t spend enough time setting up the events in their story, so they have unmotivated characters flitting from experience to experience for no discernible reason. On the other hand, other authors spend too much time setting things up, with the result that the story slows down and drags severely. Events occur at a snail’s pace as conversations, descriptions, and aftermaths linger for far longer than needed.

Both of these tendencies are problems with pacing. The first paces a story too quickly, without the requisite background, so the audience loses or can’t even find the thread of causes and effects. The second paces a story too slowly and needs to cut material in order to focus on the events that are actually crucial in the narrative.

The solution to these issues is to include everything that is necessary for a story to be told in the right way and not more. Of course, the problem is figuring out exactly what all and only those things really are. But figuring that out is just the process of gaining experience and becoming a writer. Our skills will increase with practice, and we will come to be able to pace a story better as we understand what is necessary to include and exclude in our stories.

section.title: Pacing and Climax
section.para: A final general point about pacing relates to the climax of a story. The climax is the point at which a story’s conflicts reach their breaking point, and the stakes and excitement are highest. It is the culmination of a story.

figure.label: Figure 10.13
figure.title:
Climax means fast pacing.
Photo by Snapwire via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A wooden fence with the stakes placed close togther.

section.para: The climax of the original Star Wars movies is the lightsaber battle between Luke Skywalker and Darth Vader and their subsequent escape from the doomed Death Star. The climax of The Lion King is the fateful battle between Simba and Scar for control over the savannah and Pride Rock. In the book The Hunger Games, the climactic moment comes when Katniss and Peeta agree to ingest toxic berries at the same time, forcing the administrators of the Games to declare both of them the winners.

Consider all these examples and others you know. As conflicts grow and characters find themselves drawn toward a resolution, there will be a moment when all the events come to a head. The stakes reach their maximum, the conflicts can be postponed no longer, and characters have put everything on the line.

In those climactic moments, we will probably want the pacing of the story to be fast. We won’t need much description because we’ve already done the description previously; we’ve explained who our characters are, what they want, and how they’re trying to achieve it. As the consequences of the climax play out, we’ll usually be able to let them happen at a quick pace. The audience will be able to discern their connections if we’ve done enough work beforehand. Just as in real life, our stories will contain crucial moments in which the repercussions of past actions cannot be controlled, and events explode all around us.

As we think about how to pace our stories, we should consider the stakes and make the rate at which events happen equal to those stakes. We’ll also want to consider genre, characters, goals, conflicts, and other aspects of our stories.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 10.14
figure.title:
Stakes.
Photo by Pixabay via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: Stakes in a wooden fence.

section.para: The stakes of a story are what’s on the line, or what characters stand to gain or lose as a result of their participation in the narrative. Stakes can be possessions, like money or property, but they also can be psychological things like a person’s self-image or identity as a member of a certain group.

Stakes work with conflicts to create and maintain narrative tension. As the stakes go up, narrative tension goes up. As long as the stakes in a story fit in with the characters, events, and conflicts, then raising the stakes usually leads to an increase in tension.

In this topic, we discussed six ways of raising the stakes in our stories. We can use these techniques and others to force our characters to risk more and to be more personally invested in their risks. Pacing, or the rate at which events occur in our stories, helps raise stakes naturally and in proportion to other story elements.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: Welcome to Week 5. This week, you will read the following topics:

listitem.para: : The Needs—Audiences and How to Satisfy Them
: Story Structure and Successful Communication

section.para: We’ll step back to take a broader perspective this week. Our goal is to understand how audiences affect storytelling and how we can use stories to share the kinds of messages we want to send in our groups and organizations.

chapter.label: Topic 11
chapter.title: The Needs—Audiences and How to Satisfy Them

section.title: Audiences and Their Needs
section.para: We have already had a great deal to say in our course about audiences. Audiences are the people who experience our stories—they might be readers, TV or movie viewers, theatergoers, or anyone else who engages with our work. We don’t need to create stories for any audience other than ourselves, but most authors are interested in sharing what they produce.

To share a story with an audience means to invite that audience into the world of the story. If the audience members want to experience the story as fully as possible, they will need to accept features of the story as though they were true aspects of reality (at least in the context of the story). If the story involves dragons or aliens, then the audience will have to take it as given that dragons and aliens can actually exist in the story. If the story involves a government secretly spying on its citizens in order to quash resistance, then the audience will have to take it as given that such a government exists. The human ability to suspend disbelief about these kinds of things, and even believe that they are real in another context, is one reason why stories are such a powerful medium for communication.

section.title: Stepping into a Story’s World

figure.label: Figure 11.1
figure.title:
Stepping into a story.
Daniil Peshkov © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man steps into a book with a sunset coming out of the page.

section.para: The fact that audiences experiencing a story must step into the story’s world has important consequences for how we communicate those worlds. In short, the audience knows only what we tell them about the world, and if we aren’t clear or thorough enough, our audience will be stepping into a half-baked world that makes little sense to them. We’ll return to this issue later in the topic.

Audiences don’t just step into our worlds as passive observers, either. Rather, they make an active contribution to the reality of the story: all the imagination, tension, conflict, and stakes seem real when they occur and are felt inside the minds of audience members. Once the creator of a story has finished her work, it is the audience’s participation in that work that brings the world, characters, and conflicts to life. The imaginations of the story creator and the audience will work together to realize a vision about what is possible.

This topic is about these issues and others. Understanding audiences, their expectations, their needs, and their involvement in stories is crucial to giving them something they will value. There’s no problem with developing a world or characters just for ourselves, but if we want to share that world with others, we have to keep that audience in mind not only after we finish but also while we’re creating.

section.title: Learning about Our Audiences and Their Needs
section.para: As writers, we will create stories and messages for many different audiences. Sometimes these audiences will be small and well-defined; other times they’ll be large and undefined. Either way, the more we know about our audience, the better off we’ll be in crafting messages that will reach it.

section.title: Writing a Memo

figure.label: Figure 11.2
figure.title:
Writing a memo.
Photo by Oleg Magni via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man types on his laptop.

section.para: Let’s start with an example. Suppose we have an assignment to write an office memo. The memo will explain our company’s new policy regarding the snack machines in the break room: no more shaking them to drop illicit chips or candy bars. Our job is to craft a piece of communication to send that message to employees at the company.

section.title: Subject Matter and Audience
section.para: The proper framing for a message should be determined at least in part by the audience. An audience of office workers has certain expectations about how they will be treated, how they will receive information, and how they will act in response. When receiving instructions from management, they rightly expect to hear clear messages that tell them exactly what to anticipate and what will be required of them. A lack of clarity on important information or policies is obviously a danger not only for employees but also for the company itself.

section.title: Knowing about Audiences: Small and Defined
section.para: Let’s focus on what we know about our audience and how we should frame our memo based on that knowledge. The employees at our company are an audience we know well because we are part of that audience. We know their expectations because they are more or less like our expectations. We know their preferences because they are more or less like our preferences. We even know the names of many of them, along with specific facts about their lives. This is a small, well-defined audience about which we are fortunate to have detailed knowledge, so we can tailor our message accordingly.

section.title: Knowing about Audiences: Large and Undefined
section.para: In many professions, however—and certainly with many of the stories we’ll write—it isn’t always possible to have such detailed knowledge about our audiences. For one thing, if the audience for a story we write is “fans of vampire fiction,” then the group we’ll be targeting will number into the millions, at least potentially. This audience is much larger than the employees at our company. This audience also differs because it is far less determinate than others. The audience of “employees at our company” is a very specific group of people, and for any given individual, we can easily determine whether they belong to the audience by figuring out whether they work at our company or not.

figure.label: Figure 11.3
figure.title:
Vampire fiction.
lightfieldstudios © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A vampress shows her pointy teeth.

section.para: The group of “fans of vampire fiction” does not work the same way. The boundaries are undefined. While there are certain core fans who would be into anything vampire-related, at the periphery of the audience are people who perhaps have only a passing interest in vampires. This subsection of our audience might be interested in our story if it included vampires in the right way: if it was a vampires + steampunk story or a vampires + romance story or a vampires + Abraham Lincoln story, and so on. So, for any given individual, we won’t automatically be able to tell whether that person belongs to our audience. That person might belong if we write our story in a certain way; if we don’t, then that person isn’t in our audience, not even potentially.

In our careers as storytellers, we’ll encounter audiences on both ends of this spectrum, as well as everything in between. Sometimes we’ll know who we’re writing for in such detail that we could name them. Other times, we’ll be creating a story whose audience is so broad that anyone might enjoy it.

section.title: Discovering Our Audiences
section.para: Regardless of the identity of the audience members, however, one principle holds true: the more we know about them, the better we’ll be able to reach them. In particular, knowing certain things about our audience members will allow us to create stories that speak to them on more individual levels. Here are some of those things:

listitem.para: What are the needs of our audience?
What is the background of our audience?
What are the expectations of our audience with respect to the kind of story we want to tell them?
What feelings, if any, does our audience already have toward our other stories or to us as storytellers?

section.para: As suggested by the title of this chapter, the first question is the most important. It encompasses parts of the others—an audience’s background and expectations help form their needs—and an audience’s needs will be the driving force in whether they choose to experience our stories or not. An audience can need to feel narrative tension, need to watch a chick flick or action movie, need to escape the humdrum of reality, need a friend, and so on.

Knowing about the needs of an audience will allow us to fulfill them. When we’re fulfilling an audience’s needs, the audience members will be interested in continuing to read or watch our stories. It’s simple, at least in theory.

section.title: High-Level Knowledge about Audiences
section.para: Considering that many of our audiences will be large and a bit undefined, we’ll have to be content with gathering information about our audiences at a high level. Sometimes all we’ll know about them is that they are at least potentially interested in mashups between My Little Pony and zombie movies. But that information by itself might be enough for us to go on and create a story that they’ll be interested in. Other times, we’ll have access to much more detailed knowledge about the needs and habits of audience members, and when we have that information, we can tailor our stories and messages accordingly.

section.title: The Needs of Audiences

figure.label: Figure 11.4
figure.title:
Audience needs.
Photo by Andrea Piacquadio via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man sits behind a stack of books.

section.para: Let’s close this section with a note on why we speak in terms of needs rather than wants. Of course, our audiences have wants in addition to needs. In some ways, it’s more accurate to think of their “needs” as basic biological things, like eating and drinking, while their “need” for narrative tension or an exciting fantasy world looks more like a desire. We’ll continue to refer to what our audience needs, however, for two reasons.

section.title: Audiences Need Good Stories
section.para: The first reason is that, at least from our perspective as storytellers, our audience does need one thing from us: good stories. Most of the time, our stories will be the only way we interact with audience members, so as far as we’re concerned, their desires might as well be needs. They are the needs that we, at least through stories, are able to fulfill.

section.title: Audiences Have Expectations
section.para: The second reason we speak of audience needs is that the term helps us to remember an audience’s expectations. Like the employees at our company or fans of vampire fiction, audiences make certain assumptions about what authors will do in their stories. Some of these assumptions are obvious and not worth discussing—like that authors will use intelligible words and write meaningful sentences. But other assumptions are not so obvious, and not every assumption is shared by every audience. Some audiences will expect our main characters to be likable and relatable, for example, and will refuse to read a book if the main character isn’t portrayed that way. Other audiences will look for violence in everything they read and will move on to look somewhere else if they don’t find it in our stories.

It is useful to think of these expectations as needs in the sense that our writing must fulfill them in order to engage our audience. As authors, we invite readers to enter worlds of our own design, but they do not enter blindly or with no preconceptions about what they will experience. We do not create every part of the world for our readers. That would be impossible since they experience our world in their own minds. The preconceptions that our readers bring to our writing will affect how they experience our stories. From their perspective—and from ours as authors as well—readers’ expectations for the story are just as important as ours in bringing a story to life. Violating our audience’s expectations or preconceptions too severely will alienate audience members and make them believe our stories aren’t worth experiencing.
Many of these audience needs are determined by genre, which we’ll discuss in section .

section.title: Audience, Genre, and Expectations
section.para: In , we introduced the notion of a genre. A genre is the storytelling category a story belongs to, such as romance, western, and horror. Genres can be nested inside each other. For example, “fantasy” is a very large genre, encompassing many subgenres like high fantasy, urban fantasy, and Harry Potter fanfiction. Works belonging to the same genre are likely to have some general features in common, such as subject matter or the historical period of the setting.

section.title: Determining Genre

figure.label: Figure 11.5
figure.title:
What is a genre?
Photo by Nick Fewings via Unsplash.

imagedata.alt: Many books on a bookshelf.

section.para: What makes a story belong to a particular genre is just the presence or absence of some general features the readers expect the genre to have. If a story involves wizards and a magic system, then it is a fantasy story. It could also be a western and a romance too—a story doesn’t need to belong to a single genre. But even if a story of wizards and magic does include features more characteristic of other genres, it will also be a fantasy, in addition to whatever else it is.

section.title: Needs Can Be Idiosyncratic
section.para: This observation about genre is important for thinking about the needs of our audience. The idea of needs reminds us that audiences bring a set of expectations to our stories. Some of these expectations come from individual members of the audience themselves. We may have a particular taste for strong female leads, cute and cuddly sidekicks, or conspiracy theories. All of these story elements could occur in any genre, and none are unique or even characteristic of a particular genre. We can find strong female leads in any kind of story in any setting. The need a person has for a story with that feature would be unique to them and not something that authors could anticipate easily.

section.title: Genre Determines Other Needs
section.para: But other needs of an audience are purely genre-driven, and these are needs that authors can anticipate. So, these needs ought to be an important part of how we design and execute our stories.

section.title: An Example: The Romance Genre

figure.label: Figure 11.6
figure.title:
Romance genre.
Photo by freestocks.org via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: An open book with cut-out hearts sprinkled in the pages.

section.para: Think of it this way: let’s imagine we’re in a bookstore, browsing through the aisles. We come across the romance aisle and decide to take a look. We see rows and rows of romance novels with inhumanly attractive people gracing their covers. Let’s say we grab a book at random and sit down to read it. What will we expect to find? What can we know in advance about what the book will contain? Some things we definitely cannot know in advance, like the setting. A story of romance could take place in any time period and in any place, so the genre by itself tells us nothing about that. The same is true for other parts of the story—we can’t know the exact nature of the conflicts, the backgrounds of the characters, or the details of the storytelling.

But there are other things we can be reasonably sure about based on the genre alone. There will be a love story with much passion felt by everyone involved. The protagonist will probably have multiple love interests and may have to make an agonizing choice between them. The romantic tension between the characters will increase slowly, with tortured longing, before their relationship finally becomes physical and so on. We don’t need to read the book to know any of these things about it. We know them because we plucked the book from the romance section of the bookstore.

Now, imagine that we randomly grab another book from the same section, but this time, we buy it and go home. We start reading and discover that while the book does have a discernible plot, almost all the conversations between characters are about how to build interesting things out of Lincoln Logs. We look in vain for the love story, waiting for it as we turn page after page, but it never arrives. Each chapter just brings more ideas for the logs.

What will we think about that book? It might be a fine book, and maybe it has good ideas about building—but it isn’t a romance. It’s not a romance because it lacks features that are crucial to the genre. We could even return it to the store for a refund. When the store asks why we’re returning it, we wouldn’t have to say it’s a bad book or even that we didn’t like it. The problem is that the book was sold as a romance and categorized as belonging to that genre without actually being a romance.

section.title: Genre and Audience Needs
section.para: As readers, we bought the book because it appeared to belong to a particular genre, and we went into our experience of the story with expectations set by the genre. Our needs as an audience were things like wistful glances, lingering touches, and tormented pining. We adopt those needs because we like stories with those features, but we chose that particular book because we legitimately expected it to fulfill our needs. These needs derive from the genre alone.

figure.label: Figure 11.7
figure.title:
Readers have genre expectations.
Photo by cottonbro via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A woman looks away from an open book in her lap.

section.para: This example teaches us an important lesson about genre. If we’re designing a story, we must understand what genre our story will belong to. This knowledge may help us design the story, but it matters primarily for the purpose of knowing our audience.
