Writing a story in a particular genre and presenting it to people as an exemplar of that genre will fix expectations in our audience’s mind. They will come to our story seeking certain things. If our story doesn’t provide at least some of those things, then we’ve missed a chance to fulfill their needs with the world of our story.

Genre plays a fundamental role in determining the needs of our audience. Some needs are idiosyncratic to certain individuals, but the defining features of a genre are not mere conventions. We ignore them at our own peril.

section.title: Audiences and Genre Expectations
section.para: Conversely, if a story we’ve written isn’t connecting with audiences, it may not be that we’ve written a bad story. It could be that we’re presenting it as belonging to a certain genre when it really doesn’t. A great horror story will fail as a biography but may be great for fans of the macabre.

The best way to discover the expectations imposed by a genre is to get to know them firsthand by reading widely within a genre. After several stories, we’ll begin to notice patterns that go beyond characters, hooks, or conflicts. Those patterns will indicate tacit genre requirements that authors follow to fulfill the needs of their audience.

section.title: The Payoff

figure.label: Figure 11.8
figure.title:
Resolution of the story’s conflicts.
ismagilov © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man seems at peace with a lightbulb floating over his head with a lot of chalk drawings in the background.

section.para: Our discussion of audience needs leads us to the last storytelling element we’ll discuss in our course: the payoffThe result or outcome of events in a narrative. . The payoff of a story is the result or outcome of the events in the narrative. It’s the series of events that is the culmination of all other events. The payoff is the resolution of the story’s conflicts and the final determination of the stakes. For audiences, it’s an ultimate relief of their narrative tension because it’s when everything has been decided, and all the questions have been answered.

section.title: The Payoff of Harry Potter
section.para: As an example of a payoff, let’s consider the ending of the Harry Potter series of novels.Rowling, J.K. (1997–2007). Harry Potter [Book series]. Bloomsbury; Arthur A. Levine/Scholastic; Raincoast. Events in the books, especially the later ones, lead inexorably to a war involving all the supporters of both Harry and his nemesis, Voldemort. The war takes place on the grounds of Hogwarts, the setting for most events in the story. The stakes have never been higher—all participants on both sides are fighting for their lives, their values, their relationships, and their futures. Individual conflicts that readers have followed throughout the book, such as those between Harry and Snape or between the Weasely family and pureblood wizards, are subsumed into the larger conflicts and receive their individual resolutions as part of the outcome.

A good payoff brings together many aspects of a story and knits them all together in an explosion of discovery, twists, and action. Characters reach their breaking point in order to push the stakes to their utmost limit and finish the narrative in a satisfying way.

section.title: Coherent Payoffs
section.para: The payoff, perhaps more than any other part of the story, must make sense in light of everything else that has come before. The scale of the payoff’s stakes and conflicts must be proportionate to other events in the story. The causal relationships between the payoff and what leads to it should feel inevitable, like there was no other way the story could have ended besides the way it did.

figure.label: Figure 11.9
figure.title:
Hogwarts.
marina113 © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A castle on a hill.

section.para: Author J. K. Rowling’s understanding of this point is one reason why many fans of the Harry Potter books were satisfied with their ending. Given the past events in the story, the story’s characters and their goals, the conflicts, and the stakes, the payoff in the seventh book had to happen as Rowling depicted it. There had to be a battle involving all of Harry’s and Voldemort’s supporters. The battle had to happen at Hogwarts, the site of so many other developments. And Harry and Voldemort had to have a final showdown, a one-on-one confrontation, in which they could settle the score once and for all. It made sense for the payoff to play out this way.

In contrast, imagine our reactions as readers if Harry and Voldemort had merely decided to work out their differences over a round of golf. The resolution to everything could have been so simple: by the eighteenth green, they could have set aside their differences in appreciation for each other’s sportsmanship.

section.title: Payoffs Make Sense in the Story World
section.para: No one would want that ending, of course. It would be no payoff at all—it would make no sense given the characters, their goals and conflicts, and the stakes. In order to drive toward an ending like that one, Rowling would have had to have changed almost everything in the previous books. The characters and events in the narrative would have been completely different. It would have been an entirely different story.

As an element of a story, the payoff is also a crucial need of the audience. If our story has built the narrative tension to max levels, then our audience will expect us to deliver an explosive ending that answers the major questions and follows the conflicts to their natural climaxes. If the conflicts in our story are more psychological or based on relationships, then there may not be actual explosions, but the principle is the same. The characters have reached the end of their journey, and their goals will either be achieved or forever lost. They will either become new people or learn nothing and refuse to change. They will reap the consequences of their decisions, and the truth about each character will be known.

Creating a payoff like this one requires us to continue developing our narrative, conflicts, and events in the ways we have discussed in other topics. We deepen conflicts, make character goals more incompatible, and raise the stakes for the purpose of driving toward the payoff. We’re on the right track when the end we envision brings together the story’s previous conflicts and intensifies them to the point that they cannot be set aside any longer. They will demand to be resolved. Our job as storytellers is then simple—we resolve them with a payoff.

section.title: A Failed Payoff: Lost

figure.label: Figure 11.10
figure.title:
Lost.
Photo by Francesco Ungaro via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A thick jungle with some mist.

section.para: We can see that the payoff is a true need of an audience by looking at a recent example of a payoff failure. In the television series Lost,Abrams, J. J., Lindelof, D., Burk, B. Cuse, C., Bender, J., Pinkner, J., Williams, S., Kitsis, E., Horowitz, A., Higgins, J., & Sarnoff, E. (Executive Producers). (2004–2010). Lost [TV series]. Bad Robot Productions; Touchstone Television; ABC Studios. survivors of a plane crash are marooned on a desert island. For the first few seasons, the show weaves an enigmatic tale of island inhabitants and mysterious societies with major plot twists in almost every episode. In time, though, the plot becomes so convoluted that viewers begin to realize the show’s writers have woven themselves into a corner. The plot twists stop being exciting developments and start becoming last-ditch attempts to impose order on an unruly narrative.

The ending of Lost is a payoff in that it attempts to explain how all the threads from previous seasons were connected. But many fans and critics believed that the attempt was a pretty bad one, doing more explaining away than actual explaining. Countless conflicts were left unresolved, and major questions were left unanswered. The payoff trivialized the high stakes of earlier events by being a low-stakes, inappropriately serene event itself.

Given everything that had come before, the payoff of Lost just didn’t make sense. It fulfilled almost none of its audience’s needs and had the ultimate effect of making people wonder why they had spent so much time watching the show in the first place.

Payoffs are important elements of stories, but just like conflicts and stakes, they are an important part of creating and then finally resolving narrative tension. Their interaction with the audience makes them part of the audience’s needs, so we must keep payoffs in mind as we design events and conflicts in our stories.

section.title: Playing with Audience Expectations
section.para: As we’ve seen, a story’s genre imposes certain expectations about narrative, character, and other aspects of the story. Some of these expectations are fairly inviolable, and if we fail to meet them, it could mean our story belongs to some other genre.

section.title: Breaking Expectations
section.para: But not all genre and audience expectations are so unbreakable. For others, we have room to maneuver, and playing with expectations can have a powerful and good effect on the stories we tell.

title.emphasis: A Song of Ice and Fire

section.para: Our example here will come from the George R. R. Martin book series A Song of Ice and Fire,Martin, G. R. R., (1996–2011). A Song of Ice and Fire [Book series]. Bantam Books; Voyager Books. better known as Game of Thrones. Martin’s books are unabashed fantasies: there are swords, castles, land and sea battles, dragons, and other things typical of the fantasy genre. But Martin also plays with some fantasy conventions in ways that make his story unique and memorable to audiences.

One such convention is the rule that main characters don’t die, and if they do, they go down with a glorious death at the end of the story. Martin breaks this convention by showing his willingness, from early on in the book, to kill off important and even leading characters. In many fantasy stories, protagonists are protected by plot armorA feature of many main characters who survive all threats and dangers because they must continue to live in order to advance the narrative. —an incredible ability to survive any encounter, no matter how dangerous, in order to advance the narrative. Martin’s characters enjoy no such protection, and the brutal, unfeeling world they inhabit exacts its price on them in each and every book.

section.title: Shedding the Plot Armor

figure.label: Figure 11.11
figure.title:
Plot armor.
Photo by Mike via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A knight's armor.

section.para: Martin’s willingness to play with and ultimately violate this fantasy convention has a powerful impact on his story. The constant threat of death hanging over every character means that the story could go in any direction at any time. The audience cannot rely on their favorite characters surviving until the end; for all they know, an untimely end awaits on the very next page. The effect on narrative tension is noticeable. Martin meets many other expectations about fantasy stories, but by violating the one about character deaths, he ups the stakes and creates enormous narrative tension.

A Song of Ice and Fire is popular because the narrative is well-crafted and the characters are deep, but the author’s approach to some genre expectations shows that the series takes risks and does things that other stories don’t usually do. In combination with Martin’s technical skill, the result is one of the best fantasy series ever written.

As authors, we’re in control of our stories, and we can decide which audience needs we’ll fulfill and which we’ll ignore. Both have consequences. If we want to remain within a certain genre, then we don’t have much choice about some of those needs. But for other needs, we can go in new directions, forge new paths within and between genres, and establish ourselves as storytellers who risk it all to share compelling narratives.

section.title: Writing with the Audience in Mind
section.para: In this topic, we’ve discussed the needs of our audiences. The more we know about them and what those needs are, the better we’ll be able to fulfill them. We’ll be able to make our stories more interesting, create greater narrative tension, and deliver fantastic payoffs to satisfy our readers.

To accomplish those goals, we must keep our audience in mind as we write. The audience brings needs and expectations to our stories, and if we aren’t thinking of those things as we create, then it may only be a coincidence or good luck that our stories meet the audience’s needs. By remembering the audience, we can build a narrative and characters that give audiences what they want.

section.title: Writing Only Says What It Carries

figure.label: Figure 11.12
figure.title:
Writing only says what it carries.
Photo by Karolina Grabowska via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man holds a book outside with trees in the background.

section.para: We’ll finish this topic by discussing another important point we should remember about our audience while we write our stories. The point is that any communication we write, story or otherwise, only says what it carries with it. That is, the only material the audience has to understand our writing is the material we give them. We cannot rely on them having anything else or, more importantly, any particular piece of background knowledge that isn’t already in the writing.

What does this mean for storytelling? It means that everything an audience needs in order to fully experience, understand, and enjoy our stories should be contained therein. If we’re building a world unlike the real one, then all the background knowledge needed for understanding that world should be in the story. Readers shouldn’t have to buy another book, visit a website, or hear the author speak in order to grasp what’s going on in the story. It is our job to make sure the story carries everything it needs in order to be understood by its audience.

What we’re saying here may seem obvious—of course, our stories only say what they carry with them. How could they say anything else? In reality, though, many stories (and more broadly, communications of all kinds) suffer from a pervasive failure to appreciate this point. In many professions and areas of writing, the author does not do enough to clearly explain what she means, leaving the job of deciphering her message up to the audience instead. But it is not the audience’s job to decipher or sift through dozens of poorly written pages in our novel just to find out how our imagined government system works. If we’ve invented such a government, our job is to explain it clearly, providing only what our audience needs, with enough detail, to understand our vision.

section.title: The Illusion of Transparency
section.para: The failure to recognize and act on differences between what authors and audiences know is called the illusion of transparencyThe belief that the contents of one’s own mind are as clear and accessible to others as they are to oneself. . We suffer from this illusion when we believe that our audiences will be able to see inside our minds as easily as we can. We suffer from it when we assume that our audience shares our background knowledge about a certain subject. We suffer from it when we believe our audience will grasp the meaning of our writing as readily as we do when we read our own work.

We call these beliefs and assumptions an “illusion” because they’re just that—misleading at best, completely false at worst. It is not true that what’s inside our heads is as clear to everyone else as it is to us. It is not true that our audience shares our background knowledge about a certain subject, especially a technical one. And it is not true that our audience can pick up on our intentions in our writing as easily as we do.

section.title: Upshots of the Illusion of Transparency

figure.label: Figure 11.13
figure.title:
Stories should contain everything an audience needs.
Photo by Hong SON via Pexels.

imagedata.alt: A man reads a book at a table.

section.para: We’ll draw two practical conclusions for storytelling. The first is that if we want audiences to see or understand something in our stories, then we must include it and make it prominent and clear enough for people to notice and comprehend. Our stories only say what they carry, so if we want to tell our audience a story that we intended as a metaphor for something else, then we must make sure that the story contains everything an audience needs in order to see and follow the metaphor. We cannot expect audiences who lack our familiarity with our own work—to say nothing of our written notes—to see what we have in mind unless we give it to them unambiguously.

The second conclusion is that consequences will follow if there are times when people don’t understand our stories. Most of the time, unclarity or misunderstanding is not the audience’s fault but the author’s fault. Most audiences try to read fairly and charitably and will make a reasonable effort to follow what the author is saying. If audiences don’t understand our meaning, then it’s probably because we didn’t give it to them clearly enough.

The solution to this problem is to practice and try again. Writing is hard to begin with, and writing clearly is even harder. Telling stories is hard too, and telling good stories is even harder. But we’ll get better as we practice, and we should be eager to identify places where an audience fails to understand us because those places are opportunities for growth.

We write with our audience in mind not only in designing interesting stories but also in trying to communicate those stories clearly. Remember that our audience can only use the material we give them to understand what we write. It is our job to give them what they need.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 11.14
figure.title:
Audience.
rawpixel © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: People standing in a row reading books.

section.para: In this topic, we have focused on audiences. Audiences have needs: they are looking to get certain things out of our stories. The better we understand these needs, the more we will be able to fulfill them.

Many audience needs stem from the genre of our writing. The genre of a work determines many of its features, and those features become expectations of the audience. If we don’t remember those expectations in storytelling, then we won’t be able to meet those needs.

One storytelling element closely related to an audience’s needs is the payoff. Payoffs bring together the many narrative threads in a story to resolve conflicts and settle the stakes. Payoffs are our chance to deliver answers to questions and satisfying endings. We play around with payoffs and other genre conventions at our own risk—violating audience expectations too much will set our work apart, but not in a good way. Our writing only says what it carries with it, and if what it carries is uninteresting or unclear, then audiences don’t have any reason to pay attention.

section.title: Putting the Pieces Together
section.para: Our course has covered many different parts of storytelling. Let’s introduce this topic by reviewing some of those parts.

section.title: Writing

figure.label: Figure 12.1
figure.title:
Writing.
hakinmhan © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man writes on a sticky note that is surrounded by crumpled sticky notes and pencils.

section.para: Our early focus was on writing itself. Although we couldn’t discuss every aspect of writing technique or practice, we had topics on sentences (), paragraphs (), grammar, word choice, and revision (). Throughout these topics, our focus was on writing simply and directly. We write simple and direct sentences by making them short and to the point, using strong subjects, and keeping the subject and predicate close together. We write effective paragraphs in various ways, including by following the uneven “U” model of paragraph building. This model encourages us to frame a paragraph with a lead sentence, then support that sentence with particular items of evidence or examples. The final sentence then connects the paragraph to the work’s larger purpose.

Nearly all of our discussion on writing applies both to storytelling and to writing in other contexts and for other audiences. Simple and direct sentences lead to clarity in any genre, and with some modifications, the uneven “U” paragraph model is suitable for writing fiction and stories.

section.title: Narrative and Character
section.para: Our next two topics focused on the most important elements in stories: narrative () and character (). A narrative is a sequence of events that unfolds over the course of a story. The events are just the things that happen, and when they’re connected by threads of cause and effect, we’ve got a narrative. Characters are the entities that things happen to in a story. Most of the time, characters are people, animals, or other living things, but they don’t need to be. A character could be anything that can act to cause or experience the events in a narrative.

Narrative and character work together to turn a group of storytelling elements into an actual story. Without characters, a narrative is just a sequence of events that an audience has no reason to invest themselves in. Without a narrative, characters are just things with nothing to do. Pairing the events in a narrative with characters to experience them gives us a story.

section.title: Interesting Stories

figure.label: Figure 12.2
figure.title:
Interesting stories.
ra2studio © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: An open book with trees, a house, the sun, and hot air balloons coming out of the page.

section.para: The last few topics have expanded our knowledge of stories by introducing techniques like hooks (), stakes (), and conflicts (). None of these elements is as necessary to stories as narrative and character. Their purpose isn’t to make something into a story but to make something into an interesting story. A hook draws interest from an audience at the beginning of a work, tempting potential readers with interesting details or situations. Conflicts create narrative tension, or the anticipation an audience feels about wanting to go on. Raising the stakes raises the tension, which reaches a breaking point near the conclusion of a story. Like narrative and character, these other elements work together to make audiences want to keep experiencing our stories, sometimes many times over.

We use all these story elements and techniques in the context of creating stories for audiences. Audiences have needs, and knowing those needs allows us to fulfill them. We’ve also had the opportunity to work with some stories and discover how they go from ideas in an author’s mind to reality as words that audiences can read.

Now, we just summarized eleven whole topics in six paragraphs. That’s a lot of material! We’ve seen countless examples of writing and storytelling, both good and bad, and have seen the theory behind them as well. We’ve also had the opportunity to work over some stories ourselves as we think about how they go from ideas in an author’s mind to reality as words that audiences can read.

section.title: Great Storytelling Takes Time
section.para: As we move forward, however, we should remember that it won’t be possible for us to put all these pieces together successfully the first time we try. No one becomes a great storyteller the first time they put words on a page. Even with good ideas, the execution of a plot is a difficult task. Don’t be frustrated by apparent inadequacies or mistakes, especially at the start.

figure.label: Figure 12.3
figure.title:
Storytelling takes time.
Elnur Amikishiyev © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man surrounded by books holds a clock and points.

section.para: We have designed this course to be somewhat modular so that students can extract and use certain skills immediately. You don’t have to be writing a full-on novel; you can use conflicts and stakes to enhance a presentation or use a story frame to pitch job application materials. You can apply the storytelling skills you have learned in many contexts—and you can start applying them right away.

For both the short-term and the long-term, the key is to remember that storytelling, like writing, is a skill that we improve with practice. Using a story frame for marketing purposes may be all that some students need right now, while others may be aiming for a career as an author or playwright. Both will gain experience by using the techniques discussed in our course, and both will improve. Practice is fundamental. The more we try to use what we’ve learned, the more successful we’ll be. Failures along the way are only failures if we don’t learn from them.

section.title: Growing as a Writer and Storyteller
section.para: In , we discussed the idea of the Keats fallacy. Named after the British poet John Keats, the fallacy is the idea that being a good writer is an innate gift that some people are born with but others lack. Those who believe this fallacy see successful or prolific writers as the few who are lucky enough to be blessed with the gift. Everyone else can only read their work but never hope to produce something similar because they don’t have the gift.

section.title: The Keats Fallacy

figure.label: Figure 12.4
figure.title:
Good writing takes practice.
Tim Hester © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A piece of paper with a drawing of a lightbulb surrounded by crumpled paper.

section.para: Hopefully, it’s clear that the Keats fallacy is not only an erroneous belief but also a silly one. Writing well and telling interesting stories is like playing a sport or cooking. The more we do those things, the better we get at them. The more time we spend studying and practicing, the more we develop a natural sense of what works and what doesn’t. Every skill works like this. Of course, there are differences between people who have a natural talent and those who must work for it, but—especially in crowded fields like writing and storytelling—those differences will wash out over time and, in many cases, will not be the determining factor in whether an author’s work becomes successful.

Intelligent, dogged persistence will be far more important than talent in the long run. By “intelligent,” we mean a persistence that seeks out the best information about what it is trying to achieve and then creates a plan to put it into action. By “dogged,” we mean a persistence that drives us to show up every day and write out words onto a page, even when we know full well that what we’ve written isn’t very good.

section.title: Source of the Keats Fallacy
section.para: But where does the Keats fallacy come from? The source is the comparison we make between professional writers and ourselves as beginning writers. Observing professional authors from the outside, we see only the product—the end result—of all their hard work. We see nothing of the process or the hours per day they spend writing, to say nothing of the years of experience they’ve gained through the same dogged persistence we’ve recommended above. Because of that, we end up comparing their finished product to what we’re able to produce—which for many people is nothing so far—and of course, we don’t come out looking very good on that comparison. We see only their successes, failing to notice the decades of steady work and hundreds of failures it took them to get where they are now. And since writing good stories is so difficult, we explain their prolific success by ascribing to them some innate gift that they must simply have.

Seeing the source of the Keats fallacy should open our eyes to its falsity. It is simply not true that we cannot become good storytellers or published authors. We can. Do not be mistaken, though—it will take hard work, and we will have many failures. But they’re just stepping-stones along the way toward something much greater.

section.title: Growth Mindset

figure.label: Figure 12.5
figure.title:
Growth mindset.
Igor Zakharevich © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A bookshelf shaped like a head is full of books.

section.para: This way of thinking about our writing is part of having a growth mindsetThe belief that we can learn new things, change ourselves, and become successful at something that we might not be good at now. about our writing and storytelling abilities. A growth mindset is an attitude that we can learn new things, change ourselves, and become successful at something that we might not be very good at now. When we approach writing from a growth mindset, we try to learn what we can about technique, and then we try it out ourselves by putting it into practice. We seek new information about how to do things better, and we aren’t offended when others correct us. When we fail—as we inevitably will, especially at the beginning—we do not interpret our failure as a mark against our abilities or as evidence that we are not one of the “chosen ones” with an innate gift. Failures are just lessons we learn so that we don’t have to make the same mistakes in the future.

section.title: Fixed Mindset
section.para: The opposite of a growth mindset is a fixed mindsetThe belief that our abilities, intelligence, and talents are fixed and cannot change or develop. . According to a fixed mindset, the abilities you have now are fixed and cannot change. Your character and level of knowledge are fixed as well. Those with a fixed mindset fear the correction of others because they see it as a personal attack or condemnation. Because they believe they cannot change, they must take failure as the ultimate proof of their own inadequacy.Dweck, C. S. (2006). Mindset: The new psychology of success. Random House.

The growth mindset is the correct one to adopt about ourselves and our abilities. Not only is it the true mindset—we can change and improve, and who we are is not fixed—it is also the mindset that is much more likely to lead to success. For those who are very invested in a fixed mindset or who have built their identity on a certain reputation for knowledge, then the growth mindset can be difficult to accept. But in the end, it’s a no-brainer, especially when it comes to storytelling and writing. Each one of us can improve in these skills.

section.title: Improving Our Writing
section.para: The idea of beginning to improve may seem daunting. The challenge may get even worse when you think about trying to please audiences. Where is the starting point? The best place for us to begin is with any idea that’s interesting to you. As you’ve progressed through this course, you’ve probably had ideas for events, plotlines, characters, or other elements of stories. Perhaps you’ve even written them down. If those ideas spark something in you, then begin there. What’s interesting to you will be interesting to at least some other people. There is an audience for your story, no matter how small.

section.title: Writing Practices
section.para: We’ll close this section with a note on writing practices, or the habits and routines that authors use to write consistently. Every writer will need to develop writing practices in order to create a finished product. To learn more about your own writing practices, answer the following questions:

figure.label: Figure 12.6
figure.title:
Writing practices.
Roman Samborskyi © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A man and woman hold pencils to their chins while thinking.

listitem.para: How regularly do you write?
At what time of day do you write?
What software do you use to write?
What software do you use to organize your ideas?
When and how do you revise?
What are your short- and long-term goals for writing?

section.para: We could ask many other questions to elicit other aspects of writing practices, but these will do for now. If we’re just beginning, then we may not have the answers to any of these questions yet. That’s fine. But if we’re serious about growing in our writing, then we’ll probably want to have answers eventually.

One of the reasons we haven’t discussed these points much is simply that writing practices vary so much from author to author. The important thing is to figure out what works for you. Try many different approaches, pieces of software, and brainstorming techniques. What works for one successful author may not work for you, but something else will. The only way to know is to try different things and figure it out yourself.

In all of these efforts toward growth and improvement, keep in mind that the best thing you can ever do for your writing is to write. Learning techniques is important, and we’ve discussed many of the nuts and bolts of story creation in our course. Talking about writing is good, reading about writing is good, and theorizing about writing is good. But only writing is actually writing, and the only way to solve writing problems—including that pervasive problem of not having a completed draft—is to write.

section.title: Saving Ideas
section.para: As you’ve read through our topics and completed the assessments, you’ve probably had ideas for stories of your own. They might be individual scenes, characters, or snappy pieces of dialogue, or maybe a full-fledged narrative has dropped into your head. These ideas might also be refinements of something you’ve mulled over for a long time, or maybe they were completely new.

section.title: Keeping Ideas Around

figure.label: Figure 12.7
figure.title:
Keeping ideas around.
everythingpossible © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Lightbulbs that end in pencil points with paper balls in them. One paper ball is bright and yellow.

section.para: Now answer these questions: What did you do with those ideas when you had them? Did you write them down? Or did you entertain them only for a moment, then let them go? Do you remember them at all now?

Designing and writing stories—whether we intend them to be short stories, novels, scripts, plays, or anything else—is like building a house. In order to build a house, we must have a huge number of individual pieces that we then assemble into something house-shaped. But before we can assemble the pieces, we must design and build the pieces themselves.

section.title: Building a Story
section.para: The trouble is that we can’t always know how the piece we’re working on now will actually fit into the whole later on. Let’s say we’re designing a character for a story, for example, and we’re calling her Evie. We envision Evie to be a dark, sarcastic antihero. We write her backstory, flesh out her personality, and come up with ideas for some plots she’ll be involved in.

But as we’re building out this character, we’re also working on other aspects of our story. It’s entirely possible that, after designing more of the narrative, conflicts, and other characters, we conclude that Evie just no longer fits with the story. Her character may lose her spot to someone else, or that spot may be eliminated completely as the story goes in a direction we weren’t anticipating originally.

section.title: Becoming Comfortable with Uncertainty
section.para: A remarkable thing about writing stories is not just that we don’t know in advance how all the pieces will fit together; it’s that we don’t know in advance whether the pieces we are working on now will fit in at all. Evie might be completely wrong for what we’re writing now, but she might be completely right for some other story, including one that we haven’t even thought of yet.

To build the house of our story, we have to design many individual pieces that will combine into a narrative, characters, conflicts, and everything else. But we can’t always be sure that the pieces we are currently designing will go with the house we intend to build or whether they will go better with something else.

For this reason, the best thing to do with random story ideas is to save them. Scraps of paper, computer files, email, and audio recordings will all do the trick. Some of these methods are better than others. But some method of saving ideas is better than nothing.

section.title: Noticing Patterns

figure.label: Figure 12.8
figure.title:
We’ll begin to notice patterns.
Oleg Chumakov © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A magnifying glass, some pens, a pair of glasses, and a notebook.

section.para: As we save ideas for stories and review them regularly, we’ll begin to notice patterns. Certain ideas for characters and plots will naturally begin to associate themselves in our minds and in our notes, and those associations are the basis for new stories. Once a group of ideas becomes prominent enough, we can begin to develop that story in its own right rather than just add ideas to it as they come to us.
Whatever we write down and save, we can come back to. We should save all our ideas, if possible. We never know what they might be useful for.

Questions about how to organize story ideas after saving them go beyond the scope of this course, both because organizing ideas is a problem for writers more generally and because there are simply too many options to cover them adequately. There are many free and paid options available online, and the best way to proceed is to try out a few to see what works.

section.title: The Origin of Harry Potter
section.para: To illustrate some of the points we’ve made here, we’ll finish by reviewing the story of how J. K. Rowling developed the idea for the Harry Potter series. The first book in the series was published in 1997, but according to Rowling, she conceived the idea for the Harry Potter character in 1990. The idea just “fell into my head,” she later remembered,Newsweek. (2016, October 16). How J. K. Rowling created Harry Potter. https://www.newsweek.com/how-jk-rowling-created-harry-potter-510042. referring to the idea that gave rise to seven books that eventually sold more than 500 million copies.Scholastic. (n.d.). 20 facts about the Harry Potter book series. Mediaroom. http://mediaroom.scholastic.com/files/20-HARRY-POTTER-FACTS_SEPT2018.pdf

When Rowling got home that day in 1990, she wrote down her ideas and continued to develop them. But what happened in the next seven years? Life. Her mother passed away, Rowling was married and then divorced, and she moved several times in an attempt to escape poverty. Finally, she completed her first manuscript more than six years after having the original idea, showing the kind of intelligent, dogged persistence we’re advocating here.

Obviously, more went into designing the Harry Potter series than just saving her original ideas. Rowling spent countless hours refining and reworking her story and persevered through very difficult circumstances. But none of it would have been possible had she not taken herself seriously enough as a writer—long before she was successful—to save her ideas in a way that she could develop them later.

section.title: Feedback and Writing Groups
section.para: Developing and writing our stories will eventually bring us to the point where we have a completed manuscript or several chapters of one. At that time, it will be important to solicit feedback from others.

section.title: Blind Spots
section.para: When we are deeply involved in writing something important to us, we can become completely caught up in our new world and consumed by the characters and events of the story. This passion is a powerful driving force to create and finish a product, but it also has the somewhat harmful side effect of making us blind to the imperfections of our work. Our manuscript for a novel, for example, may feature annoying characters, unbelievable events, or coincidences just too good to be true. Or, much more simply, it may just be boring. Yet our connection to the story may make it impossible for us to see these things in our own work, even when they are immediately obvious to other people.

section.title: Getting Feedback from Others

figure.label: Figure 12.9
figure.title:
Getting feedback from others.
rawpixel © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Many people in a row holding signs in the shape of dialogue boxes.

section.para: This is the most important reason to solicit feedback from others: we need another pair of eyes on our writing to point out the things that we cannot see. It simply isn’t possible for us to notice all the shortcomings in our own writing. As we become better writers, we’ll get better at more quickly identifying things like overly long sentences or grammar mistakes. It’s the larger issues with our stories, which go completely unnoticed in our revision and self-editing, that we need others to point out for us.

section.title: An Example
section.para: I’ll share an example from my own work editing the stories of other people. I once read and commented on a draft of an interesting science-fiction novel that wasn’t an early manuscript but wasn’t near being finished either. The point of view in the story was third-person limited, focusing particularly on a young female lead character.

Remember that a third-person point of view means that the author uses “she” and “her” pronouns to describe the action as though the audience were observing the protagonist. A third-person limited point of view adds a restriction to the story, requiring the author to only provide information available to the point-of-view character at the time.

section.title: Hidden Snipers
section.para: In the story I was editing, the author had mostly done a good job of staying consistent with the limited point of view, but one particular passage violated the restriction on information available. Soldiers were to march the main character across a frozen lake with cliffs rising on either side, and the story noted that “snipers lay hidden in the bluffs above.” This is an interesting detail to add to a story and definitely increases the tension, but think about it from the perspective of points of view. This story was described from the third-person limited point of view—but if that’s true, and the snipers really were hidden, then how could the lead character have known about them? She couldn’t have noticed them during her march because then they wouldn’t have been “hidden,” so mentioning them at all violated the limited point of view.

For me, as a reader, the passage was a little jarring because the author had done such a good job with the point of view until that moment. The mention of “hidden snipers” broke my immersion in the story.

The remarkable thing about such a passage is that this author had probably read through that very paragraph at least five or six times without noticing the mistake. Focusing on building the world and increasing narrative tension, this author had failed to see that there was a logical mistake in her use of point of view.

section.title: Others’ Eyes on Our Work
section.para: The “hidden snipers” mistake is exactly the kind of thing that is so difficult for us to see in our own work, but these issues will pop out to any attentive reader who isn’t us. We cannot hope to identify all these mistakes and shortcomings in our writing without getting the help of other people.

The best way to get feedback from other people is just to ask them to read your story. Not everyone will agree, and not everyone will be the best reader, but more eyes on the page means a greater chance of catching weaknesses in narrative, character, and writing.

A good way to have others read our work is to form or join writing groups. A writing group is a group of people who share passages or chapters from their work with each other in order to give and receive feedback. Meetings can take many different forms, including live sharing of new material. Most often, one or more members of the group circulate their work beforehand so that the others can prepare comments and share their feedback at the meeting.

figure.label: Figure 12.10
figure.title:
Writing groups.
Wavebreak Media Ltd © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: Many people gathered in a circle holding notebooks and pencils.

section.para: Writing groups have many advantages, the most important being that they are groups whose purpose is to give feedback. They have built-in accountability mechanisms: one member receives feedback by giving feedback to others. In addition, members of writing groups are usually invested in learning and developing their own writing, so everyone can improve together. Writing groups also expose authors to genres outside of the ones they write in. That exposure offers new possibilities and techniques for their own work.
Many communities already have established writing groups or organizations. Such groups can offer opportunities to receive feedback and mentoring for new authors.

Receiving feedback on our writing can be scary. But the only way to improve is to understand where we are weak. With a growth mindset, feedback becomes an opportunity to learn something new and develop new skills. If we see ourselves as students of writing, then even harsh feedback is nothing to be scared of. The ability to write successfully is not an innate gift, and being told we produced something uninteresting does not mean we cannot succeed. Take the feedback, learn what to do differently, and move on.

section.title: Communicating through Stories Is Effective—And Fun
section.para: We noted in the introduction to our course that stories are a powerful way of communicating. In many cultures, stories shared through oral traditions are the only source of history and self-understanding that some people have. Until it was possible to use other mediums for storing information in reliable and widespread forms, stories were the way that people organized and remembered both individual and group experiences.

Oral traditions continue to exist in contemporary cultures, though in different forms. When we get together with old friends from high school or sit down with family for a Thanksgiving dinner, there’s a good chance we’ll end up swapping stories with everyone present. Some stories will be shared experiences we remember from years ago, and others will be things we experienced ourselves that our friends and family weren’t present for. In either case, we’re carrying on the oral tradition of storytelling, and the stories we tell play the same role in self-understanding and in community bonding.

section.title: The Power of Stories

figure.label: Figure 12.11
figure.title:
The power of stories.
Kirill Cherezov © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: An open book with light coming out of it.

section.para: More formal ways of contemporary storytelling, such as writing a novel or producing a movie, tap into the power of stories. Most of the time, we don’t know the authors of the books we read or the producers of the movies we watch, but their stories can still matter to us in the same way. Based on the material we’ve discussed in this and other topics, consider ways that you could use stories to frame the messages and communications you share with others. For most people, this won’t mean that they start writing a novel or join an online group for people writing their first screenplay. What it means is to consider ways that you could use narrative, character, conflicts, hooks, stakes, and other parts of stories to enhance the communications you already have to send. Let’s look at two examples of how to use these storytelling elements in a professional setting.

section.title: Using the Story Frame: Narrative
section.para: The first is a cover letter for a job. Applications for many professional positions require a cover letter in which candidates express their interest in the position and describe some of their qualifications. There are many ways to compose such a document, but why not frame the letter as a story? We can write about ourselves in a way that charts a narrative course from past education and other accomplishments to where we are today, with a future involving the position we’re applying for.

Framing a cover letter as a story isn’t risk-free; some hiring managers or search committees may feel it’s too informal or otherwise not appropriate for their workplace. We usually won’t have access to enough information about our audience to know whether a story frame for a cover letter is the right one. But corresponding to that risk is a high reward, which is that a cover letter written this way will stand out strongly among a batch of uniformly safe and boring descriptions of past job experiences. When most of the candidates in a stack of applications are qualified for the job, getting a foot in the door for an interview may require something more than just sending a résumé.

section.title: Using the Story Frame: Hook
section.para: The second storytelling element that we can easily adapt for many purposes is the hook. In our previous example, the simple fact of writing a cover letter through a story frame may be a hook in itself, but we can use hooks in many other ways too.

If we have to give a presentation to our team or a group of managers, for example, why not start out with a bang? We could begin with the most important information, a funny joke, a video, or anything else to get people listening. Anyone who has sat through boring presentations and talks from coworkers knows that any kind of spark at the beginning of someone’s remarks is a lifeline. An interesting hook will breathe life into our words, and if we can follow it up with a compelling story of our work, then we’ll have given people something to remember.

section.title: Frame Matters

figure.label: Figure 12.12
figure.title:
Frame matters.
stuartburf © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A black picture frame that is empty.

section.para: In many cases, the important part of the messages we send is not the content but the frame. Why be boring when we can use what we’ve learned about stories to be interesting?

Stories have another added benefit, which is that they make the communication more fun for us as authors. Writing stories is fun! Designing worlds, characters, conflicts, and hooks is an enjoyable thing to do. We usually think of stories as fun for the audience experiencing them, but they’re fun for creators as well.

Many working adults do not have opportunities to be creative. Stories are a creative outlet, and even using elements of stories without designing an entire world is a way of injecting personality and heart into professional responsibilities.

We’re not saying that using ideas of narrative or conflict in a presentation is going to turn a boring job into something great. But stories are interesting and fun regardless of where we encounter them, and we can use their power to connect with others in any role we occupy.

section.title: Summary

figure.label: Figure 12.13
figure.title:
Putting the pieces of a story together.
Jozef Polc © 123RF.com

imagedata.alt: A desk with myriad office supplies.

section.para: Putting the pieces of stories together into a coherent whole is a difficult process. Although designing a narrative, characters, and other parts of stories is fun, it’s also hard work. We should be patient with our failures, but we should also remember that we will grow and get better. Good writing is like any other skill—it improves with effort.

Most of all, we want to have a growth mindset toward our ability to tell a good story. We can grow and improve, and others have useful things to teach us. The opposite of a growth mindset is a fixed mindset, where we believe our skills are static, and any failure is an indictment of our value. Fixed mindsets are both incorrect and harmful, especially when it comes to writing and storytelling.

In the end, stories draw on a deep human need to impose order on our experience. We understand ourselves, our past and future, and our relation to others by means of stories. We can learn to use stories for many purposes and in many diverse settings.
